sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A self join reads the same table under different aliases. Each alias plays a different role, allowing one row to be matched with another row from the same table.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Employees and managers have the same stored fields, so one employees table can describe both. A self join turns the stored manager reference into a readable manager name.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Treat employees e as the employee and employees m as the manager. Match e.manager_id to m.id. A LEFT JOIN preserves employees whose manager reference is NULL.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Give each copy its own alias: employees e is the employee and employees m the manager. Match m.id = e.manager_id. For unordered coworker pairs, a.id < b.id removes self-pairs and the reversed copy of each pair. Add the same-department or same-manager condition with AND. Ordinary equality does not match two NULL manager references.
sections.code: SELECT e.id, e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id ORDER BY e.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
A self join looks up one employee’s manager in the same employee table.

Each non-NULL manager_id refers to another row in employees. The aliases e and m give the table two roles in the query.

id | name | manager_id
— | — | —
1 | Morgan | NULL
2 | Noor | 1
3 | Owen | 2
4 | Pia | 1

```sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.id IN (2, 3, 4) ORDER BY e.id;
```

**Result**

employee | manager
— | —
Noor | Morgan
Owen | Noor
Pia | Morgan

Noor is an employee in one pair and a manager in another. The table is not copied or changed: the query reads its rows in two roles.
sections.code: SELECT e.id, e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id ORDER BY e.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: For employee pairs in a department, e1.id < e2.id excludes a person paired with themself and avoids listing both (A,B) and (B,A). Equality on department limits pairs to colleagues.
sections.code: SELECT e1.id AS first_id, e2.id AS second_id FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.department = e2.department AND e1.id < e2.id ORDER BY first_id, second_id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The table below is the result of the query in Read the syntax. All six Retail employees appear. Morgan's NULL manager reflects a missing relationship, not an employee named NULL.

id | employee | manager
— | — | —
1 | Morgan | NULL
2 | Noor | Morgan
3 | Owen | Noor
4 | Pia | Morgan
5 | Quinn | Pia
6 | Rae | Noor

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: The aliases refer to the same stored table, not separate copies. Unqualified id or name is ambiguous. A foreign key can require a manager to exist without preventing every possible cycle in the hierarchy.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A self join follows a fixed number of links. Recursive CTEs, taught later, can follow an unknown number of levels; pair joins need a deliberate rule for whether direction and duplicates matter.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Label each alias's role before joining. Check a top-level employee, a subordinate, and colleague pairs, and explain why a pair should appear once or twice.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use distinct aliases for distinct roles in one table. Join the correct link, preserve missing relationships when required, and control self-pairs and mirrored pairs explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A join's cardinality is the number of matching result rows. Joining one order to several order lines repeats that order's columns once for each line. This repetition is expected, but it changes how totals must be calculated.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: An order total and a line total describe different units. A report can look plausible while counting the same order amount several times after a one-to-many join.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: First state what one result row represents: an order, an order line, or a customer. Connect each relationship by its keys. If a later join multiplies existing summaries, aggregate the many-side data before joining it.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Join orders to customers by customer_id, to order_items by order_id, and to products by product_id. quantity * unit_price is a line amount. An order with two lines appears twice after joining, so COUNT(*) counts two lines and COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) one order. SUM(o.total) there would add the order total twice. For product or category sales, sum the line quantities or line amounts and group by the requested keys.
sections.code: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, i.quantity, i.quantity * i.unit_price AS line_total FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id ORDER BY o.id, p.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
When an order has two items, a four-table join returns two item rows.

Order 101 belongs to Ada and has total 29.00. Its item rows point to Notebook and Pen through product_id.

order_id | product_id | quantity | unit_price
— | — | — | —
101 | 1 | 2 | 12.50
101 | 2 | 2 | 2.00

```sql
SELECT c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, i.quantity, i.quantity * i.unit_price AS line_total FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id WHERE o.id = 101 ORDER BY p.id;
```

**Result**

customer | product | quantity | line_total
— | — | — | —
Ada | Notebook | 2 | 25.00
Ada | Pen | 2 | 4.00

The line amounts are 25.00 and 4.00, which add to 29.00. Summing the repeated order total after this join would incorrectly give 58.00.
sections.code: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, i.quantity, i.quantity * i.unit_price AS line_total FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id ORDER BY o.id, p.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The customer summary uses count(DISTINCT o.id) for orders and count(*) for lines. After joining order_items, an order with several lines must contribute once to order_count but several times to line_count.
sections.code: SELECT o.customer_id, count(DISTINCT o.id) AS order_count, count(*) AS line_count FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.customer_id;

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: SUM(o.total) after joining order lines repeats an order total per line. SUM(DISTINCT o.total) is also unsafe: different orders can have identical totals. Fix the level of aggregation, not just visible duplicates.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: JOIN combines related rows, GROUP BY changes the summary level, and EXISTS tests membership without multiplying outer rows. Choose the pattern that matches the intended unit of your report.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Write the unit of each metric beside its formula. Check an order with multiple lines and two orders with equal totals; both cases expose common overcounting mistakes.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Follow the keys and track what one row means after every join. Aggregate at the correct level so repeated detail rows do not inflate higher-level measures.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: EXISTS is true when its subquery returns at least one row. NOT EXISTS is true when it returns none. Both produce a definite true or false result, not an unknown result.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Questions such as 'has any order?' need one answer per customer, even when that customer has many orders. An existence test avoids multiplying output rows just to check a relationship.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A correlated subquery refers to an outer query alias. Its condition defines which rows count as matches. SELECT 1 conventionally signals that only row existence matters; NULL values in those rows do not make EXISTS unknown.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: For each customers c row, EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) asks whether at least one matching order exists. NOT EXISTS asks whether none exists, including customers with no orders at all. Add a status condition inside to ask about paid or pending orders specifically. The inner query may also join order lines to orders using the same join rules already learned.
sections.code: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
To find customers without orders, test whether a matching order exists.

Ada (ID 1) has orders 101, 103 and 108; Fara (ID 6) has none. Check those two customers.

```sql
SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE c.id IN (1, 6) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;
```

**Result**

name
—
Fara

For Ada, the inner query finds a row, so NOT EXISTS is false. For Fara it finds none, so NOT EXISTS is true. Several matches would still produce only one yes-or-no decision per customer.
sections.code: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The product example uses NOT EXISTS with order_items joined to paid orders. A product qualifies only if no paid order contains it; appearing solely in cancelled orders does not disqualify it.
sections.code: SELECT p.id, p.name FROM products p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.id = i.order_id WHERE i.product_id = p.id AND o.status = 'paid') ORDER BY p.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The table below is the result of the query in Read the syntax. Five Retail customers have at least one order. Each is returned once because the query selects customer rows, not matching order pairs.

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada
2 | Ben
3 | Cleo
4 | Davi
5 | Eli

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Forgetting the correlation can make EXISTS depend on any order anywhere rather than that customer's orders. Nullable NOT IN results differ from NOT EXISTS; the predicates are not interchangeable without checking NULL behavior.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: EXISTS expresses a matching requirement, sometimes called a semi-join; NOT EXISTS expresses an absence requirement, or anti-join. These names describe row-selection behavior rather than extra SQL keywords you need to write here.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test zero, one, and several matching rows. Add a nonqualifying related row, such as a cancelled order, and check that the business condition remains inside the subquery.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use EXISTS for at least one qualifying match and NOT EXISTS for none. Make the correlation and the qualifying conditions explicit.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A scalar subquery supplies one value inside another expression. It must return one column and no more than one row. Zero rows give NULL; multiple rows cause an error.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A query often needs a calculated benchmark, such as the average price of all products. A subquery calculates that benchmark from current data rather than hardcoding a number.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Put the inner SELECT in parentheses where a value is expected. An aggregate without grouping usually supplies one summary row; its value may still be NULL if there are no qualifying inputs.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The inner SELECT avg(price) FROM products returns one value that the outer WHERE uses as a benchmark. A comparison with max or min also keeps every tied row. A scalar subquery can appear in a calculation: stock::numeric / NULLIF((SELECT sum(stock) FROM products), 0). The cast keeps fractions, NULLIF handles a zero total, and round(..., 4) rounds to four decimal places.
sections.code: SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products) ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
A scalar subquery supplies one benchmark value to a comparison.

The eight product prices are 12.50, 2.00, 75.00, 250.00, 15.00, 45.00, 8.00 and 4.00. Their total is 411.50 and their average is 51.4375.

```sql
SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | name | price
— | — | —
3 | Keyboard | 75.00
4 | Monitor | 250.00

The inner AVG returns one value. The outer WHERE compares every product with that same value; only Keyboard and Monitor cost more.
sections.code: SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products) ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The stock-share example divides each product's stock by a scalar sum of all stock. Casting stock to numeric preserves fractions; NULLIF(..., 0) leaves the share unknown when the total is zero.
sections.code: SELECT id, round(stock::numeric / NULLIF((SELECT sum(stock) FROM products),0),4) AS stock_share FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The table below is the result of the query in Read the syntax. Keyboard and Monitor are above the Retail average. The average itself is used for comparison and is not an extra displayed output column.

id | name | price
— | — | —
3 | Keyboard | 75.00
4 | Monitor | 250.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A filter returning one row today may return several tomorrow. Use a key or an appropriate aggregate when one row is required; adding LIMIT 1 without a meaningful rule can hide ambiguity.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A scalar subquery produces a value. A subquery in FROM produces a table, while EXISTS checks row presence. Choose the form matching what the surrounding query needs.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Identify the inner query's row and column counts before embedding it. Check no qualifying rows, a NULL aggregate result, and an unexpectedly duplicated lookup key.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A scalar subquery must provide at most one row and exactly one column. Account for NULL when no value is available, and make uniqueness intentional.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A correlated subquery uses a value from an outer query row. Its question therefore depends on that row, such as 'what is the average price in this product's category?'

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Comparing every product with the overall average may hide category differences. A correlated calculation supplies a benchmark for the group to which each product belongs.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Give inner and outer sources different aliases. A reference to the outer alias links the inner condition to the current outer row. This describes the query's meaning; the execution plan determines whether work is repeated or transformed.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: products p is the current outer product. Inside, p2.category = p.category restricts the average to that product's category. The same pattern can match a department or customer. A correlated count can also be an output column: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS order_count. COUNT returns 0 when that customer has no matching orders.
sections.code: SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price FROM products p WHERE p.price > (SELECT avg(p2.price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category) ORDER BY p.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
A correlated subquery can choose a different benchmark for each outer row.

Office prices are 12.50, 2.00 and 4.00; Tech prices are 75.00, 250.00 and 8.00; Home prices are 15.00 and 45.00.

```sql
SELECT p.name, p.category, p.price FROM products p WHERE p.price > (SELECT avg(p2.price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category) ORDER BY p.id;
```

**Result**

name | category | price
— | — | —
Notebook | Office | 12.50
Monitor | Tech | 250.00
Lamp | Home | 45.00

The condition p2.category = p.category restricts each average to the current product’s category. Notebook exceeds the Office average, Monitor exceeds 111.00 for Tech, and Lamp exceeds 30.00 for Home.
sections.code: SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price FROM products p WHERE p.price > (SELECT avg(p2.price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category) ORDER BY p.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The customer example counts orders whose customer_id matches each outer customer ID. COUNT returns zero when no order matches, so customers without orders remain in the output.
sections.code: SELECT c.id, (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS order_count FROM customers c ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The table below is the result of the query in Read the syntax. Notebook, Monitor, and Lamp exceed their own category averages in Retail. This differs from comparing all products with one overall average.

id | name | price
— | — | —
1 | Notebook | 12.50
4 | Monitor | 250.00
6 | Lamp | 45.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Omitting p2.category = p.category turns the benchmark into an overall average. Reusing aliases or leaving ambiguous references unqualified can accidentally change which source a column belongs to.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Correlation concerns dependency, not a particular execution speed. Joins or grouped summaries can express related calculations; compare plans and results before assuming one form is faster.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Write the outer row's question in words. Then point to the exact inner condition using its value, and test rows from different groups and rows with no related records.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A correlated subquery answers a row-specific question through an explicit outer reference. Clear aliases and a complete correlation condition protect its meaning.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A derived table is a query used as a source in FROM. LATERAL allows such a query to refer to sources on its left, making a related table result for each outer row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Separate query layers make a summary of summaries possible. LATERAL also expresses questions such as the two most expensive products in each category without mixing their limits together.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A FROM subquery can return many rows and columns; an alias names its output for the outer query. Unlike an ordinary independent subquery, a LATERAL subquery may use a preceding source's values.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: A query in parentheses after FROM makes a derived table. Give it an alias and use its output columns in the outer SELECT, for example averaging previously counted orders. A LATERAL query may read a preceding alias. Put ORDER BY and LIMIT inside it to choose the first, latest, or top two rows separately for each customer or category. LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) latest ON true keeps an outer row even when there is no result. CROSS JOIN LATERAL (...) keeps only outer rows with a result.
sections.code: SELECT round(avg(order_count),2) AS average_orders FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id) counts;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
LATERAL lets a FROM subquery read the customer selected to its left.

Ada has orders 101 on May 1, 103 on May 10 and 108 on June 10, 2024. Fara has no orders. We need each customer’s latest order while keeping both customers.

```sql
SELECT c.name AS customer, latest.id AS order_id, latest.ordered_on FROM customers c LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT o.id, o.ordered_on FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY o.ordered_on DESC, o.id DESC LIMIT 1) latest ON true WHERE c.id IN (1, 6) ORDER BY c.id;
```

**Result**

customer | order_id | ordered_on
— | — | —
Ada | 108 | 2024-06-10
Fara | NULL | NULL

ORDER BY and LIMIT run inside the per-customer lookup, so Ada contributes order 108. LEFT JOIN keeps Fara when the subquery returns no rows. The second sort key makes equal dates deterministic.
sections.code: SELECT round(avg(order_count),2) AS average_orders FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id) counts;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The LATERAL example starts from distinct categories. For each category it sorts matching products by price descending, then ID, and takes at most two. The final ORDER BY arranges the combined output.
sections.code: SELECT c.category, p.id, p.price FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) c CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT id, price FROM products p WHERE p.category = c.category ORDER BY price DESC, id LIMIT 2) p ORDER BY c.category, p.price DESC, p.id;

average_orders
—

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops an outer row if the inner query returns no rows. LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true preserves it with NULLs. Sorting inside a subquery does not establish the final output order.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A scalar subquery returns a single value; a derived table supplies rows and columns. LATERAL makes a table-producing subquery dependent on an earlier source, like correlation with a table-shaped result.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check who belongs to the inner summary before averaging it. For top-N queries, verify that LIMIT applies separately per category and that equal prices have a tie-breaker.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use a derived table to separate calculation stages. Use LATERAL for a related row set per outer row, choosing CROSS or LEFT behavior when matches are absent.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A common table expression, or CTE, gives a query result a name for use within one statement. WITH introduces these named stages before the main query.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Breaking a long calculation into named stages helps a reader follow where rows are filtered, grouped, and compared. The names describe the calculation rather than creating permanent tables.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Write WITH name AS (query), then use name as a source. Multiple CTEs are comma-separated and may read earlier CTEs. Their names last only for the current statement.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: WITH paid AS (...) defines a stage keeping paid order IDs and totals. The final SELECT reads paid, filters totals above 50, and sorts by ID. The inner and outer filters serve separate readable stages. If a CTE calculates sum(total) AS spend, its outer query can filter the spend column. A later stage can read the same CTE again, for example to calculate an average for comparison.
sections.code: WITH paid AS (SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid') SELECT id, total FROM paid WHERE total > 50 ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
A CTE names an intermediate result so the next step reads naturally.

Orders include paid order 102 for 75.00, paid order 103 for 250.00 and pending order 109 for 250.00. The CTE reads all orders and keeps only paid ones.

```sql
WITH paid AS (SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid') SELECT id, total FROM paid WHERE total > 100 ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | total
— | —
103 | 250.00

The outer query keeps amounts above 100 from paid. Order 103 is the only match: order 102 is too small and 109 never entered paid. paid is a query-local name, not a saved table.
sections.code: WITH paid AS (SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid') SELECT id, total FROM paid WHERE total > 50 ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: category_sales groups revenue from paid order lines by category. The final query compares each category's revenue with the mean of those category totals, reusing the named calculation.
sections.code: WITH category_sales AS (SELECT p.category, sum(i.quantity*i.unit_price) AS revenue FROM products p JOIN order_items i ON i.product_id=p.id JOIN orders o ON o.id=i.order_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY p.category) SELECT category, revenue FROM category_sales WHERE revenue > (SELECT avg(revenue) FROM category_sales) ORDER BY category;

sections.body:
The table below is the result of the query in Read the syntax. Four Retail paid orders have totals above 50: IDs 102, 103, 105, and 111. The CTE name does not add another output column or result table.

id | total
— | —
102 | 75.00
103 | 250.00
105 | 90.00
111 | 75.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A CTE name exists for one statement and does not create a stored table. An aggregate alias such as spend becomes a column of that CTE, so the outer WHERE may filter it. Specify the final ORDER BY explicitly.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A derived table gives a query layer an inline position; a CTE gives it a name before the main query. Neither automatically persists data. Recursive and data-changing CTEs have additional rules taught separately.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Name each stage by what it represents. Trace its columns and row filters, then verify that a later comparison uses totals at the intended level rather than raw rows.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use WITH to make query stages clear and reusable within one statement. Treat materialization as a planning choice, not an automatic property of every CTE.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: UNION stacks compatible query results and removes duplicate whole rows. UNION ALL also stacks results, but keeps every input row, including duplicates.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Data from separate sources can share one report format. Choosing ALL preserves repeated transactions that happen to have the same displayed values.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Both branches need the same number of columns with compatible types in corresponding positions. Columns match by position, not by name; output headings normally come from the first branch. Only a final ORDER BY guarantees combined ordering.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: SELECT city AS place ... UNION SELECT warehouse ... puts values into one output column and removes repeats. UNION ALL keeps every row from both branches. A quoted value such as 'order' AS source can label a branch. In the activity task, (check_out - check_in) * nightly_rate uses the earlier booking-charge calculation. Add one final ORDER BY after the branches to arrange their combined output.
sections.code: SELECT city AS place FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL UNION SELECT warehouse FROM inventory ORDER BY place;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
UNION combines two compatible columns and removes repeated values.

Known customer cities are London, Paris, London, Berlin and Paris. Inventory warehouse values repeat North and South across products.

```sql
SELECT city AS place FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL UNION SELECT warehouse FROM inventory ORDER BY place;
```

**Result**

place
—

sections.body: UNION is not a join: it adds rows rather than attaching columns. Dropping ALL can silently discard valid repeated transactions. NULLs count as equal for duplicate removal; UNION ALL preserves them as separate rows.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Use JOIN for related columns on the same row and UNION for similarly shaped rows from different queries. Branch-specific ORDER BY or LIMIT needs parentheses when combined with a set operation.

sections.title: Recap

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: INTERSECT returns rows found in both query results. EXCEPT returns rows found in the first result but absent from the second. By default, both remove duplicate whole rows.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: These operations express overlap and difference directly: customers with two kinds of orders, or products that appear in lines but never in paid orders.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types in corresponding positions. Plain INTERSECT and EXCEPT remove duplicates. INTERSECT keeps values present in both results, and EXCEPT keeps values from the first result that are absent from the second. For set comparison, NULL values match each other, so filter unknown IDs when the task excludes them.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The two branches select non-NULL customer IDs from paid and pending orders. INTERSECT keeps IDs present in both. ORDER BY customer_id sorts the final overlap.
sections.code: SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status='paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status='pending' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
INTERSECT finds values that occur in both query results.

Among known customers, paid orders belong to IDs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Pending orders belong to IDs 2 and 4. Some IDs occur on several orders.

```sql
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY customer_id;
```

**Result**

customer_id
—
2
4

Only 2 and 4 occur in both sets. Plain INTERSECT returns each matching ID once, even if either input contains duplicates.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: EXCEPT is directional: reversing its branches changes the question. NULLs count as equal for set comparisons. INTERSECT binds more tightly than UNION or EXCEPT; parentheses make a mixed expression's meaning explicit.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: NOT EXISTS can express related absence questions while retaining other outer columns. A nullable NOT IN has different NULL behavior, so it is not a direct substitute for set difference.

sections.title: Practice deliberately

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: INTERSECT finds common rows; EXCEPT finds a directional difference. Choose duplicate handling and parentheses deliberately, and sort the final result when order matters.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: INSERT adds new rows to a table. RETURNING produces a result from the rows actually inserted, making their stored values available immediately to the caller.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: An application needs to know what was saved, including generated identifiers and defaults. RETURNING avoids guessing those values or issuing an unrelated lookup afterward.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: List INSERT's target columns and put matching VALUES in the same order. Missing columns use a default or NULL, subject to constraints. INSERT INTO target(columns) SELECT ... copies query rows into that target. To create the target first, write CREATE TABLE name(column type, ...). Here integer holds whole numbers, text holds strings, PRIMARY KEY requires a unique non-NULL key, and NOT NULL makes a value required. numeric(10,2) stores amounts to two decimal places. In customers, vip defaults to false, so omitting it creates a non-VIP customer.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) names five target columns. VALUES (50,'Ruler','Office',3.50,15) supplies their values. RETURNING chooses fields from the saved row. For dates use DATE '2024-08-01'. An existing timestamp column accepts a quoted value such as '2024-08-01 12:00'. A JSONB column accepts a JSON object inside a SQL text literal, for example '{"device":"tablet","pages":2}'. JSON keys and text values use double quotes inside the single SQL quotes. A statement without a column list uses table-definition order, so an explicit list is safer.
sections.code: INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES (50,'Ruler','Office',3.50,15) RETURNING id,name,price,stock;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
An explicit column list makes an insertion easy to check. RETURNING shows the inserted row.

The practice products table contains IDs 1 through 8. ID 60 is unused. Add a stapler with a price of 8.50 and 10 units in stock.

```sql
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, stock) VALUES (60, 'Stapler', 'Office', 8.50, 10) RETURNING id, name, price, stock;
```

**Result**

id | name | price | stock
— | — | — | —
60 | Stapler | 8.50 | 10

The five VALUES entries match the five named columns by position. RETURNING displays only the new row and the requested columns; it does not list the older products.
sections.code: INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES (50,'Ruler','Office',3.50,15) RETURNING id,name,price,stock;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The archive example creates paid_archive with an order primary key, then copies paid order IDs and totals using INSERT ... SELECT. It copies values, not a live link to the orders table.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE paid_archive(order_id integer PRIMARY KEY,total numeric(10,2)); INSERT INTO paid_archive SELECT id,total FROM orders WHERE status='paid';

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Mismatched column/value positions can put data in the wrong place or raise a type error. Duplicate keys and other constraint violations fail unless specifically handled. A successful preview does not make exercise changes permanent outside its isolated run.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: INSERT changes rows; SELECT normally reads them. RETURNING turns changed rows into output. Upserts later add conflict-handling rules, while transactions determine whether a group of changes is committed together.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check both the returned row and the resulting table state. Confirm omitted-column defaults and constraint behavior, and remember that each practice execution starts from its controlled dataset.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: List INSERT columns explicitly, match values by position, and use RETURNING for saved values. Verify actual table changes separately from command output.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: UPDATE changes values in existing rows. It keeps the rows and changes only the columns listed in SET.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Use it to adjust stock, correct a price, or move an order to its next status.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: WHERE chooses the rows to change. SET lists only the columns receiving new values, so other columns keep their values. A formula such as stock=stock+2 reads the old stock and writes the calculated result.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: UPDATE products SET stock=10 WHERE stock=0 changes only out-of-stock products. For values from another table, use UPDATE products AS p SET stock=i.quantity+2 FROM inventory AS i WHERE i.product_id=p.id. FROM supplies the source, and WHERE pairs each source row with its target. round(price*1.10,2) raises a price by 10 percent and keeps two decimal places.
sections.code: UPDATE products SET stock=10 WHERE stock=0;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Compare a product that needs restocking with one whose stock should stay unchanged.

In products, Notebook (id 1) has stock 40 and Mug (id 5) has stock 0. Apply UPDATE products SET stock=10 WHERE stock=0 before reading these rows.

```sql
UPDATE products SET stock=10 WHERE stock=0;
SELECT id,name,stock FROM products WHERE id IN (1,5) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | name | stock
— | — | —
1 | Notebook | 40
5 | Mug | 10

Mug changes to 10. Notebook stays at 40 because its old stock did not satisfy WHERE.
sections.code: UPDATE products SET stock=10 WHERE stock=0;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: UPDATE ... FROM matches each product to inventory by product_id, then uses quantity+2 as the new stock. The source must supply at most one matching row per product.
sections.code: UPDATE products p SET stock=i.quantity+2 FROM inventory i WHERE i.product_id=p.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, this separate check reads all product stocks after UPDATE: product 5 is now 10 and the others are unchanged. UPDATE itself does not return this table.

id | stock
— | —
1 | 40
2 | 120
3 | 12
4 | 5
5 | 10
6 | 8
7 | 50
8 | 20

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Without WHERE, UPDATE changes every row. With multiple source matches in UPDATE ... FROM, the chosen source row is unpredictable. First inspect the intended rows with SELECT.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: JOIN explains how source rows match. Constraints still apply during UPDATE, and a transaction lets several related changes succeed together.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check both changed and unchanged products. Confirm that a second source match cannot accidentally choose a different quantity.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose rows carefully, calculate new values, then verify the resulting data.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: DELETE removes rows from a table. A foreign key can prevent deletion of a row that other rows still reference.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Removing old or unwanted data must leave relationships between the remaining rows valid.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DELETE FROM names the target table and WHERE selects rows to remove. A NOT EXISTS subquery can keep rows that still have a related record. TRUNCATE events removes every event while keeping the table definition. It has no WHERE clause.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: When deletion depends on another table, write DELETE FROM order_items AS i USING orders AS o WHERE o.id=i.order_id AND o.status='cancelled'. Only order_items is the deletion target. For text matching, body !~* 'SQL' means the case-insensitive regular expression does not match. Combine date and kind conditions with AND to remove only the intended events.
sections.code: DELETE FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Delete only early visit events, then read the surviving rows.

Among events 1–4, events 1 and 3 are visits on July 1, event 2 is a purchase on July 1, and event 4 is a visit on July 2. Delete visits before July 2.

```sql
DELETE FROM events WHERE kind='visit' AND occurred_at<TIMESTAMP '2024-07-02';
SELECT id,kind FROM events WHERE id<=4 ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | kind
— | —
2 | purchase
4 | visit

The purchase remains, as does the visit exactly on the boundary date. Both parts of the deletion condition must be true.
sections.code: DELETE FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: TRUNCATE events removes every event but preserves the table definition. It does not run row-level DELETE triggers; it can run TRUNCATE triggers.
sections.code: TRUNCATE events;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, this separate check lists the five customers left after deleting customers without orders. It is not direct DELETE output.

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada
2 | Ben
3 | Cleo
4 | Davi
5 | Eli

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Omitting WHERE deletes all rows. Referencing rows may block DELETE unless a foreign-key action allows it. PostgreSQL can roll back TRUNCATE, but it takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Unlike DELETE, it can make a table appear empty to a concurrent transaction using an older snapshot.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: NOT EXISTS expresses an absence test. Foreign-key actions such as CASCADE or SET NULL define what happens to dependent rows.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Before deleting, run the same condition with SELECT. Check that customers with orders remain and that the resulting relationships are valid.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: DELETE chooses rows to remove; TRUNCATE empties tables. Understand dependencies before either operation.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An upsert tries to insert a row and handles a specified uniqueness conflict instead of simply failing.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: It helps imports and synchronisation jobs decide what to do when an identifier already exists.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: An INSERT may meet an existing PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE value. ON CONFLICT(key) chooses that conflict. DO NOTHING keeps the existing row. DO UPDATE SET changes only the listed columns of that row. Other errors still fail.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: EXCLUDED holds the proposed insert values. In SET quantity=inventory.quantity+EXCLUDED.quantity, inventory.quantity is the stored quantity and EXCLUDED.quantity is the incoming amount. Assign EXCLUDED.quantity alone to replace rather than add. Multiple parenthesized VALUES groups propose several rows. Columns omitted from INSERT use their defaults, or NULL when permitted.
sections.code: INSERT INTO inventory VALUES (1,'Central',60,DATE '2024-08-01') ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET warehouse=EXCLUDED.warehouse,quantity=EXCLUDED.quantity,updated_on=EXCLUDED.updated_on;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Use an incoming inventory quantity as an addition, while preserving the stored warehouse.

Inventory row 1 has warehouse North and quantity 40. An incoming row proposes Central and quantity 5. The conflict action adds quantity only.

```sql
INSERT INTO inventory VALUES(1,'Central',5,DATE '2024-08-01') ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET quantity=inventory.quantity+EXCLUDED.quantity;
SELECT product_id,warehouse,quantity FROM inventory WHERE product_id IN (1,2) ORDER BY product_id;
```

**Result**

product_id | warehouse | quantity
— | — | —
1 | North | 45
2 | North | 120

The quantity becomes 45, but the warehouse remains North because warehouse was not assigned in DO UPDATE. Row 2 is untouched.
sections.code: INSERT INTO inventory VALUES (1,'Central',60,DATE '2024-08-01') ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET warehouse=EXCLUDED.warehouse,quantity=EXCLUDED.quantity,updated_on=EXCLUDED.updated_on;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The second example adds EXCLUDED.quantity to the existing quantity. It changes the date but deliberately keeps the existing warehouse.
sections.code: INSERT INTO inventory VALUES(2,'North',5,DATE '2024-08-01') ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET quantity=inventory.quantity+EXCLUDED.quantity,updated_on=EXCLUDED.updated_on;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
In the original syntax example, the incoming values replace product 1’s inventory row: Central, quantity 60, date 2024-08-01. This check reads the stored result; the other inventory rows are unchanged.

product_id | warehouse | quantity | updated_on
— | — | — | —
1 | Central | 60 | 2024-08-01
2 | North | 120 | 2024-07-01
3 | South | 12 | 2024-07-02
4 | South | 5 | 2024-07-02

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: DO UPDATE needs a suitable non-deferrable unique key or index; exclusion constraints cannot be its conflict target. Other errors still fail. Repeating an additive upsert adds again, so not every upsert is safe to retry unchanged.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A primary key is a common conflict target. Compare replacement with accumulation: both use upsert, but their business meaning differs.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test the existing-key and missing-key cases. Read each assignment and decide whether it replaces, preserves, or adds to a value.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose the conflict key and merge rule explicitly; EXCLUDED contains the attempted insert.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A transaction groups changes into one unit: commit all of them or discard them. A savepoint marks a place inside that unit to return to.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A bank transfer must not debit one account without crediting the other.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BEGIN opens a transaction. COMMIT keeps all its changes, while ROLLBACK discards them. The account updates in a transfer belong to one transaction so they succeed or fail together.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: SAVEPOINT name records an intermediate point. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name cancels changes made after it and keeps the transaction open. For example, add 10, set a savepoint, add 100, roll back to the savepoint, then commit: only the first 10 remains. A PL/pgSQL block is introduced later and has a different use of BEGIN.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Transfer a small amount between two accounts as one transaction.

Accounts 1 and 2 start at 1000.00 and 500.00. Transfer 20 by subtracting it from account 1 and adding it to account 2 inside BEGIN and COMMIT.

```sql
BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-20 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+20 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;
SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN (1,2) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | balance
— | —
1 | 980.00
2 | 520.00

The two balances change together and their combined total remains 1500.00. Replacing COMMIT with ROLLBACK would preserve both starting balances.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The savepoint follows the first addition of 10. Rolling back to it cancels only the later addition of 100, so committing preserves the first addition.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+10 WHERE id=1; SAVEPOINT before_extra; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=1; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_extra; COMMIT;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example transfers 100 between accounts 1 and 2. This check reads balances 900 and 600 after COMMIT; the UPDATE commands do not directly return these rows.

id | balance
— | —
1 | 900.00
2 | 600.00
3 | 750.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: After a statement error, the transaction normally refuses further work until rollback. Rolling back to a suitable earlier savepoint can recover it. Atomicity alone does not validate missing account IDs or every concurrent business rule.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Constraints reject invalid balances. Isolation and row locks address concurrent transactions; those are separate from grouping statements atomically.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check both balances and their sum. Trace exactly which changes survive a savepoint rollback. Each practice execution starts with a fresh isolated dataset.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Transactions control what is kept; savepoints allow a partial undo before the final commit.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A data-changing CTE puts INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE inside WITH. Its RETURNING rows can feed the rest of the same SQL statement.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: This connects a change to a report or follow-up insert without passing changed rows through application code.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A modifying CTE puts INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE inside WITH. RETURNING supplies rows for the next part of that same statement. Read that returned relation to use changed values instead of rereading the original table.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: WITH changed AS (UPDATE ... RETURNING id,price) SELECT ... FROM changed reads the rows changed by UPDATE. To archive deletions, use WITH removed AS (DELETE ... RETURNING ...) INSERT INTO archive SELECT ... FROM removed. Create a destination first with CREATE TABLE archive(id integer PRIMARY KEY,title text): names and types go inside parentheses, and PRIMARY KEY makes id unique and required.
sections.code: WITH changed AS (UPDATE products SET price=price-1 WHERE category='Home' RETURNING id,price) SELECT id,price FROM changed ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Return the new stock directly from an UPDATE inside a CTE.

Notebook (id 1) starts with stock 40, and Mug (id 5) with stock 0. The CTE adds one to these two rows and returns the new values.

```sql
WITH changed AS (UPDATE products SET stock=stock+1 WHERE id IN (1,5) RETURNING id,stock) SELECT id,stock FROM changed ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | stock
— | —
1 | 41
5 | 1

The final SELECT reads the returned rows, producing 41 and 1. Other products are not part of the changed relation.
sections.code: WITH changed AS (UPDATE products SET price=price-1 WHERE category='Home' RETURNING id,price) SELECT id,price FROM changed ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The added CTE inserts Eraser and returns its id and name. The final SELECT reads that output as a small result table.
sections.code: WITH added AS (INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES(51,'Eraser','Office',1.25,30) RETURNING id,name) SELECT id,name FROM added;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, this separate check reads all products after lowering Home prices. The modifying CTE’s direct SELECT returns only changed rows, so that output has a different scope.

id | price
— | —
1 | 12.50
2 | 2.00
3 | 75.00
4 | 250.00
5 | 14.00
6 | 44.00
7 | 8.00
8 | 4.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Sibling modifying CTEs share a snapshot; their physical order is not a reliable communication mechanism. Use RETURNING dependencies and avoid changing the same row twice in one statement.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Ordinary CTEs organise queries; modifying CTEs also have effects. A transaction can group several statements when one WITH statement is unnecessary.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Distinguish returned changed rows from a later whole-table check. Verify both the new values and the rows that must stay unchanged.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use RETURNING as the explicit data flow between a modification and its consumer.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A data type tells PostgreSQL what a value means and which operations it supports: numbers, text, or true/false values.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: The right type prevents invalid values and avoids surprising comparisons or calculations.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: smallint, integer and bigint store whole numbers in increasing ranges. numeric stores exact decimal values within its declared limits. text stores characters and boolean stores true or false. NULL represents a missing value of any of these types.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: pg_typeof(value)::text displays a type name. The literal 42 fits integer, while 10000000000 needs bigint. The text operator || joins strings, so 'product-' || id::text builds a label. NOT vip reverses a Boolean value. COALESCE(condition,false) changes an unknown condition result to false.
sections.code: SELECT pg_typeof(1)::text AS integer_type, pg_typeof(1.5)::text AS decimal_type, pg_typeof('x'::text)::text AS text_type, pg_typeof(true)::text AS boolean_type;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Build a text label and a Boolean priority value from customer data.

Ada (1) is a VIP in London. Cleo (3) is not a VIP but is in London. Eli (5) is not a VIP and has no city.

```sql
SELECT id,'customer-'||id::text AS label,COALESCE(vip OR city='London',false) AS priority FROM customers WHERE id IN (1,3,5) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | label | priority
— | — | —
1 | customer-1 | t
3 | customer-3 | t
5 | customer-5 | f

Text IDs form readable labels. Both London customers have true priority. Eli’s unknown OR result becomes false through COALESCE. PostgreSQL displays Boolean values as t and f.
sections.code: SELECT pg_typeof(1)::text AS integer_type, pg_typeof(1.5)::text AS decimal_type, pg_typeof('x'::text)::text AS text_type, pg_typeof(true)::text AS boolean_type;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The expression 'product-' || id::text combines a text prefix with the product ID converted to text.
sections.code: SELECT id, 'product-' || id::text AS label FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example returns one row of type names, not the original values. A value’s type and its display format are different things.

integer_type | decimal_type | text_type | boolean_type
— | — | — | —
integer | numeric | text | boolean

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: numeric(p,s) limits precision and scale and may round input. varchar(n) limits characters, not bytes. Text 'true' is not itself a boolean, even though an explicit conversion can produce one.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Casts convert values between compatible types. Constraints express additional rules such as positive quantities or required text.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Read the type as well as the displayed value. Check whether a calculation requires exact decimals, an integer range, or text formatting.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose types for meaning and valid operations; use explicit casts where conversion is needed.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A UUID is a 128-bit identifier. An enum is a named type that accepts only a declared set of text labels.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: UUIDs help create identifiers across systems. Enums restrict a column to a small, deliberately maintained set of states.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A UUID can be read from text with ::uuid, which checks its format. Uppercase and lowercase hexadecimal letters describe the same UUID. An enum is a named type with a fixed list of allowed labels and an order declared by that list.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: CREATE TYPE priority AS ENUM ('low','normal','high') creates the type. CREATE TABLE tickets(id integer PRIMARY KEY,priority priority) then uses it as a column type. Insert an enum label as quoted text. ORDER BY priority uses declaration order. A uuid PRIMARY KEY combines UUID values with uniqueness and NOT NULL.
sections.code: SELECT '123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000'::uuid AS identifier;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Order tickets by the declared meaning of an enum rather than alphabetically.

Insert three tickets in this order: (1, high), (2, low), (3, normal). Define the enum order as low, normal, high.

```sql
CREATE TYPE lesson_priority AS ENUM('low','normal','high'); CREATE TABLE lesson_tickets(id integer PRIMARY KEY,priority lesson_priority); INSERT INTO lesson_tickets VALUES(1,'high'),(2,'low'),(3,'normal');
SELECT id,priority::text AS priority FROM lesson_tickets ORDER BY lesson_tickets.priority,id;
```

**Result**

id | priority
— | —
2 | low
3 | normal
1 | high

Sorting the enum follows its declared priority, producing IDs 2, 3, 1. Casting the displayed label to text does not change the enum column used for sorting.
sections.code: SELECT '123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000'::uuid AS identifier;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: request_log uses a UUID primary key and a required note. Inserting a known identifier illustrates storage without depending on random generation.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE request_log(request_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,note text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO request_log VALUES('00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001','imported');

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example returns one fixed value under identifier. Its stored type is uuid; the displayed hyphens are its standard text representation.

identifier
—
123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Enum labels are case-sensitive and sort in declaration order, not alphabetically. Removing labels requires more work than adding them. A UUID does not by itself enforce a table key; declare PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare an enum with a CHECK constraint or a lookup table. A lookup table is often easier when states need their own editable metadata.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Keep fixed identifiers in reproducible exercises. Check that an enum accepts only declared labels and that its ordering matches the intended rule.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use UUIDs for identifiers and enums for carefully chosen finite states; their roles are different.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: String functions inspect or transform text. Here, normalisation means applying the same cleanup rules before comparing or storing values.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Extra spaces and inconsistent letter case often make equivalent input look different.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: lower and upper change case. trim removes surrounding spaces by default. Functions can be nested: upper(trim(value)) trims first, then changes case. These expressions return cleaned values without changing the table.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: length(name) counts characters. left(name,3) returns the first three characters, or the whole string if shorter. concat_ws(', ',name,city) joins present values with a comma and space and skips NULL arguments. Sort a computed length with ORDER BY name_length DESC,id to resolve equal lengths consistently.
sections.code: SELECT id, lower(email) AS normalized_email FROM customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Create readable customer labels even when a city is missing.

Customer 1 has name Ada and city London. Customer 5 has name Eli and a NULL city.

```sql
SELECT id,concat_ws(', ',name,city) AS label,left(name,2) AS prefix FROM customers WHERE id IN (1,5) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | label | prefix
— | — | —
1 | Ada, London | Ad
5 | Eli | El

The label for Eli has no dangling separator because concat_ws skips the missing city. left(name,2) independently returns each name’s first two characters.
sections.code: SELECT id, lower(email) AS normalized_email FROM customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: length(name) produces name_length. Descending length puts longer names first; id resolves ties consistently.
sections.code: SELECT id,name,length(name) AS name_length FROM customers ORDER BY name_length DESC,id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example lowercases known email addresses. They already use lowercase in Retail, so their appearance stays the same; Cleo is absent because her email is NULL.

id | normalized_email
— | —
1 | ada@example.test
2 | ben@example.test
4 | davi@example.test
5 | eli@example.test
6 | fara@example.test

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: length counts characters; octet_length counts bytes. trim does not remove all possible internal whitespace. Case conversion depends on locale and is not a universal rule for all identifiers or email systems.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: This text cleanup differs from relational normalisation, which concerns table design. Expression indexes can support frequently used text transformations.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test missing text, leading spaces, and equal-length names. Decide whether you want a transformed result or an UPDATE of stored data.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose a clear cleanup rule and apply it consistently; know whether it changes output or storage.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: DATE stores a calendar day without a time of day. Date arithmetic can count days or move to another calendar date.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Bookings, deadlines, and follow-up dates need clear rules about which days are included.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Subtracting one DATE from another returns a whole number of days. Adding an integer moves a date by that many days. For bookings, check_out-check_in counts nights when checkout is excluded.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: DATE '2024-08-01' states an unambiguous calendar date. shipped_on-ordered_on measures shipping days only when shipped_on is known. ordered_on+7 creates a follow-up date. Use WHERE status='pending' to calculate reminders only for pending orders.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest,check_out-check_in AS nights FROM bookings ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Calculate booking nights and a follow-up date using calendar days.

Ada’s booking runs from July 1 to July 4. Davi’s runs from July 1 to July 2. Checkout is the first unoccupied day.

```sql
SELECT id,guest,check_out-check_in AS nights,check_out+1 AS follow_up_on FROM bookings WHERE id IN (1,4) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | guest | nights | follow_up_on
— | — | — | —
1 | Ada | 3 | 2024-07-05
4 | Davi | 1 | 2024-07-03

The differences are three nights and one night. Adding 1 to checkout creates the next calendar date for a follow-up.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest,check_out-check_in AS nights FROM bookings ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: For pending orders, ordered_on+7 gives a follow-up date one week later. The query returns dates without changing the order rows.
sections.code: SELECT id,ordered_on+7 AS follow_up_on FROM orders WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example returns 3, 3, 2, 1, and 3 nights for the five bookings. These are whole-day date differences, not elapsed timestamp hours.

id | guest | nights
— | — | —
1 | Ada | 3
2 | Ben | 3
3 | Cleo | 2
4 | Davi | 1
5 | Eli | 3

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A calendar month is not a fixed number of days. DATE subtraction differs from age(), which expresses calendar years, months, and days. Be explicit about inclusive and exclusive boundaries.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Timestamps add time of day and time-zone questions. Half-open ranges help represent stays whose checkout day is excluded.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check a one-night stay and a month boundary. Verify that adjoining stays can share a checkout/check-in date without overlapping nights.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: DATE arithmetic works with calendar days; state the boundary rule before calculating.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: timestamp without time zone stores calendar and clock fields. timestamptz identifies an instant; its displayed clock time depends on the session time zone.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A local appointment and a globally timed event need different treatment, even if their text looks similar.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For timestamp without time zone, AT TIME ZONE interprets the clock fields in a named zone and produces an instant of type timestamptz. For timestamptz, the same operation produces the local clock fields of the named zone. The original zone name is not stored.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: EXTRACT(HOUR FROM occurred_at)::integer reads an event’s hour. To treat a zone-less event time as UTC and show Tokyo time, apply both conversions: (occurred_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Tokyo'. TIMESTAMPTZ '2024-07-01 12:00:00+02' supplies an explicit instant. Named regions such as America/New_York apply the rules for that date, including seasonal clock changes.
sections.code: SELECT id,EXTRACT(HOUR FROM occurred_at)::integer AS event_hour FROM events ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Interpret stored event times as UTC, then display the same instants in Tokyo.

The first two events store July 1 at 09:00 and 09:10 without a time zone. For this report, the business rule says these fields represent UTC.

```sql
SELECT id,occurred_at,(occurred_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Tokyo' AS tokyo_time FROM events WHERE id IN (1,2) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | occurred_at | tokyo_time
— | — | —
1 | 2024-07-01 09:00:00 | 2024-07-01 18:00:00
2 | 2024-07-01 09:10:00 | 2024-07-01 18:10:00

The same instants appear as 18:00 and 18:10 in Tokyo. Changing the display zone does not change which moments the events represent.
sections.code: SELECT id,EXTRACT(HOUR FROM occurred_at)::integer AS event_hour FROM events ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The first AT TIME ZONE treats occurred_at as UTC. The second displays that instant as Tokyo local time, returning a timestamp without time zone.
sections.code: SELECT id,(occurred_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Tokyo' AS tokyo_time FROM events ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example reads the stored timestamp hours directly: 9, 9, 10, 8, 10, and 11. It applies no time-zone conversion and makes no UTC assumption.

id | event_hour
— | —
1 | 9
2 | 9
3 | 10
4 | 8
5 | 10
6 | 11

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Do not assume a zone-less timestamp means UTC. Daylight-saving transitions can make a local time ambiguous or nonexistent. Explicit offsets or a clear input policy avoid guessing.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: DATE contains no time of day. Reporting with timestamptz also needs a chosen zone before extracting dates or grouping days.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace the type after each AT TIME ZONE. Check a conversion that crosses midnight, not only one that changes the hour.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: First identify whether you have clock fields or an instant, then apply the intended zone.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An interval expresses a span using months, days, and smaller time units. date_trunc finds the start of a calendar period containing a timestamp.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reports need consistent month boundaries; elapsed-time calculations need a clear starting point and unit.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: date_trunc('month', value) returns the start of its month. Use 'day' for midnight and 'week' for Monday at midnight. A cast to ::date hides the time fields when only a calendar date is needed. GROUP BY the truncated value to count or sum each period.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: TIMESTAMP '2024-07-01 00:00:00' is a fixed reference time. Subtract it from occurred_at to obtain an interval. EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM interval) gives seconds, so divide by 60 for minutes. An interval literal such as INTERVAL '48 hours' can be added to a date or timestamp. A date plus an interval produces a timestamp.
sections.code: SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Place events into daily and weekly reporting buckets.

Events 1, 4 and 6 occur on July 1, 2 and 3 at different times. July 1, 2024 is a Monday.

```sql
SELECT id,date_trunc('day',occurred_at)::date AS event_day,date_trunc('week',occurred_at)::date AS week_start FROM events WHERE id IN (1,4,6) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | event_day | week_start
— | — | —
1 | 2024-07-01 | 2024-07-01
4 | 2024-07-02 | 2024-07-01
6 | 2024-07-03 | 2024-07-01

Daily truncation keeps three different dates. Weekly truncation gives the same Monday for all three, which makes them one group in a weekly report.
sections.code: SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Subtracting the fixed midnight timestamp gives the time since that start. Dividing extracted seconds by 60 expresses the interval in minutes.
sections.code: SELECT id,EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (occurred_at-TIMESTAMP '2024-07-01 00:00:00'))/60 AS minutes_since_start FROM events ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results

— | —

2024-07-01 | 374.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A month has varying length, and a local day across daylight-saving changes may not be 24 hours. now() stays at transaction-start time; clock_timestamp() changes as time passes. Choose the reporting zone for timestamptz.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: DATE arithmetic counts calendar days. Time buckets and running totals answer different questions: one groups periods, the other accumulates rows.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An array stores an ordered collection whose elements share a type, such as several text tags on one product.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Arrays suit small values that belong together. A separate relationship table is often better when elements need their own keys or references.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ARRAY[...] creates an ordered list of values of one type. value=ANY(array) asks whether any element matches. cardinality(array) counts elements. array_position(array,value) returns the first matching position, or NULL if no element matches.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Array operators compare collections: tags && ARRAY['work','light'] means at least one shared element, while @> requires all elements of the right-hand array. To count each tag, CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(p.tags) AS t(tag) makes one row per product tag, then GROUP BY t.tag. An array normally starts at position 1, although custom lower bounds are possible.
sections.code: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE 'usb'=ANY(tags) ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Compare an array overlap test with the position of one particular tag.

Notebook has tags paper and study. Keyboard has usb and work. Lamp has light and work.

```sql
SELECT id,tags,tags && ARRAY['work','light'] AS matches,array_position(tags,'usb') AS usb_position FROM products WHERE id IN (1,3,6) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | tags | matches | usb_position
— | — | — | —
1 | {paper,study} | f | NULL
3 | {usb,work} | t | 1
6 | {light,work} | t | NULL

Keyboard and Lamp overlap the requested tags. Only Keyboard has usb, at position 1. The absent position stays NULL rather than becoming zero.
sections.code: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE 'usb'=ANY(tags) ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: LATERAL unnest(p.tags) produces one row per tag for each product. GROUP BY tag then counts those expanded rows.
sections.code: SELECT t.tag,count(*) AS product_count FROM products p CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(p.tags) AS t(tag) GROUP BY t.tag ORDER BY product_count DESC,t.tag;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example returns products 3 and 7 because their tag arrays contain usb. A membership test keeps product rows; it does not expand each tag into a separate row.

id | name
— | —
3 | Keyboard
7 | Cable

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: An empty array differs from a NULL array. If no comparison is true but an element is NULL, = ANY may be unknown. Repeated tags count repeatedly after unnest; the product_count example assumes unique tags within each product.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare unnest with a one-to-many join: both can increase row count. Containment ignores repeated occurrences, unlike an expanded count.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check empty arrays, NULLs, and duplicate tags. Decide whether you are counting tag occurrences or distinct products.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Arrays keep collections together; unnest expands them, so track the resulting row count.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: json stores JSON text. jsonb stores a processed representation suited to structural operations and indexes. Both can hold objects, arrays, and scalar values.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: JSON is useful for variable optional attributes, while regular columns remain useful for stable shared fields and constraints.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: -> extracts a JSON value. ->> extracts text, so attributes->>'rating' must be cast to numeric before numeric comparison or addition. #>> follows a path of keys and returns text. A missing key produces SQL NULL.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Use (attributes->>'rating')::numeric >= 4.5 to compare ratings as numbers. Use payload->>'device' as a group key, cast payload->>'amount' to numeric, and SUM it for purchases. IS NULL also works on extracted text to find missing fields. JSON null and SQL NULL are different, but ->> returns SQL NULL for both a missing key and a JSON null value.
sections.code: SELECT id,attributes->>'color' AS color FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Extract readable colors and numeric ratings, keeping products with missing keys.

Notebook has attributes color blue and rating 4.7. Cable has only length 2, while Folder has an empty JSON object.

```sql
SELECT id,attributes->>'color' AS color,(attributes->>'rating')::numeric AS rating FROM products WHERE id IN (1,7,8) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | color | rating
— | — | —
1 | blue | 4.7
7 | NULL | NULL
8 | NULL | NULL

The query keeps all three products. Missing keys produce NULL, and the rating of Notebook is a number after the cast.
sections.code: SELECT id,attributes->>'color' AS color FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: For purchase events, the query extracts device and converts amount to numeric before summing by device.
sections.code: SELECT payload->>'device' AS device,sum((payload->>'amount')::numeric) AS amount FROM events WHERE kind='purchase' GROUP BY device ORDER BY device;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example extracts color from every product. Monitor, Cable, and Folder produce SQL NULL, which is different from the text string NULL.

id | color
— | —
1 | blue
2 | black
3 | black
4 | NULL
5 | white
6 | blue
7 | NULL
8 | NULL

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: JSON null and SQL NULL differ, although ->> returns SQL NULL for either a missing key or JSON null. jsonb keeps only the last duplicate object key and does not preserve formatting or key order. A numeric cast fails on nonnumeric text.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: JSONB containment checks structure without extracting every field. Constraints and relational columns can protect fields that must always be valid.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check absent keys, JSON null, and numeric strings. Inspect whether an operator returns JSON or text before combining it with other operations.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose the extraction operator by the result type you need, and convert numeric text explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: JSONB can be searched by structure and transformed into a new document. These operations work on values; storing the new document requires a write such as UPDATE.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: You can filter optional attributes or change one field while keeping the rest of a document.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: attributes @> '{"color":"blue"}'::jsonb checks whether an object contains that key and value, even when other keys exist. attributes ? 'rating' checks whether the top-level key exists. A present key containing JSON null still exists.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: jsonb_set(attributes,'{featured}','true'::jsonb,true) sets the path featured and creates that key when missing. The new value is JSON true, not the text string "true". attributes-'color' removes a top-level key. attributes||'{"promotional":false}'::jsonb merges top-level object keys, with right-hand values replacing duplicate keys. Other object keys remain.
sections.code: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"color":"blue"}'::jsonb ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Change two JSONB keys while leaving other product attributes intact.

Product 1 has color blue and rating 4.7. Remove color and add featured=true only to that product. Product 2 starts with color black and rating 4.2.

```sql
UPDATE products SET attributes=(attributes-'color')||'{"featured":true}'::jsonb WHERE id=1;
SELECT id,attributes->>'color' AS color,attributes->>'featured' AS featured,attributes->>'rating' AS rating FROM products WHERE id IN (1,2) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | color | featured | rating
— | — | — | —
1 | NULL | true | 4.7
2 | black | NULL | 4.2

Product 1 loses its color but keeps its rating and gains featured. Product 2 is unchanged. ->> displays the JSON Boolean as the text true.
sections.code: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"color":"blue"}'::jsonb ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: UPDATE stores jsonb_set's returned document for Office products. '{featured}' is the path; 'true'::jsonb is a Boolean JSON value, not a text string.
sections.code: UPDATE products SET attributes=jsonb_set(attributes,'{featured}','true'::jsonb,true) WHERE category='Office';

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example returns products 1 and 6 because their JSONB objects contain color=blue. Extra keys do not prevent this structural match.

— | —
1 | Notebook
6 | Lamp

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: JSON number 2 differs from JSON string "2". A missing intermediate path is not built automatically by jsonb_set; only the final item can be created when its parents exist. Updating the document replaces the stored value, so keep the original as the function's input.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Use ->> when you need a text value, @> when you need a structural match. Important relationships may still belong in relational columns.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check that only Office documents change and that unrelated keys survive. Distinguish JSON true from the JSON string "true".

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Match JSON structure deliberately, then store the transformed document when an actual change is needed.
