sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Keys protect identity and relationships. PRIMARY KEY identifies a row uniquely and forbids NULL; UNIQUE prevents repeated key values; FOREIGN KEY requires a referenced row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Database-enforced keys keep data consistent regardless of which application writes it.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PRIMARY KEY identifies each row and forbids duplicate or NULL key values. UNIQUE prevents repeated known values. NOT NULL separately requires a value. REFERENCES customers(id) requires a present customer ID to exist in customers.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Write these rules beside a column in CREATE TABLE, for example customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id). A column can be both PRIMARY KEY and REFERENCES, giving at most one child row per parent. For an existing table, ALTER TABLE products ADD CONSTRAINT name UNIQUE(name) adds uniqueness. Ordinary UNIQUE allows several NULLs; UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT permits only one NULL.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_notes(id integer PRIMARY KEY,customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),body text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO customer_notes VALUES(1,1,'Call after 5');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Create customer aliases with a foreign key and a deliberate NULL uniqueness rule.

Customers 1 and 2 already exist. Create a separate alias table, allowing an absent alias but using UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT, then insert one missing alias and one billing alias.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lesson_aliases(id integer PRIMARY KEY,customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id),alias text UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT); INSERT INTO lesson_aliases VALUES(1,1,NULL),(2,2,'billing');
SELECT id,customer_id,alias FROM lesson_aliases ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | customer_id | alias
— | — | —
1 | 1 | NULL
2 | 2 | billing

Both rows are valid. A second missing alias would violate this uniqueness rule, while a nonexistent customer ID would violate the foreign key.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_notes(id integer PRIMARY KEY,customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),body text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO customer_notes VALUES(1,1,'Call after 5');

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: customer_alias uses UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT on alias. Unlike ordinary UNIQUE, this rule allows at most one NULL alias.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_alias(customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id),alias text UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, this metadata check lists the created table’s column types and nullability. It does not display customer notes, and declared key constraints require their own checks.

column_name | data_type | is_nullable
— | — | —
id | integer | NO
customer_id | integer | NO
body | text | NO

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Ordinary UNIQUE allows multiple NULLs. A foreign key does not automatically index the referencing column. By default, any NULL in a foreign key with several columns skips the match. MATCH FULL allows all key columns to be NULL together and rejects a mix of NULL and present values.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A primary key identifies the note, while a foreign key identifies its relationship. An index helps access data; a constraint states a rule.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Inspect keys as well as columns. Try reasoning about duplicate IDs, missing customers, and NULL aliases before submitting a table design.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Separate row identity, uniqueness rules, and required relationships; declare each one explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: CHECK rejects a row when a condition is false. DEFAULT supplies an omitted value. A foreign-key action says what to do when a referenced row changes or is deleted.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: These rules keep ordinary writes simple while protecting required business conditions.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CHECK(condition) rejects a false condition. Unknown passes, so combine it with NOT NULL when the value is required. DEFAULT supplies a value when a column is omitted or DEFAULT is requested. A check may compare two columns, such as CHECK(end_day>start_day).

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: ON DELETE CASCADE on a foreign key removes child rows when their parent is deleted. ON DELETE SET NULL instead clears that reference if NULL is permitted. ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN promoted boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false adds a column and supplies false to existing rows as well as future inserts that omit it. Changing only an existing column’s default does not backfill old values.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE reservations(id integer PRIMARY KEY,quantity integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK(quantity>0)); INSERT INTO reservations(id) VALUES(1);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Follow what happens to a child row when its parent is deleted with CASCADE.

Create draft 1 and one line referencing that draft. Before deletion, each table has one row. The line’s foreign key declares ON DELETE CASCADE.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lesson_drafts(id integer PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE lesson_draft_lines(id integer PRIMARY KEY,draft_id integer REFERENCES lesson_drafts(id) ON DELETE CASCADE); INSERT INTO lesson_drafts VALUES(1); INSERT INTO lesson_draft_lines VALUES(1,1); DELETE FROM lesson_drafts WHERE id=1;
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM lesson_drafts) AS draft_count,(SELECT count(*) FROM lesson_draft_lines) AS line_count;
```

**Result**

draft_count | line_count
— | —
0 | 0

Deleting the draft also removes its line. Both counts become zero, without a separate DELETE against the line table.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE reservations(id integer PRIMARY KEY,quantity integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK(quantity>0)); INSERT INTO reservations(id) VALUES(1);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Adding promoted with NOT NULL DEFAULT false gives existing products false and supplies false for future inserts that omit the column.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN promoted boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, the checker reads the new reservation with id 1 and quantity 1. CREATE TABLE itself does not return that saved row.

id | quantity
— | —
1 | 1

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Changing an existing column's default does not rewrite its old values. This differs from adding a new column with a default. CHECK is not a safe way to maintain rules that depend on other rows. Cascading deletes can remove many dependent rows.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Foreign keys handle relationships; CHECK handles conditions on a row. Defaults provide values but do not replace validation.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check omitted, explicit NULL, and invalid values separately. For a referential action, trace exactly which dependent rows will change.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use defaults for convenience and constraints for validity; keep their roles separate.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An identity column gets values from an associated sequence, an object that hands out numbers. Generation and uniqueness are separate rules.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Automatic IDs avoid making every insert choose a new number manually.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: An identity column uses a sequence to supply numbers when the ID is omitted. GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY normally rejects explicit IDs. GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY permits them. Add PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE because identity alone does not enforce uniqueness.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: CREATE SEQUENCE ticket_number START WITH 100 INCREMENT BY 5 declares a separate counter. Each nextval('ticket_number') consumes and returns the next number. Identity options go in parentheses, as IDENTITY(START WITH 100). An explicit inserted ID does not advance a BY DEFAULT sequence: after inserting 50, its first automatic ID can still be 1. Sequence numbers may have gaps after rollback.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE activity_log(id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,message text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO activity_log(message) VALUES('Started'),('Finished');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Read two successive numbers from a sequence with a five-unit step.

A new ticket sequence starts at 100 and advances by 5. No numbers have been allocated yet.

```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE lesson_ticket_number START WITH 100 INCREMENT BY 5;
SELECT nextval('lesson_ticket_number') AS first_ticket,nextval('lesson_ticket_number') AS second_ticket;
```

**Result**

first_ticket | second_ticket
— | —
100 | 105

Two nextval calls allocate 100 and 105. A later call would allocate 110, not reread either displayed number.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE activity_log(id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,message text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO activity_log(message) VALUES('Started'),('Finished');

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: BY DEFAULT allows the explicit legacy ID 50. That insert does not advance the sequence to 50, so the following generated ID on this fresh table is 1.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE imported_log(id integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,message text); INSERT INTO imported_log VALUES(50,'Legacy'); INSERT INTO imported_log(message) VALUES('New');

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, the checker reads Started and Finished with generated IDs 1 and 2. These are saved rows read after creation and insertion.

id | message
— | —
1 | Started
2 | Finished

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Sequence numbers are not reclaimed after rollback and can have gaps. Manual IDs do not automatically keep a sequence ahead of existing rows. An ID is neither a row count nor a guaranteed commit-time order.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: UUIDs offer another identifier strategy. Primary keys protect identity regardless of how values are generated.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Distinguish ALWAYS from BY DEFAULT. Check what a manual insert does to the next generated value and whether uniqueness is enforced.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A sequence generates numbers; a key makes them unique. Expect gaps.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Normalisation organises data so that each property is stored with the entity it describes. A relationship table links two entities when each can relate to many of the other.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Keeping one authoritative copy of a property reduces inconsistent updates and accidental data loss.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Find the separate entities and ask which key determines each property. A many-to-many relationship uses a link table: customer_id REFERENCES customers(id), product_id REFERENCES products(id), PRIMARY KEY(customer_id,product_id). The pair prevents duplicate links.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: To build a category lookup, first SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products. Then row_number() OVER(ORDER BY category) assigns 1, 2, 3 in alphabetical order; ::integer makes the ID type explicit. We will study other window functions later. INSERT INTO categories SELECT ... stores these rows. Reporting still uses earlier GROUP BY/HAVING and LEFT JOIN rules; count(DISTINCT product_id) counts each linked product once. If a city occurs n times, storing it once removes n-1 repeated copies: use count(*)-1 for that grouped measure.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE favorites(customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id),product_id integer REFERENCES products(id),PRIMARY KEY(customer_id,product_id)); INSERT INTO favorites VALUES(1,3),(2,1);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Build a category lookup from repeated product category names.

Products repeat the labels Home twice, Office three times and Tech three times. A category lookup needs one row for each label.

```sql
SELECT row_number() OVER(ORDER BY category)::integer AS category_id,category FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) c ORDER BY category_id;
```

**Result**

category_id | category
— | —
1 | Home
2 | Office
3 | Tech

DISTINCT reduces eight products to three labels. row_number gives each label a reproducible ID in alphabetical order.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE favorites(customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id),product_id integer REFERENCES products(id),PRIMARY KEY(customer_id,product_id)); INSERT INTO favorites VALUES(1,3),(2,1);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The categories example extracts distinct category names and assigns deterministic IDs in alphabetical order. It creates a lookup table; it does not yet replace products.category with a foreign key.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE categories(id integer PRIMARY KEY,name text NOT NULL UNIQUE); INSERT INTO categories SELECT row_number() OVER(ORDER BY category)::integer,category FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) c;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, the checker reads two saved customer/product links. The pair key prevents a duplicate link, while one customer or product may occur in several different pairs.

customer_id | product_id
— | —
1 | 3
2 | 1

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Normalisation does not mean making a table for every column. Splitting a design without preserving keys and dependencies can lose meaning. Denormalise only with a clear consistency strategy and a measured need.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Primary and foreign keys make relationships enforceable. JOIN combines normalised tables when a report needs their properties together.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: For each new table, state what one row represents and what identifies it. Check whether repeated text is a property or a relationship.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Store each property in the right place and represent many-to-many links explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A schema is a named container for database objects. Catalogs are database tables and views describing objects such as tables, columns, and constraints.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Schemas organise names; metadata queries let tools inspect a database without hardcoding every table definition.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A schema groups named objects. schema.table identifies a table explicitly; search_path controls which schemas an unqualified name searches. current_schema() reports the current creation schema. information_schema contains queryable descriptions of tables and columns, rather than their business rows.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: In columns, filter table_schema and table_name; column_name and data_type describe each column, ordinal_position preserves its position, and numeric_precision/numeric_scale describe numeric capacity. tables with table_type='BASE TABLE' selects stored tables. table_constraints names each constraint and its constraint_type. Join key_column_usage by constraint catalog, schema and name for key columns. constraint_column_usage identifies the referenced columns of the single-column foreign keys used here.
sections.code: SELECT column_name,data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema=current_schema() AND table_name='customers' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Read the first three customer-column descriptions instead of customer records.

A customers row might contain (1, Ada, London). The table definition calls those first three fields id, name and city.

```sql
SELECT column_name,data_type,ordinal_position FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema=current_schema() AND table_name='customers' AND ordinal_position<=3 ORDER BY ordinal_position;
```

**Result**

column_name | data_type | ordinal_position
— | — | —
id | integer | 1
name | text | 2
city | text | 3

The metadata query returns the column definitions, not Ada’s values. ordinal_position follows the table’s declared column order.
sections.code: SELECT column_name,data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema=current_schema() AND table_name='customers' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Filtering information_schema.tables to BASE TABLE excludes views. The current-schema condition avoids mixing similarly named objects in other schemas.
sections.code: SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=current_schema() AND table_type='BASE TABLE' ORDER BY table_name;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example lists all six customers columns with their types: id, name, city, email, joined_on, and vip. It describes the table, not the customer rows. Metadata visibility can depend on role privileges.

column_name | data_type
— | —
id | integer
name | text
city | text
email | text
joined_on | date
vip | boolean

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A schema is not a separate database. current_schema() is the first effective schema in search_path, not every searched schema. Letting untrusted users create objects in a searched schema can change name resolution.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: The schema browser uses similar metadata. Roles and search_path matter for secure functions and administrative tooling.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Distinguish table data from metadata. Always check schema filters when a table name could exist in several places.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Qualify object names when needed, and use catalogs to inspect the database definition.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A migration is a recorded, repeatable change to database structure or data. It should leave both existing data and application expectations consistent.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Applications evolve while real data must survive. An ordered migration is safer to verify than ad hoc edits.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For an existing table, add a column, fill old rows, then enforce rules on the filled data. For example, ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN segment text creates an initially nullable column. UPDATE ... SET segment=CASE ... END fills it, and ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN segment SET NOT NULL makes it required.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: ALTER TABLE products RENAME COLUMN stock TO stock_units changes the name while keeping values. ADD CHECK(reorder_point>0) adds a validity rule after filling the new column. ADD COLUMN dispatched boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false supplies false to old and future rows; a later UPDATE can set dispatched=(shipped_on IS NOT NULL) for old rows without changing the default for future inserts.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN segment text; UPDATE customers SET segment=CASE WHEN vip THEN 'priority' ELSE 'standard' END; ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN segment SET NOT NULL;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Add a required reorder point safely by filling existing rows before enforcing constraints.

Products initially have no reorder_point column. Product 1 is Office, product 3 is Tech and product 5 is Home. Add the column, fill it by category, then make it required and positive.

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN reorder_point integer; UPDATE products SET reorder_point=CASE WHEN category='Tech' THEN 10 ELSE 20 END; ALTER TABLE products ALTER COLUMN reorder_point SET NOT NULL; ALTER TABLE products ADD CHECK(reorder_point>0);
SELECT id,category,reorder_point FROM products WHERE id IN (1,3,5) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | category | reorder_point
— | — | —
1 | Office | 20
3 | Tech | 10
5 | Home | 20

Every shown row has a valid reorder point before the constraints are added. Existing product IDs and categories are preserved.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN segment text; UPDATE customers SET segment=CASE WHEN vip THEN 'priority' ELSE 'standard' END; ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN segment SET NOT NULL;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Adding reviewed_at without a default leaves existing orders NULL. This represents an unknown or not-yet-recorded review time.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN reviewed_at timestamp without time zone;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, this separate check reads the completed customer segments: priority for VIP customers and standard for the others. It is not direct ALTER TABLE output.

id | segment
— | —
1 | priority
2 | standard
3 | standard
4 | priority
5 | standard
6 | standard

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Adding NOT NULL before filling NULL rows fails. This example does not set a future default, so later inserts must supply segment. Large tables may need staged backfills, lock planning, and compatible application deployment.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Defaults, constraints, and transactions each solve part of migration safety. Backups and restore tests protect against changes that cannot simply be reversed.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Verify old rows and the final schema. Ask what a new insert must provide after the migration, not just whether today's rows look correct.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Plan the order of change, backfill existing data, and check the rules for future writes.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A window function calculates using related rows while retaining each individual result row. This lets a detail row carry a group total beside it.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reports often need both an employee's salary and the total for that employee's department.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OVER turns an aggregate into a window calculation: it adds a value to each row rather than replacing many rows with one summary. PARTITION BY department limits each calculation to that employee's department. With no ORDER BY inside OVER, sum, avg, and count use the whole partition. NULL partition keys belong to one shared partition. WHERE filters the input before the window is calculated, so a paid-order share uses only paid orders in both its numerator and denominator.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Write sum(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS department_total. Replacing sum with avg gives the department average, so salary-avg(salary) OVER (...) measures a difference from that average. For a share, divide the row value by its partition total: stock::numeric / NULLIF(sum(stock) OVER (PARTITION BY category),0). The cast keeps fractional digits; NULLIF avoids division by zero; round(...,4) sets four decimal places. count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) counts every order, including those in the NULL-customer partition. An outer ORDER BY controls display order.
sections.code: SELECT id,department,salary,sum(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department) AS department_total FROM employees ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Put a department total beside each employee salary without reducing the detail rows.

Engineering has three employees: IDs 2, 3, and 6 earn 90000.00, 80000.00, and 80000.00.

```sql
SELECT id,salary,sum(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS department_total FROM employees WHERE department='Engineering' ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | salary | department_total
— | — | —
2 | 90000.00 | 250000.00
3 | 80000.00 | 250000.00
6 | 80000.00 | 250000.00

All three rows remain. Each salary now sits beside the same department total, 250000.00.
sections.code: SELECT id,department,salary,sum(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department) AS department_total FROM employees ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: count(*) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id) repeats the customer's order count on each order. NULL customer IDs form their own partition rather than disappearing.
sections.code: SELECT id,customer_id,count(*) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_order_count FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example retains all six employee rows. Each department’s total repeats beside its employees because the window adds a calculation without collapsing the rows.

id | department | salary | department_total
— | — | — | —
1 | Leadership | 120000.00 | 120000.00
2 | Engineering | 90000.00 | 250000.00
3 | Engineering | 80000.00 | 250000.00
4 | Sales | 70000.00 | 140000.00
5 | Sales | 70000.00 | 140000.00
6 | Engineering | 80000.00 | 250000.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: GROUP BY changes result row granularity; a window does not do that grouping. WHERE and HAVING filter before window calculations. To filter by a window result, calculate it in a subquery or CTE first.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Ordinary aggregates produce summaries; window aggregates attach summaries to detail. A window ORDER BY, introduced next, can also change the calculation's frame.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Compare input and output row counts. Check that every department has its own total and that NULL partition keys are handled deliberately.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: PARTITION BY chooses related rows; OVER keeps the detail rows while calculating across them.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: row_number assigns a different number to each ordered row. rank gives tied rows the same rank and leaves gaps; dense_rank gives ties the same rank without gaps.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Use these functions for leaderboards, ordered positions, and selecting a limited number of rows within each group.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ORDER BY inside OVER defines the sequence used by a ranking function. PARTITION BY starts it again for each group. row_number gives every row a unique position; include id after the main sort key when equal values need a consistent order. rank and dense_rank give equal sort values equal ranks. For 90,80,80,70, rank gives 1,2,2,4 and dense_rank gives 1,2,2,3. Adding id to those ranking keys would split the salary ties.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) numbers expensive products first within each category. Use rank() or dense_rank() with ORDER BY salary DESC when equal salaries must tie. Window values cannot be tested in the same SELECT's WHERE: first calculate them in a CTE, then filter outside it, as in WITH numbered AS (SELECT id,row_number() OVER (ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS rn FROM products) SELECT id FROM numbered WHERE rn<=2 ORDER BY rn. rn<=2 keeps at most two rows; dense_rank=2 keeps every row at the second distinct value. WHERE status='paid' filters orders before numbering.
sections.code: SELECT id,category,row_number() OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS position FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Compare ordinary and dense salary ranks on actual employees with tied salaries.

The six salaries in descending order are 120000, 90000, 80000, 80000, 70000, 70000.

```sql
SELECT id,salary,rank() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS salary_rank,dense_rank() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_salary_rank FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC,id;
```

**Result**

id | salary | salary_rank | dense_salary_rank
— | — | — | —
1 | 120000.00 | 1 | 1
2 | 90000.00 | 2 | 2
3 | 80000.00 | 3 | 3
6 | 80000.00 | 3 | 3
4 | 70000.00 | 5 | 4
5 | 70000.00 | 5 | 4

Both 80000 salaries receive rank 3. The next salary receives rank 5, but dense rank 4: only RANK leaves a gap after the tied rows.
sections.code: SELECT id,category,row_number() OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS position FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The CTE first numbers employees within departments, then rn<=2 keeps at most two from each. The ID tie-breaker chooses a consistent result when salaries match.
sections.code: WITH ranked AS (SELECT *,row_number() OVER(PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC,id) AS rn FROM employees) SELECT id,name,department,salary FROM ranked WHERE rn<=2 ORDER BY department,salary DESC,id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example numbers products within categories. Tech positions are Monitor 1, Keyboard 2, and Cable 3, although the final table is displayed by ID.

id | category | position
— | — | —
1 | Office | 1
2 | Office | 3
3 | Tech | 2
4 | Tech | 1
5 | Home | 2
6 | Home | 1
7 | Tech | 3
8 | Office | 2

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: The outer ORDER BY does not define window order. Adding id to rank removes salary ties. Decide whether 'top two' means exactly two rows or every row in the top two ranks.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A subquery or CTE lets WHERE filter a computed window value. DISTINCT ON is another option when only one row per group is needed.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test equal salaries. Compare which employees survive row_number<=2 versus rank<=2 before choosing the function.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose numbering for a row limit and ranking for meaningful ties; define the window order explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: lag reads a value from an earlier row in the window's order; lead reads one from a later row. Neither requires a self join.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Compare successive orders, salaries, or events while retaining each current row.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LAG reads an earlier row and LEAD reads a later row in the window order. Their default offset is one row. PARTITION BY keeps independent sequences separate; ORDER BY ordered_on,id makes the previous or next order unambiguous even on the same date. The lookup stops at a partition boundary. Without a supplied default, a missing neighbour gives NULL. PostgreSQL does not skip neighbours whose stored value is NULL.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: lag(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id) adds the previous total. Subtract it from total to compare amounts. lead(ordered_on) OVER (...) - ordered_on subtracts dates and returns days until the next order. Subtracting two timestamps instead gives an interval: extract(epoch FROM occurred_at-lag(occurred_at) OVER (...))/3600 converts it to hours; round(...::numeric,2) rounds the result. LEAD works on quantities too: order inventory within each warehouse by product_id. A third argument, as in lag(total,1,0), supplies 0 only when no previous row exists, not when an existing row contains NULL.
sections.code: SELECT id,customer_id,total,lag(total) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id) AS previous_total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Read one customer’s previous order total beside each current order.

Customer 1 has orders 101, 103, and 108 in this chronological order, with totals 29.00, 250.00, and 16.00.

```sql
SELECT id,total,lag(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id) AS previous_total FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 ORDER BY ordered_on,id;
```

**Result**

id | total | previous_total
— | — | —
101 | 29.00 | NULL
103 | 250.00 | 29.00
108 | 16.00 | 250.00

Each order gains the previous order’s total. The first row has no predecessor, so its previous_total is NULL.
sections.code: SELECT id,customer_id,total,lag(total) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id) AS previous_total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The salary example subtracts the preceding employee's salary in hire-date order within the same department. It compares employees, not salary history for one employee.
sections.code: SELECT id,salary-lag(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department ORDER BY hired_on,id) AS salary_change FROM employees ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
In the original syntax example, NULL previous_total marks the first order in each customer sequence. In other data it could also mean the preceding row’s total is NULL. The preview may show only part of the full result.

id | customer_id | total | previous_total
— | — | — | —
101 | 1 | 29.00 | NULL
102 | 2 | 75.00 | NULL
103 | 1 | 250.00 | 29.00
104 | 3 | 15.00 | NULL
105 | 4 | 90.00 | NULL
106 | 2 | 20.00 | 75.00
107 | 5 | 25.00 | NULL
108 | 1 | 16.00 | 250.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A default argument does not replace a NULL in an existing neighbouring row. Date ties need a tie-breaker. The final display order can differ from the order used by lag or lead.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Window partitions define independent sequences. A self join can express similar comparisons but often needs more key-handling code.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define the sequence first; lag and lead then read neighbours inside that sequence.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A window frame is the portion of a partition used for the current calculation. It can grow with each row to produce a running total.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Running revenue answers 'how much so far?' without losing individual orders.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A frame selects the rows used for the current window calculation. ROWS counts positions in the window's ORDER BY, not calendar days. UNBOUNDED PRECEDING means the partition's first row; CURRENT ROW means the current position. ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW grows one row at a time. PARTITION BY restarts that process per customer, and WHERE filters orders before the window calculation. Add id after the date so same-day rows have a definite order.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: sum(total) OVER (ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) is a running sum. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING is its shorter form. For a three-order mean, use avg(total) with ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. To exclude the current order and average only its two predecessors, use ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING. At the beginning, the frame contains only the available preceding rows; if none exist, AVG and SUM return NULL. count(shipped_on) over a running frame counts non-NULL shipment dates; COUNT on an empty frame returns 0.
sections.code: SELECT id,ordered_on,sum(total) OVER(ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' ORDER BY ordered_on,id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Average only the preceding orders, leaving the current order outside the frame.

The first four orders by date and ID total 29.00, 75.00, 250.00, and 15.00.

```sql
SELECT id,total,round(avg(total) OVER (ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING),2) AS prior_two_mean FROM orders ORDER BY ordered_on,id LIMIT 4;
```

**Result**

id | total | prior_two_mean
— | — | —
101 | 29.00 | NULL
102 | 75.00 | 29.00
103 | 250.00 | 52.00
104 | 15.00 | 162.50

The current amount is excluded. For order 104 the two preceding amounts are 75.00 and 250.00, whose mean is 162.50. The first order has an empty frame.
sections.code: SELECT id,ordered_on,sum(total) OVER(ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' ORDER BY ordered_on,id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: PARTITION BY customer_id restarts accumulation for each known customer. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING is shorthand for a frame ending at the current row.
sections.code: SELECT id,customer_id,sum(total) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_spend FROM orders WHERE status='paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: With an ordered window, the default RANGE frame includes all peers at the current sort value. A total can jump across equal dates. Use an explicit frame and a tie-breaker when row-by-row steps matter.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A whole-partition sum repeats one total; a running sum uses a changing frame. The outer ORDER BY still controls how the result is displayed.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test same-day orders and two customers. Check that filtering happens before summing and that a new partition starts again.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Specify partition, order, and frame to make a running calculation unambiguous.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: first_value and last_value read the first and last value of the current window frame. ntile splits an ordered partition into numbered groups of rows.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: These functions compare rows with a chosen endpoint or divide a ranked list into roughly equal-sized groups.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: first_value and last_value read the endpoints of the current frame in window order. Ascending price puts the minimum first; descending price puts the maximum first. To read the last row of the entire partition, use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. Otherwise the default ordered frame normally ends at the current row's equal-key group, so LAST_VALUE can return a value from the middle of the partition. NTILE(n) instead splits an ordered partition into n numbered buckets with nearly equal row counts; earlier buckets get any extra rows.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: first_value(price) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) repeats each category's maximum. Subtract the ascending first price from price to find the premium above the cheapest product. last_value(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) repeats the final order total. A WINDOW clause names a reusable definition: write first_value(hired_on) OVER w and last_value(hired_on) OVER w, then WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY hired_on,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) after FROM/WHERE and before the final ORDER BY. ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC,id) gives salary-order buckets, not four equal numeric salary ranges.
sections.code: SELECT id,first_value(price) OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS category_max FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Reuse one full window to show the cheapest and most expensive Office prices.

Office prices are 12.50 for Notebook, 2.00 for Pen, and 4.00 for Folder.

```sql
SELECT id,price,first_value(price) OVER w AS minimum_price,last_value(price) OVER w AS maximum_price FROM products WHERE category='Office' WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY price,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | price | minimum_price | maximum_price
— | — | — | —
1 | 12.50 | 2.00 | 12.50
2 | 2.00 | 2.00 | 12.50
8 | 4.00 | 2.00 | 12.50

The shared full frame gives every row the same endpoints: minimum 2.00 and maximum 12.50. ORDER BY id displays them independently of price order.
sections.code: SELECT id,first_value(price) OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS category_max FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.body: ntile(4) divides all six employees in salary/ID order into four buckets. The buckets have 2, 2, 1, and 1 rows on this dataset.
sections.code: SELECT id,ntile(4) OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC,id) AS quartile FROM employees ORDER BY id;

sections.body: The default ordered frame usually ends at the current peer group, so last_value may not mean 'last in the partition'. ntile divides rows, not value ranges, and can split equal salaries into different buckets. NULLs are not skipped.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: max() OVER can express a whole-partition maximum directly. Ranking and bucketing differ: rank preserves ties, while ntile aims for balanced row counts.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Endpoint functions follow the frame; ntile balances ordered rows, not numeric intervals.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: DISTINCT ON is a PostgreSQL feature that keeps one representative row for each group of key values. The ordering decides which row wins.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: It is a compact way to select a latest event or highest-priced item per group while keeping that row's other columns.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each key group after ordering. Its key expressions must match the leftmost ORDER BY expressions. The remaining sort keys decide which row wins: date DESC chooses the latest date, then id DESC chooses the greatest ID if dates tie. Omitting a tie-breaker can make the chosen row unpredictable. NULL keys form one group unless WHERE removes them.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id,id,ordered_on FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id,ordered_on DESC,id DESC picks the latest order of any status per customer. For the cheapest item use ORDER BY category,price,id with DISTINCT ON (category). For the highest JSON rating, extract text with attributes->>'rating', cast it to numeric, then sort that expression DESC NULLS LAST and id ascending. NULLS LAST matters: DESC otherwise puts NULL first in PostgreSQL, which could select a missing rating instead of a real score. Keep an explicit outer ORDER BY when a wrapping query needs another display order.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT ON(customer_id) customer_id,id AS order_id,ordered_on FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY customer_id,ordered_on DESC,id DESC;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Select a complete cheapest-product row for each category.

Home has Mug at 15.00 and Lamp at 45.00. Office has prices 12.50, 2.00, 4.00; Tech has 75.00, 250.00, 8.00.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT ON (category) category,id,name,price FROM products ORDER BY category,price,id;
```

**Result**

category | id | name | price
— | — | — | —
Home | 5 | Mug | 15.00
Office | 2 | Pen | 2.00
Tech | 7 | Cable | 8.00

Ordering puts the cheapest product first within each category. DISTINCT ON keeps that complete product row, leaving three rows.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT ON(customer_id) customer_id,id AS order_id,ordered_on FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY customer_id,ordered_on DESC,id DESC;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The event example applies the same rule to occurred_at, using the highest event ID to break identical timestamps.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT ON(customer_id) customer_id,id AS event_id,occurred_at FROM events ORDER BY customer_id,occurred_at DESC,id DESC;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The original syntax example chooses the latest order of any status. Customer 4’s pending order 109 therefore remains; this example does not filter to paid orders.

customer_id | order_id | ordered_on
— | — | —
1 | 108 | 2024-06-10
2 | 111 | 2024-07-04
3 | 110 | 2024-07-03
4 | 109 | 2024-07-01
5 | 107 | 2024-06-05

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: DISTINCT removes duplicate whole output rows; DISTINCT ON selects one row per key. To display chosen rows in a different overall order, wrap the selection in another query. PostgreSQL groups NULL keys together unless you filter them out.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: row_number with a filter can express a similar rule in more SQL systems. Both approaches need an explicit definition of 'first'.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check equal dates, different statuses, and NULL customers. Make sure the selected row matches the intended business rule.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Name the group keys, define the winning row, and keep the ORDER BY prefix compatible.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A view is a stored query definition that you can query by name. An ordinary view stores the definition, not a separate copy of its result rows.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A shared view keeps a reporting rule in one place instead of repeating it in every query.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE VIEW gives a SELECT a reusable name without storing its result rows. Each SELECT from the view reads current underlying data. Computed columns need clear aliases, such as price*stock AS stock_value. A view can contain joins and grouping; that makes it a reusable report but generally not an automatically writable view. To keep customers with no paid orders in a report, LEFT JOIN paid orders using the status condition in ON, then COALESCE the grouped sum to zero.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Write CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ...; then query it with SELECT ... FROM name ORDER BY .... The caller still needs its own ORDER BY. A simple view over one table can be updated through its plain column names. Append WITH LOCAL CHECK OPTION after the defining SELECT to reject inserts or updates through that view whose new row fails the view's own WHERE condition. For example, an pending_orders view filtered by status='pending' can accept a changed total but must not accept changing status to 'paid'. UPDATE view_name SET total=22.00 WHERE id=106 targets only that visible row. CREATE VIEW report(category,revenue) AS SELECT ... can instead assign the output names in parentheses.
sections.code: CREATE VIEW paid_orders AS SELECT id,customer_id,ordered_on,total FROM orders WHERE status='paid';

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Update a pending order through a filtered view, then read that view.

Orders 106 and 109 are pending, with totals 20.00 and 250.00. Other statuses are outside this view.

```sql
CREATE VIEW lesson_pending AS SELECT id,status,total FROM orders WHERE status='pending' WITH LOCAL CHECK OPTION; UPDATE lesson_pending SET total=22.00 WHERE id=106;
SELECT id,status,total FROM lesson_pending ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | status | total
— | — | —
106 | pending | 22.00
109 | pending | 250.00

Updating through the view changes order 106 to 22.00 in the base table. Both orders remain pending and visible; CHECK OPTION guards the view condition.
sections.code: CREATE VIEW paid_orders AS SELECT id,customer_id,ordered_on,total FROM orders WHERE status='paid';

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: customer_spending starts from every customer. The paid-status condition stays in the LEFT JOIN, and COALESCE changes a missing sum to zero, preserving customers without paid orders.
sections.code: CREATE VIEW customer_spending AS SELECT c.id AS customer_id,COALESCE(sum(o.total),0) AS paid_spend FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, the checker reads the created paid_orders view. The preview may show only its first rows; each caller must specify ORDER BY when order matters.

id | customer_id | ordered_on | total
— | — | — | —
101 | 1 | 2024-05-01 | 29.00
102 | 2 | 2024-05-02 | 75.00
103 | 1 | 2024-05-10 | 250.00
105 | 4 | 2024-06-01 | 90.00
107 | 5 | 2024-06-05 | 25.00
108 | 1 | 2024-06-10 | 16.00
110 | 3 | 2024-07-03 | 45.00
111 | 2 | 2024-07-04 | 75.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A view does not inherently make its query faster or guarantee a caller's row order. Privileges and row-security behavior depend on how the view is defined; do not assume it is automatically a security boundary.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A CTE names a query within one statement. A materialized view stores results and needs refresh; an ordinary view reads current underlying data under the query's snapshot.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check view columns and filters. For customer totals, confirm that customers with no paid orders remain and receive zero.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use views to reuse a query definition, and specify ordering and permissions deliberately.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A materialized view saves the rows produced by a query. Its contents stay as saved until an explicit refresh recomputes them.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A stored summary can make repeated reads cheaper when slightly old results are acceptable.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW name AS SELECT ... runs a query and stores its result rows. Later source changes do not update that stored copy. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW name reruns the whole defining query and replaces the saved rows. Refresh after the INSERT or UPDATE that the report should include. A monthly summary can group by date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date; a count summary can contain one row even when there are no matching orders.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: A normal refresh can block readers. To allow SELECT while refreshing, use REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY name. It needs an already populated materialized view and a qualifying unique index: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX index_name ON view_name(customer_id). The indexed column or column combination identifies each result row uniquely. This index must cover all rows and use column names directly, without expressions or a WHERE condition. Build the materialized view first, then its index, then refresh it. For one row per month, month_start is the natural key.
sections.code: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW category_snapshot AS SELECT category,sum(stock) AS stock_units FROM products GROUP BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Compare current product stock with a snapshot saved before the stock changed.

Product 1 starts with stock 40 and product 2 with 120. The snapshot is created before adding 5 to product 1.

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW lesson_stock AS SELECT id,stock FROM products; UPDATE products SET stock=stock+5 WHERE id=1;
SELECT p.id,p.stock AS current_stock,s.stock AS snapshot_stock FROM products p JOIN lesson_stock s ON s.id=p.id WHERE p.id IN (1,2) ORDER BY p.id;
```

**Result**

id | current_stock | snapshot_stock
— | — | —
1 | 45 | 40
2 | 120 | 120

The source now shows 45, while the saved snapshot still shows 40. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW lesson_stock would bring the saved value to 45.
sections.code: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW category_snapshot AS SELECT category,sum(stock) AS stock_units FROM products GROUP BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: customer_totals is initially populated, then receives a unique customer_id index. That full, column-only unique index makes the concurrent refresh eligible.
sections.code: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW customer_totals AS SELECT customer_id,sum(total) AS total FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id; CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customer_totals_key ON customer_totals(customer_id); REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY customer_totals;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, the checker reads category_snapshot: Home has 8 units, Office 180, and Tech 67 in Retail. The creation command itself does not return that table.

category | stock_units
— | —
Home | 8
Office | 180
Tech | 67

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A concurrent refresh requires an already populated view and a unique index on ordinary columns covering all rows. The index must use columns directly, without expressions or a WHERE clause. Only one refresh may run per materialized view at a time.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: An ordinary view reads its sources on demand; a materialized view trades freshness and storage for reusable results. Indexes can also support reads of the stored summary.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Ask when the summary was last refreshed. Check the defining query, refresh requirements, and whether callers can tolerate old results.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A materialized view is a saved result, so plan both its reads and its refresh schedule.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A set-returning function produces rows rather than one scalar value. generate_series creates a sequence of numbers or times that can serve as a query's data source.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Generated calendars let reports include days with no recorded events and expand stays into individual nights.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: generate_series(start,stop,step) supplies rows directly in FROM. With integers the step defaults to 1. Both endpoints are included when the step reaches them; generate_series(1,5) therefore gives five rows. A positive step with start greater than stop gives no rows; a zero step is an error. Dates can be passed with an interval step such as INTERVAL '1 day' or '1 month'; cast the generated value to date for a date-only report.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: FROM generate_series(0,100,20) AS s(target) creates thresholds named target. LEFT JOIN products p ON p.stock>=s.target, then GROUP BY s.target and count(p.id), keeps every threshold and counts only matched products. The same pattern creates a complete calendar: join orders to generated dates and count(o.id), not count(*), so empty dates have zero orders. For monthly revenue, put both date bounds and status='paid' in ON: ordered_on>=month_start AND ordered_on<month_start+INTERVAL '1 month'. COALESCE(sum(total),0) supplies zero for an empty month. For booking nights use CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(b.check_in,b.check_out-1,INTERVAL '1 day'): LATERAL lets each booking supply its own inclusive start and exclusive checkout boundary.

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Generate stock thresholds and count the products that reach each one.

The eight product stocks are 40, 120, 12, 5, 0, 8, 50, and 20. We want a row for each generated target: 0, 20, 40.

```sql
SELECT s.target AS target_stock,count(p.id) AS product_count FROM generate_series(0,40,20) AS s(target) LEFT JOIN products p ON p.stock>=s.target GROUP BY s.target ORDER BY s.target;
```

**Result**

target_stock | product_count
— | —
0 | 8
20 | 4
40 | 3

Every target remains in the report. Four products have at least 20 units; three have at least 40. The generated values supply the report rows.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A SQL function gives a reusable calculation or query a name, typed arguments, and a declared result type. It can then be called in SQL expressions.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A shared calculation, such as a tax rule, is easier to reuse when its inputs and result are explicit.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A SQL function declares input names and types, a return type, and a SQL body. The last query's result supplies the returned value. Dollar quotes $$ ... $$ enclose the body without requiring escapes around its string literals. Creating the function defines it; SELECT function_name(arguments) calls it. Use IMMUTABLE only when the same arguments always produce the same result independently of database contents. A function reading products or orders should instead be STABLE here: it reads a consistent snapshot within one calling statement, but later statements may see changed data.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: CREATE FUNCTION fee(amount numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT round(amount*0.05,2) $$; defines a rounded calculation. Parameters can also be used in a query: SELECT name FROM products WHERE id=pid. A unique ID gives at most one name; no matching row returns NULL. count(*) returns bigint, whereas sum(total) returns numeric and needs COALESCE(...,0) if no matches should mean zero. For a percent discount use amount*(1-percent/100). STRICT, also called RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT, makes a NULL argument produce NULL without running the body. Otherwise the body is called with NULL and its expressions decide the result.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION add_vat(amount numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT round(amount*1.20,2) $$;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Define a reusable discount function and call it for three product prices.

Products 1, 2, and 3 cost 12.50, 2.00, and 75.00. A reusable function will calculate a ten-percent discount.

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION lesson_discount(amount numeric,percent numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE STRICT AS $$ SELECT round(amount*(1-percent/100),2) $$;
SELECT id,price,lesson_discount(price,10) AS discounted FROM products WHERE id IN (1,2,3) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | price | discounted
— | — | —
1 | 12.50 | 11.25
2 | 2.00 | 1.80
3 | 75.00 | 67.50

Each call returns the price multiplied by 0.90 and rounded to two places. The stored prices remain unchanged because the function only calculates a value.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION add_vat(amount numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT round(amount*1.20,2) $$;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: product_label reads products by its pid argument. STABLE is appropriate for this table lookup; IMMUTABLE would falsely promise that a product name can never change for the same ID.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION product_label(pid integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$ SELECT name FROM products WHERE id=pid $$;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, the checker calls add_vat on product prices after creating the function: 12.50 becomes 15.00. This is a check query’s output, not direct CREATE FUNCTION output.

id | gross_price
— | —
1 | 15.00
2 | 2.40
3 | 90.00
4 | 300.00
5 | 18.00
6 | 54.00
7 | 9.60
8 | 4.80

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A wrong IMMUTABLE declaration can let the planner reuse a stale value. NULL behavior should be deliberate; RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT skips calls for NULL arguments. Elevated SECURITY DEFINER functions require careful privilege and search_path design.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Views package a relation; functions expose typed arguments and results. PL/pgSQL adds procedural steps when one SQL body is insufficient.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check input and return types, rounding, and NULL behavior. Choose volatility from what the function actually reads or changes, not from the speed you want.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Give reusable logic a clear interface and an honest volatility declaration.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: PL/pgSQL is PostgreSQL's procedural language. It adds variables, decisions, loops, and error handling around SQL statements.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Some rules need intermediate values or branches that are clearer as a short program than as one expression.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A PL/pgSQL body is a block: optional DECLARE variables, then BEGIN, statements, and END. This BEGIN starts a program block, not a transaction. RETURN ends a function with a value. IF condition THEN ... ELSIF other_condition THEN ... ELSE ... END IF; chooses the first true branch. Test IS NULL explicitly when missing input needs its own result: ordinary comparisons with NULL are not true. Give every possible path a RETURN.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Declare a variable with charge numeric; or initialize it with total integer:=0;. Assignment uses :=. SELECT expression INTO charge FROM bookings WHERE id=bid; stores a query's value in charge; unlike CREATE TABLE AS, it creates no table. Without STRICT, no matching row stores NULL and multiple matches keep only the first, so use a unique lookup key. A counted loop is FOR i IN 1..n LOOP total:=total+i; END LOOP;. Check n<1 before the loop when the required answer is zero. For a guarded ratio, return NULL when b=0, otherwise RETURN round(a/b,2);.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION stock_label(qty integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$ BEGIN IF qty=0 THEN RETURN 'empty'; ELSIF qty<10 THEN RETURN 'low'; ELSE RETURN 'ready'; END IF; END $$;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Turn three different stock levels into labels using ordered IF branches.

Notebook has stock 40, Mug has 0, and Lamp has 8. The function checks zero first, then values below ten.

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION lesson_stock_label(qty integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$ BEGIN IF qty=0 THEN RETURN 'empty'; ELSIF qty<10 THEN RETURN 'low'; ELSE RETURN 'ready'; END IF; END $$;
SELECT id,stock,lesson_stock_label(stock) AS label FROM products WHERE id IN (1,5,6) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | stock | label
— | — | —
1 | 40 | ready
5 | 0 | empty
6 | 8 | low

The first matching branch supplies each label: ready, empty, or low. Checking zero before the broader below-ten rule prevents an empty product being labelled low.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION stock_label(qty integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$ BEGIN IF qty=0 THEN RETURN 'empty'; ELSIF qty<10 THEN RETURN 'low'; ELSE RETURN 'ready'; END IF; END $$;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: booking_charge declares charge, stores a query result with SELECT ... INTO charge, then returns it. Date subtraction gives nights before multiplication by the nightly rate.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION booking_charge(bid integer) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$ DECLARE charge numeric; BEGIN SELECT (check_out-check_in)*nightly_rate INTO charge FROM bookings WHERE id=bid; RETURN charge; END $$;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, the checker calls stock_label for the products. Stock 5 and 8 gives low, 0 gives empty, and the other shown values give ready.

id | label
— | —
1 | ready
2 | ready
3 | ready
4 | low
5 | empty
6 | low
7 | ready
8 | ready

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: In this function NULL qty reaches ELSE because neither IF condition is true; a negative qty gives low. Handle such input explicitly when required. SELECT INTO without STRICT gives NULLs when no row is found and keeps only the first row when several match. Prefer a set-based query to an unnecessary loop.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A SQL function can be simpler for one calculation. PL/pgSQL BEGIN/END are block syntax, unlike SQL BEGIN/COMMIT transaction commands.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace each branch, including NULL and boundary 10. For a lookup, check the missing-row case and whether the query can return several rows.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use procedural steps when they clarify the rule, and keep blocks distinct from transactions.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A procedure is a named server-side operation invoked with CALL. Unlike a function, it is not called as a value inside SELECT.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: It can give a multi-step business operation one clear interface, such as restocking a product.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A procedure groups commands into a named operation and is invoked with CALL, rather than as an expression in SELECT. For the input-only procedures here, CREATE PROCEDURE lists typed arguments, LANGUAGE plpgsql, and a BEGIN ... END body; it has no RETURNS clause. Argument values can be used in WHERE and SET expressions. Creating the procedure does not execute it. CALL restock(1,7) supplies pid=1 and units=7 when executing the operation.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The form is CREATE PROCEDURE name(arg type,...) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN statement; ... END $$; followed by CALL name(values);. Several statements can run in one call: debit the source account, then credit the destination. For category repricing, use price=round(price*(1+percent/100),2) with a numeric percent argument and WHERE category=cat. An intentional UPDATE without WHERE changes every inventory date. A no-argument procedure still has parentheses in both definition and CALL clear_cancelled_lines();. Its body may use DELETE FROM order_items i USING orders o WHERE o.id=i.order_id AND o.status='cancelled', which removes matching lines but keeps their order headers. These exercises leave transaction boundaries to the caller.
sections.code: CREATE PROCEDURE restock(pid integer,units integer) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE products SET stock=stock+units WHERE id=pid; END $$; CALL restock(1,7);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Call a procedure to restock one product, then inspect its stored quantity.

Notebook (ID 1) starts with 40 units; Pen (ID 2) starts with 120. The call requests seven more units for ID 1.

```sql
CREATE PROCEDURE lesson_restock(pid integer,units integer) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE products SET stock=stock+units WHERE id=pid; END $$; CALL lesson_restock(1,7);
SELECT id,name,stock FROM products WHERE id IN (1,2) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | name | stock
— | — | —
1 | Notebook | 47
2 | Pen | 120

CALL executes the stored UPDATE once. Notebook now has 47 units, while Pen remains at 120 because the procedure filters by pid.
sections.code: CREATE PROCEDURE restock(pid integer,units integer) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE products SET stock=stock+units WHERE id=pid; END $$; CALL restock(1,7);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: mark_inventory_checked accepts a date and updates every inventory row. The absence of WHERE is intentional because all records need the new checked date.
sections.code: CREATE PROCEDURE mark_inventory_checked(as_of date) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE inventory SET updated_on=as_of; END $$; CALL mark_inventory_checked(DATE '2024-08-15');

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, the checker reads products after CALL and shows stock 47 for ID 1. The procedure call itself does not return those product rows.

id | stock
— | —
1 | 47
2 | 120
3 | 12
4 | 5
5 | 0
6 | 8
7 | 50
8 | 20

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A missing pid makes this UPDATE affect no rows; negative units reduce stock. Add explicit validation when the business rule requires it. Transaction control inside procedures is limited to eligible top-level CALL/DO chains and is not allowed inside an explicit transaction block; these examples leave transaction boundaries to the caller.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Functions return values in queries. Procedures describe operations; both still obey constraints and permissions.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the intended row scope and argument meaning. Compare a targeted update with the deliberate all-row inventory update.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define an operation with CREATE PROCEDURE and run it with CALL; do not assume it validates every input automatically.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A trigger runs a function automatically when a specified table event occurs. A row trigger runs once for each affected row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A shared write rule can apply even when different applications insert or update the table.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A BEFORE row trigger runs once per affected row before INSERT or UPDATE stores it. Its function has no normal arguments, RETURNS trigger, and access to NEW, the proposed row. Assigning NEW.name:=trim(NEW.name) changes that proposed value. RETURN NEW lets the operation continue with the modified row; returning NULL would skip that row. Use the trigger to transform a value, rather than issuing another UPDATE against the same row.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: First define CREATE FUNCTION clean_name() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.name:=trim(NEW.name); RETURN NEW; END $$;. Then connect it with CREATE TRIGGER name BEFORE INSERT ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION clean_name();. BEFORE UPDATE uses the same NEW mechanism, and UPDATE OF email limits the event to statements that mention email as an update target. lower(trim(NEW.email)) removes surrounding spaces before lowercasing. A timestamp or date can likewise be assigned directly to NEW.updated_on. For JSONB defaults, IF NOT (NEW.payload ? 'device') THEN NEW.payload:=NEW.payload||'{"device":"unknown"}'::jsonb; END IF; adds only a missing key while retaining existing keys. The normal INSERT or UPDATE is what fires the installed trigger.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION trim_customer_name() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.name:=trim(NEW.name); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER normalize_name BEFORE INSERT ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION trim_customer_name(); INSERT INTO customers(id,name,joined_on) VALUES(60,'  Zara  ',DATE '2024-08-01');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Let a BEFORE INSERT trigger clean a name before the new customer is stored.

The INSERT supplies customer 50 with the name “  Mira  ”, including two spaces at each end.

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION lesson_trim_name() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.name:=trim(NEW.name); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER lesson_normalize BEFORE INSERT ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION lesson_trim_name(); INSERT INTO customers(id,name,joined_on) VALUES(50,'  Mira  ',DATE '2024-08-01');
SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE id=50;
```

**Result**

id | name
— | —
50 | Mira

The BEFORE trigger trims NEW.name before storage. SELECT reads Mira without surrounding spaces; the submitted INSERT did not need to call the function itself.

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The product trigger rounds the proposed price to one decimal place before insertion. The stored numeric(10,2) value may still display two decimal digits.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION round_product_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.price:=round(NEW.price,1); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER product_round BEFORE INSERT ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION round_product_price(); INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES(60,'Clip','Office',1.26,5);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, the checker reads customers after inserting Zara as customer 60. Her name is stored without surrounding spaces; existing customers are unchanged.

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada
2 | Ben
3 | Cleo
4 | Davi
5 | Eli
6 | Fara
60 | Zara

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Returning NULL from a BEFORE row trigger skips that row's operation; RETURN NEW is important for INSERT/UPDATE. A row trigger and a statement trigger are different scopes. Avoid accidental recursion and use a constraint when it expresses a simple validity rule more directly.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A DEFAULT provides a value; a BEFORE trigger can transform a supplied value. An AFTER trigger is suited to follow-up recording after a successful row operation.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the stored value, not just the submitted INSERT text. Confirm the trigger's timing, event, scope, and return value.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use BEFORE row triggers for deliberate row transformation, and return the row that should be stored.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An audit trigger records what changed in a separate history table. For an update, it can keep the old and new values side by side.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A change history helps explain price adjustments or record newly added customers.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: An AFTER row trigger can copy an operation's result into a separate audit table. INSERT provides NEW; DELETE provides OLD, the deleted row; UPDATE provides both OLD and NEW. For example, an update can record NEW.id, OLD.price, and NEW.price side by side. An AFTER trigger's return value is ignored, so RETURN NULL does not cancel the stored change. The audit insert belongs to the same transaction: rolling back the original operation also rolls back its history row.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Create the audit table, then a RETURNS trigger function whose body inserts the chosen OLD/NEW fields, then CREATE TRIGGER name AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION function_name();. Use AFTER INSERT with NEW for new customers and AFTER DELETE with OLD for removed events or order lines. UPDATE OF stock means stock appeared in SET, even when SET stock=stock leaves its value unchanged. To log only genuine changes, put IF OLD.stock IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.stock THEN INSERT INTO audit_table VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.stock,NEW.stock); END IF; inside the function. IS DISTINCT FROM treats two NULLs as unchanged and one NULL versus a value as changed.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE price_audit(product_id integer,old_price numeric,new_price numeric); CREATE FUNCTION audit_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO price_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); RETURN NULL; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER price_history AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_price(); UPDATE products SET price=price+2 WHERE id=1;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Record both sides of a price change in a separate history table.

Product 1 costs 12.50. An audit table and AFTER UPDATE trigger are installed before increasing its price by 2.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lesson_price_audit(product_id integer,old_price numeric(10,2),new_price numeric(10,2)); CREATE FUNCTION lesson_audit_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO lesson_price_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); RETURN NULL; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER lesson_price_history AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION lesson_audit_price(); UPDATE products SET price=price+2 WHERE id=1;
SELECT product_id,old_price,new_price FROM lesson_price_audit ORDER BY product_id;
```

**Result**

product_id | old_price | new_price
— | — | —
1 | 12.50 | 14.50

One changed product produces one history row showing both 12.50 and 14.50. The original update and the audit row succeed or roll back together.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE price_audit(product_id integer,old_price numeric,new_price numeric); CREATE FUNCTION audit_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO price_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); RETURN NULL; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER price_history AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_price(); UPDATE products SET price=price+2 WHERE id=1;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The customer example uses AFTER INSERT to copy the inserted ID and name. INSERT has NEW but no old customer row to record.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_audit(customer_id integer,name text); CREATE FUNCTION audit_customer_insert() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO customer_audit VALUES(NEW.id,NEW.name); RETURN NULL; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER customer_insertion AFTER INSERT ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_customer_insert(); INSERT INTO customers(id,name,joined_on) VALUES(61,'Yara',DATE '2024-08-01');

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
For the original syntax example, the checker reads one price_audit entry for product 1, from 12.50 to 14.50. The audit insert and the original update share the same transaction.

product_id | old_price | new_price
— | — | —
1 | 12.50 | 14.50

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: UPDATE OF price can fire even for SET price=price. To record only actual changes in another design, compare OLD.price IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.price. Rollback also removes transactional audit rows, so this is not a permanent log of failed attempts. Production history needs access rules and retention.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: BEFORE can alter the row being written; AFTER can record the result. IS DISTINCT FROM compares changes safely when values may be NULL.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the old/new pair and the audit row count. Distinguish a column mentioned in UPDATE from a value that really changed.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Audit deliberate events with OLD and NEW, and remember that this history shares the transaction's outcome.
