sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Full-text search finds words and related word forms in documents. PostgreSQL first reduces words to searchable forms called lexemes.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Use it for articles or help pages when matching different forms of a word is more useful than finding an exact substring.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: to_tsvector('english', body) turns a document into searchable word forms. A tsquery describes what to find, and @@ checks the match. Use the same language rules on both sides. plainto_tsquery treats several words as requirements joined by AND. phraseto_tsquery also keeps their order and positions.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: websearch_to_tsquery accepts familiar search text: SQL -tuning means SQL must occur and tuning must not. setweight(vector,'A') labels words from an important field; label body words B and join the vectors with ||. Weights preserve where words came from and can later affect ranking. A plain @@ test still checks the matching words, not a relevance score.
sections.code: SELECT id,title FROM documents WHERE to_tsvector('english',body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english','SQL') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Search the document bodies and show the match decision before filtering rows.

Retail has three documents. The first body mentions SQL, the second discusses indexes, and the third discusses plants. Search body, not title.

```sql
SELECT id,title,to_tsvector('english',body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english','SQL') AS matches FROM documents ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | title | matches
— | — | —
1 | SQL guide | t
2 | PostgreSQL tuning | f
3 | Garden notes | f

The Boolean column shows the test for every document. Only row 1 matches. Putting this expression in WHERE would keep that row and remove the others.
sections.code: SELECT id,title FROM documents WHERE to_tsvector('english',body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english','SQL') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: phraseto_tsquery searches for SQL queries in that order, accounting for word positions. This is narrower than requiring both words anywhere in a document.
sections.code: SELECT id,title FROM documents WHERE to_tsvector('english',body) @@ phraseto_tsquery('english','SQL queries') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example contains only SQL guide on Retail. Its id and title are shown, not its internal search vector.

id | title
— | —
1 | SQL guide

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: ILIKE matches character patterns; full-text search uses language rules and can remove common words. A search configuration must suit the document language.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare LIKE and regular expressions with word-based search. For larger collections, GIN can index prepared tsvector values; ranking is a separate calculation.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test a single word, several words, and a phrase. Check which column is searched before deciding that a missing match is an error.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Prepare the document and search with matching language rules, then use @@ to test each document.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An index is an extra structure that helps PostgreSQL find rows. A B-tree supports equality, ranges, and ordered access; a Hash index supports equality.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Indexes can reduce the rows a query must inspect. They also consume storage and add work to inserts, updates, and deletes.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A B-tree can find equal values, ranges and ordered values. A Hash index supports equality. Write CREATE INDEX name ON table USING method(columns). A multi-column B-tree stores keys in their declared order. Give an individual key DESC when the intended ordering needs it.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The orders example uses customer_id first, then ordered_on. For one status followed by newest orders, use a status key followed by descending date and id keys. Count matching rows before assuming an index will help: count(*) FILTER (WHERE condition) counts matches while another count(*) counts all input rows. A low matching fraction often favors index access, but PostgreSQL chooses the plan. An ordinary index does not replace the primary key; Hash indexes cannot enforce uniqueness.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_date ON orders USING btree(customer_id,ordered_on);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Add an index, then run an ordinary price lookup against the same product rows.

Notebook costs 12.50, Pen 2.00, Keyboard 75.00 and Mug 15.00. An index on price gives the database an additional way to find cheap products.

```sql
CREATE INDEX lesson_price_lookup ON products USING btree(price);
SELECT id,name,price FROM products WHERE price<20 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;
```

**Result**

id | name | price
— | — | —
1 | Notebook | 12.50
2 | Pen | 2.00
5 | Mug | 15.00

The result still contains ordinary product rows. Creating an index changes an access structure, so this query's meaning and values stay the same. LIMIT keeps this illustration short.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_date ON orders USING btree(customer_id,ordered_on);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The reporting query counts products below 20 and all products together. Comparing these counts shows how much of the table that condition selects.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) FILTER(WHERE price<20) AS matching_rows,count(*) AS total_rows FROM products;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example's verification shows the btree method and its two key columns. CREATE INDEX itself returns a command status, not this table.

amname | key1 | key2
— | — | —
btree | customer_id | ordered_on

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A sequential scan can be sensible on a small table. A multicolumn B-tree is usually most effective when conditions constrain its leading columns, though other access strategies exist.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Connect indexes with WHERE, ORDER BY, and EXPLAIN. An ordinary index speeds access; a unique index also enforces a uniqueness rule.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the method and column order, then reason about the matching fraction. Do not use tiny-fixture timings as evidence of a production speedup.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose an index for actual lookup conditions and ordering needs, then confirm the planner's choice with a plan.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Index methods solve different search problems. GIN finds components inside collections; GiST supports searches such as range overlap; BRIN summarizes neighboring table pages.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A JSON containment query and a date-range overlap query need different kinds of information. One index method cannot efficiently serve every operator.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Choose the method for the condition you need. GIN can index JSONB components and array elements. GiST can index date ranges for overlap tests. BRIN stores summaries for groups of nearby table pages and is useful when values tend to follow physical storage order. The operator class supplies the matching rules for a type.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Use USING gin(attributes) for a JSONB column or USING gin(tags) for an array. A range expression can be indexed as USING gist(daterange(check_in,check_out,'[)')); [) includes check-in and excludes checkout. For BRIN, WITH (pages_per_range=4) makes one summary cover four pages. Smaller ranges mean more summaries, not an automatic speed improvement.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX products_attributes_gin ON products USING gin(attributes);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Index product tags and inspect the products containing the usb tag.

Keyboard has tags {usb,work}, Monitor has {display,work}, and Cable has {usb}. The GIN index stores information about these array elements.

```sql
CREATE INDEX lesson_tags_gin ON products USING gin(tags);
SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE tags @> ARRAY['usb'] ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | name
— | —
3 | Keyboard
7 | Cable

@> asks whether tags contains usb, so Keyboard and Cable remain. The index can support this condition while the selected product rows keep their usual meaning.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX products_attributes_gin ON products USING gin(attributes);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The BRIN example summarizes occurred_at across page ranges. It is especially useful on large tables when nearby rows tend to have nearby timestamps.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX events_time_brin ON events USING brin(occurred_at);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example's verification identifies a gin index on attributes. It confirms the definition, not a speedup for every query.

amname | key1
— | —
gin | attributes

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A matching method is only a starting point. BRIN may still inspect many rows; GIN can be costly to update; supported operators vary by operator class.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Use GiST with range overlap, GIN with arrays or JSONB, and EXPLAIN to see whether a specific query can use the index.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Match each index to its intended operator. Consider table size, value order, and update frequency before comparing access methods.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose the search operation first, then an index method and operator class that support it.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A partial index stores only qualifying rows. An expression index stores a calculated search key. INCLUDE stores extra columns alongside the key.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: These options tailor indexes to frequent queries, such as pending orders, case-normalized email searches, or reports needing a few extra values.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A partial index contains only rows that satisfy its WHERE condition. An expression index stores a calculated key, such as lower(email). INCLUDE stores additional values alongside the search keys. These extra columns can help supply output but do not become search keys.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Write CREATE INDEX name ON table(key) INCLUDE(extra_column) WHERE condition, using the parts you need. For a JSONB text lookup, put the expression in an extra pair of parentheses: ((attributes->>'color')). A query must match the indexed expression, and PostgreSQL must be able to establish a partial index's condition. Indexed expressions must use immutable calculations, which return the same result for the same inputs.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_pending_date ON orders(ordered_on) WHERE status='pending';

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
A partial index covers available products; the query still decides which rows belong in the result.

Mug costs 15.00 but has stock 0. Notebook, Pen, Cable and Folder cost less than 20 and have stock available.

```sql
CREATE INDEX lesson_available_price ON products(price) WHERE stock>0;
SELECT id,name,price FROM products WHERE stock>0 AND price<20 ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | name | price
— | — | —
1 | Notebook | 12.50
2 | Pen | 2.00
7 | Cable | 8.00
8 | Folder | 4.00

The query states stock>0, so every qualifying row belongs in the partial index. Mug is excluded by the business condition, regardless of whether the planner uses that index.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_pending_date ON orders(ordered_on) WHERE status='pending';

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The covering index searches by customer_id and also stores total and ordered_on. These included columns can avoid table reads when visibility information allows it.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_cover ON orders(customer_id) INCLUDE(total,ordered_on);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example's verification shows ordered_on as the key and the pending-status condition. It describes an index, not order rows.

key1 | predicate
— | —
ordered_on | (status = 'pending'::text)

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: INCLUDE does not guarantee an index-only scan. The planner may not prove a partial condition from a parameter, and a different expression may not match an expression index.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare a search key with an included value. Relate index-only scans to VACUUM's visibility information and partial indexes to Boolean conditions.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Read each query and index side by side. Check the filter, expression, key order, and which selected columns are actually covered.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Specialized indexes help only when their definitions match the workload; every extra column also has a storage and write cost.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A query plan describes how PostgreSQL intends to produce a result. Its nodes are operations such as scanning, sorting, joining, and grouping.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: EXPLAIN helps you see where work is planned before guessing which index or rewrite might help.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: EXPLAIN goes before the statement you want to inspect. Its output describes operations such as Scan, Filter, Sort, Aggregate, Join and WindowAgg. Child operations supply rows to their parents. Costs and row counts are estimates. A cost is a planning unit, not elapsed milliseconds.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) hides estimated costs and leaves the plan structure. The SELECT after it can use the joins, EXISTS, grouping or window functions already learned. A filter can appear inside a scan, GROUP BY may require an aggregate node, and row_number() needs window processing. Read each node as work done to produce the requested result. Plain EXPLAIN normally plans the statement without running it.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE price>50;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Read the rows first, then distinguish their result from the plan that would produce them.

The only Retail prices above 50 are Keyboard at 75.00 and Monitor at 250.00. First establish what the query is supposed to return.

```sql
SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE price>50 ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | name
— | —
3 | Keyboard
4 | Monitor

This SELECT returns two rows. Add EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) before the SELECT to inspect the operations used to find them. That command returns a plan instead of these data rows, and its exact shape can vary.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE price>50;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The grouped-revenue example adds aggregation by status. Find the scan that supplies orders and the node that combines rows into status totals.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT status,sum(total) FROM orders GROUP BY status;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example is a plan containing Seq Scan and a price filter. The small table makes this a reasonable choice; another dataset may produce a different plan.

QUERY PLAN
—
Seq Scan on products
  Filter: (price > '50'::numeric)

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Do not treat every sequential scan as a problem. Plan shape may change with data, statistics, settings, or PostgreSQL versions.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Connect scans to indexes, row estimates to ANALYZE statistics, and plan trees to the logical operations in SELECT.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: For each plan, identify the data source, filter, and any sort or aggregate. Explain what each node contributes to the final result.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Read a plan as a flow of rows, and distinguish an estimated plan from measured execution.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs a statement and reports what its plan actually did, including returned rows and execution counts.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Actual measurements help you discover where estimated row counts were wrong or unexpectedly much work occurred.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. Its plan includes actual rows and loops, the number of times an operation ran. For repeated operations, actual rows is the average per loop. Compare that observed work with estimates when estimates are displayed.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF) before the SELECT in these tasks. ANALYZE runs it, TIMING OFF removes per-node timing, SUMMARY OFF removes the final summary, and COSTS OFF removes estimates. PostgreSQL 18 also reports buffers by default with ANALYZE. These options make the report easier to compare, but they do not stop execution or make every plan shape universal.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF) SELECT id FROM products WHERE stock=0;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Establish the result of a stock filter before measuring that query.

Mug, product 5, has stock 0. All other Retail products have a positive stock value.

```sql
SELECT id FROM products WHERE stock=0 ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id
—
5

The data query returns one row. Wrapping it with the lesson's EXPLAIN ANALYZE options executes that same filter and reports the work needed to find the row. Use actual row counts as evidence and avoid relying on a particular timing.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF) SELECT id FROM products WHERE stock=0;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The order-item example counts every input row into one result. Distinguish the scan's input count from the aggregate's single output row.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM order_items;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example reports one zero-stock product and seven rejected rows on Retail. Buffers describes page access; its exact counts can vary.

QUERY PLAN
—
Seq Scan on products (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
  Filter: (stock = 0)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 7
  Buffers: shared hit=1
Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=80

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: ANALYZE on UPDATE or DELETE really changes data. A rollback can undo ordinary database changes, but not every possible external or sequence side effect.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Unlike the standalone ANALYZE maintenance command, EXPLAIN ANALYZE measures execution. BUFFERS describes page activity rather than just elapsed time.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Read rows and loops together. Compare where rows enter, are removed, and leave each operation without relying on identical timing or buffer counts.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use measured plans to explain work, remembering that collecting measurements executes the statement.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A useful optimization changes how a query does its work while preserving what the result means: its rows, duplicates, NULLs, and required order.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A report is only useful when it remains correct. Improve unnecessary work after defining who and what must appear.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Before rewriting, state what one result row means and how unmatched rows and NULLs must behave. Keep an outer join's match restriction in ON when you still need unmatched left rows. EXISTS tests whether a match exists without multiplying the outer rows.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: For a zero-inclusive customer count, LEFT JOIN paid orders and count(o.id), not count(*). For customers without a kind of order, correlate NOT EXISTS by customer_id. For a calendar day or month, use >= start AND < next_start directly on the date/timestamp column. These rewrites preserve the requested meaning and can make useful access paths available. Measure a plan before claiming a speedup.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id,count(o.id) AS paid_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Compare a customer with paid orders and a customer with none.

Customer 1 has three paid orders. Customer 6 has none. Both customers belong in this report.

```sql
SELECT c.id,count(o.id) AS paid_orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' WHERE c.id IN(1,6) GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id;
```

**Result**

id | paid_orders
— | —
1 | 3
6 | 0

The paid condition limits matches inside ON. The preserved customer 6 has no order id to count, so count(o.id) gives zero. A paid filter in WHERE would remove that customer's row.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id,count(o.id) AS paid_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The June example uses a lower date bound and an exclusive July bound. This captures one month's dates without applying a function to each stored date.
sections.code: SELECT id,ordered_on FROM orders WHERE ordered_on>=DATE '2024-06-01' AND ordered_on<DATE '2024-07-01' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
In the result of the syntax example, Fara remains with paid_count=0. Preserving her row is part of correctness, not an optional display detail.

customer_id | paid_count
— | —
1 | 3
2 | 2
3 | 1
4 | 1
5 | 1
6 | 0

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Moving filters across an outer join can change its meaning. An index-friendly condition does not guarantee a faster plan on every dataset.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Relate this work to LEFT JOIN, EXISTS, NULL handling, and date ranges. Equivalent results must be established before comparing execution costs.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check missing customers, repeated matches, boundary dates, and NULLs. Only then investigate whether a rewrite reduces work.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Preserve the report's rules first; use plans and realistic data to justify performance changes.

exercises.prompt: Return id and name of customers who have no pending orders. Use NOT EXISTS so a guest order with customer_id NULL cannot poison the condition. Order by id.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: PostgreSQL uses statistics to estimate how many rows a condition will match. ANALYZE refreshes these summaries from table data.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Good estimates help the planner choose scans and joins. A common value and a rare value may justify different plans.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ANALYZE reads table data to update planner statistics. CREATE STATISTICS defines additional summaries across columns, then ANALYZE fills them. dependencies describes relationships between columns, ndistinct estimates the number of different combinations, and mcv records common combinations of values.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Write CREATE STATISTICS name (dependencies, ndistinct) ON column1, column2 FROM table, selecting the kinds requested, then run ANALYZE table. Exact report counts still use GROUP BY and count(*). To turn a group count into a share, divide count(*)::numeric by (SELECT count(*) FROM the_same_table), then round to the requested scale. The numeric cast preserves fractions.
sections.code: ANALYZE products; SELECT category,count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Refresh planner statistics without changing the product counts.

Retail has eight products split between Home, Office and Tech. ANALYZE refreshes the planner's summaries without changing those products.

```sql
ANALYZE products;
SELECT category,count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;
```

**Result**

category | product_count
— | —
Home | 2
Office | 3
Tech | 3

The SELECT counts actual rows, giving 2, 3 and 3. These exact report counts should be distinguished from the estimates a planner may derive from statistics.
sections.code: ANALYZE products; SELECT category,count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The status report divides each status count by the total number of orders. Casting to numeric preserves a fractional share before rounding.
sections.code: SELECT status,count(*) AS order_count,round(count(*)::numeric/(SELECT count(*) FROM orders),4) AS share FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example counts two Home, three Office, and three Tech products in Retail. These are exact grouped counts, not planner estimates.

category | product_count
— | —
Home | 2
Office | 3
Tech | 3

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Statistics can become stale after major changes and estimates need not be exact. Raising the statistics target adds analysis work and does not repair incorrect SQL.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare estimated rows in EXPLAIN with real counts. ANALYZE updates planner information; VACUUM handles old row versions and can optionally run ANALYZE too.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Inspect distributions and consider whether columns are related. Verify extended-statistics definitions separately from whether a particular plan uses them.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Refresh statistics after meaningful data changes, and treat planner row counts as estimates rather than guarantees.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: PostgreSQL can keep older row versions while other transactions still need them. VACUUM removes versions that are no longer needed and makes space reusable.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Frequent updates and deletes leave cleanup work behind. Maintenance also prevents transaction-ID wraparound and supports efficient visibility checks.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: VACUUM makes space from old, no-longer-needed row versions reusable and helps mark pages visible to all transactions. VACUUM (ANALYZE) also refreshes planner statistics. Run VACUUM as its own statement outside BEGIN…COMMIT. Ordinary VACUUM usually allows reading and writing, while VACUUM FULL rewrites the table with a stronger lock.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The inspection tasks use pg_class c for tables and pg_namespace n for schemas: join n.oid=c.relnamespace, filter n.nspname=current_schema() and c.relkind='r' for ordinary tables, and select c.relname as the table name. c.relpersistence::text gives p (permanent), u (unlogged), or t (temporary). For primary keys, join pg_constraint k ON k.conrelid=c.oid, filter k.contype='p', and use cardinality(k.conkey) to count key columns. An unlogged table is not crash-safe like a permanent table; a temporary table belongs to its session. current_setting('temp_file_limit') and current_setting('autovacuum') return the controlled server's settings as text. They are observations, not recommended production defaults.
sections.code: VACUUM (ANALYZE) products;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Maintain the table, then check that its current product rows remain.

The starting products table has eight current rows. Cleaning old versions must preserve these rows.

```sql
VACUUM products;
SELECT count(*) AS product_count FROM products;
```

**Result**

product_count
—
8

The count is still eight after VACUUM. The command performs storage maintenance rather than deleting current products. Its physical page effects are inspected separately by the exercise checker.
sections.code: VACUUM (ANALYZE) products;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The catalog query reports each current-schema table's persistence code. Ordinary, unlogged, and temporary tables have different durability and lifetime rules.
sections.code: SELECT c.relname AS table_name,c.relpersistence::text AS persistence FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname=current_schema() AND c.relkind='r' ORDER BY c.relname;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example's verification shows an estimate of eight product rows and visible-page information on Retail. t means true; VACUUM itself does not return this table.

estimated_rows | has_visible_pages
— | —
8 | t

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Ordinary VACUUM usually reuses space rather than fully shrinking the file. Long-running transactions can delay cleanup; VACUUM cannot run inside BEGIN…COMMIT.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Connect cleanup to MVCC and index-only scans. ANALYZE describes data for planning; it does not replace removal of obsolete row versions.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Keep maintenance commands standalone. Distinguish row estimates, visibility information, and table persistence from the business values stored in rows.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Maintain changing tables regularly; use ordinary VACUUM, statistics, and monitoring together rather than assuming deletion immediately frees disk space.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Performance troubleshooting means finding evidence for why a query is slow, rather than changing SQL at random.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: The same query can behave differently with larger data, uneven value frequencies, cached pages, or competing work.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Start with the requested result and the number of input rows. Check whether joins multiply rows, whether filtering happens before the intended grouping, and whether the report includes the right order statuses. Then inspect the plan and compare estimates with actual rows using representative data.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: A few grouped counts often explain the workload: GROUP BY with HAVING finds repeated values or products appearing on several lines. count(*) counts lines, while sum(quantity) counts units. To estimate a Cartesian result without building it, calculate one count per table in two subqueries and multiply those counts. Keep calculated prices and revenue at the requested level so joined rows are counted once.
sections.code: SELECT customer_id,count(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY order_count DESC,customer_id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Estimate a cross join from two small counts instead of constructing every pair.

The starting fixture contains six customers and eight products. Pairing every customer with every product would produce one row for each possible pair.

```sql
SELECT c.n AS customer_rows,p.n AS product_rows,c.n*p.n AS possible_pairs FROM (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM customers) c CROSS JOIN (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM products) p;
```

**Result**

customer_rows | product_rows | possible_pairs
— | — | —
6 | 8 | 48

The two one-row counts combine into one result row. Their product is 48, so the query estimates the Cartesian row count without materializing those 48 pairs.
sections.code: SELECT customer_id,count(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY order_count DESC,customer_id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The repeated-price query groups products by price and keeps groups with more than one row. On another dataset it can reveal duplicates absent from the basic fixture.
sections.code: SELECT price,count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY price HAVING count(*)>1 ORDER BY price;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example shows one to three orders per known customer on Retail. These counts describe the data, not query speed.

customer_id | order_count
— | —
1 | 3
2 | 3
3 | 2
4 | 2
5 | 1

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: One quick run does not establish a speedup. Include planning overhead, page-cache effects, current load, and representative parameter values in comparisons.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, statistics, and index knowledge together. Keep business correctness checks separate from performance measurements.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Explain what each diagnostic count tells you. Form a specific hypothesis before proposing an index or rewrite.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Measure a defined workload, identify the expensive work, and verify both speed and unchanged results after a targeted change.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A transaction groups changes into one unit. ACID stands for atomicity (all or nothing), consistency (preserving defined rules), isolation (controlled interaction with concurrent work), and durability (committed data survives a crash under normal durability settings).

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A transfer should not debit one account while leaving the credit undone. Readers also need a predictable view when other transactions change data.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A snapshot is the set of committed row versions a query can see. At READ COMMITTED, each statement starts with a fresh snapshot, so a second SELECT may see another transaction's newly committed change. REPEATABLE READ keeps the snapshot established by the first non-transaction-control statement for the rest of the transaction. SERIALIZABLE additionally detects combinations of concurrent work that could not happen in a serial order; PostgreSQL may cancel one transaction, so the application must retry the whole transaction. This single-session workspace teaches the syntax; it does not simulate another concurrent reader or writer.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; starts a transaction with that isolation level; use SERIALIZABLE in the same position when requested. Debit one account and credit the other by the same numeric amount, then COMMIT both changes together. ROLLBACK discards all changes in the transaction. SAVEPOINT draft; records an intermediate point: ROLLBACK TO draft; removes changes after that point while preserving earlier work for COMMIT. SELECT current_setting('transaction_isolation') AS isolation_level; reports the active level. Isolation does not replace constraints or checking that a transfer preserves the total balance.
sections.code: SELECT current_setting('transaction_isolation') AS isolation_level;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Cancel both sides of a draft transfer and inspect the balances afterward.

Before the draft transfer, account 1 has 1000.00 and account 2 has 500.00. The following transaction moves 10 between them, then cancels that draft.

```sql
BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-10 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+10 WHERE id=2; ROLLBACK;
SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN(1,2) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | balance
— | —
1 | 1000.00
2 | 500.00

Both balances return to their original values. ROLLBACK cancels the debit and the credit together; the total remains 1500.00.
sections.code: SELECT current_setting('transaction_isolation') AS isolation_level;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The SERIALIZABLE example starts a transaction, subtracts 5 from account 2, then rolls back. The balance change is discarded.
sections.code: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-5 WHERE id=2; ROLLBACK;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example is read committed. One session cannot demonstrate what a competing session sees during a transaction.

isolation_level
—
read committed

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: SERIALIZABLE can abort a transaction to prevent inconsistent concurrent outcomes; retry the whole transaction. PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED, and constraints remain necessary at every level.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Relate snapshots to old row versions and VACUUM. Isolation controls concurrent visibility; atomicity controls whether a transaction's changes succeed together.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Predict balances after COMMIT and ROLLBACK. Use the written concurrency scenario to compare snapshots; actual competing sessions are outside this workspace.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose transaction boundaries and isolation deliberately, preserve data rules, and handle failures with a whole-transaction recovery policy.

exercises.title: Explain two reads and one concurrent commit
exercises.prompt: A transaction reads an account balance. Another transaction commits a new balance. The first transaction reads the balance again. Explain the possible result under READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ, and explain why a SERIALIZABLE application still needs retry logic. This written answer is self-assessed against a model explanation.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT true AS discussed;
hints: Separate a statement snapshot from a transaction snapshot.
Consider whether the second SELECT obtains a new snapshot.
Distinguish isolation guarantees from a promise that every transaction will commit.
exercises.explanation: Read your answer against the model, identify missing points, and mark it reviewed when you can explain the distinction in your own words.
exercises.modelAnswer: Under READ COMMITTED, each statement obtains a new snapshot. The second SELECT can see the newly committed balance. Under REPEATABLE READ, both reads use the transaction snapshot, so a newly committed external change is not visible to the second read. SERIALIZABLE adds protection against serialization anomalies, but PostgreSQL can abort a transaction with a serialization failure. The application must retry the entire transaction, with bounded retry policy and no duplicated external side effects.

lessons.title: Row locks, NOWAIT, and SKIP LOCKED

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A row lock coordinates transactions that want to change the same row. SELECT … FOR UPDATE reads rows and locks them against conflicting changes.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Locking is useful when a decision and the following update must be based on protected rows, such as checking accounts before a transfer.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows against conflicting changes until the transaction ends. An ordinary SELECT can usually still read their earlier committed versions. NOWAIT reports a lock conflict immediately; SKIP LOCKED omits rows that cannot be locked immediately. Skipping is useful for workers claiming queue items, but it cannot provide a complete account report. In this isolated workspace no other transaction competes for the rows, so the exercises demonstrate clauses rather than actual waiting.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Place the lock clause after WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY ordered_on,id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;. The final id breaks date ties. FOR NO KEY UPDATE allows more concurrency than FOR UPDATE when a change will not alter a key used by foreign keys. FOR KEY SHARE is weaker: it protects against deletion and key-changing updates, while allowing non-key updates. Add NOWAIT or SKIP LOCKED after the chosen mode. For a real read-then-update workflow, put both statements in BEGIN ... COMMIT; without an explicit transaction the lock ends with this statement.
sections.code: SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN(1,2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Read two balances under row locks without changing either value.

Accounts 1 and 2 contain 1000.00 and 500.00. No competing transaction is running.

```sql
SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN(1,2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
```

**Result**

id | balance
— | —
1 | 1000.00
2 | 500.00

The query reads and locks these two rows without changing either balance. In autocommit mode the locks are released when the statement finishes.
sections.code: SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN(1,2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The queue example takes the oldest pending order by date and id. LIMIT 1 bounds the claim; SKIP LOCKED lets another worker choose a different available row.
sections.code: SELECT id,total FROM orders WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY ordered_on,id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example shows the original balances of accounts 1 and 2. With no competing session there is no waiting or skipped row to observe.

id | balance
— | —
1 | 1000.00
2 | 500.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: SKIP LOCKED omits rows, so it is unsuitable for a complete financial report. NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED affect row locks; required table locks can still wait. An autocommitted statement releases locks when its transaction ends.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare row locks with MVCC snapshots and table locks. FOR KEY SHARE is a weaker row-lock mode useful for protecting referenced keys.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the selected rows and lock clause. Explain the difference between waiting, failing immediately, and skipping; this single-operation workspace cannot demonstrate competing workers.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Lock only the rows needed, keep transactions short, and choose waiting behavior that matches the application.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A deadlock is a cycle of transactions waiting for one another's locks. A connection pool reuses database connections instead of opening a new one for every request.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Consistent lock order reduces deadlock risk. A pool limits connection overhead and load, but does not remove transaction failures or data-consistency requirements.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A deadlock is a cycle: each transaction holds a lock another one needs. PostgreSQL cancels one participant to break the cycle. Acquire shared resources in the same order, keep transactions short, and retry the entire transaction after a deadlock or serialization failure, with a bounded number of attempts and a delay. A connection pool reuses connections. With transaction pooling, the next transaction may use another connection, so request-specific state must not depend on a previous session.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=3 FOR UPDATE; locks 1 before 3. Follow with equal debit/credit updates and COMMIT. SET LOCAL application_name='practice'; changes a setting only until that transaction ends; current_setting('application_name') reads it. CREATE TABLE session_observation(value text); INSERT INTO session_observation SELECT current_setting('application_name'); stores the observed value. A retry-safe debit also needs a unique request ID: WITH accepted AS (INSERT INTO requests ... ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING RETURNING account_id,amount) UPDATE accounts a SET balance=a.balance-x.amount FROM accepted x WHERE a.id=x.account_id;. A repeated ID returns no accepted row, so the UPDATE does nothing. The request record and debit must commit together; rejecting reused IDs with different payloads is a further application responsibility.
sections.code: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=3 FOR UPDATE; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-15 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+15 WHERE id=3; COMMIT;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Send one debit request twice and let its unique key prevent a second debit.

Account 1 starts with 1000.00. The same request ID, 1, asks twice to debit 30.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lesson_requests(id integer PRIMARY KEY,account_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),amount numeric NOT NULL CHECK(amount>0)); BEGIN; WITH accepted AS (INSERT INTO lesson_requests VALUES(1,1,30) ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING RETURNING account_id,amount) UPDATE accounts a SET balance=a.balance-x.amount FROM accepted x WHERE a.id=x.account_id; WITH accepted AS (INSERT INTO lesson_requests VALUES(1,1,30) ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING RETURNING account_id,amount) UPDATE accounts a SET balance=a.balance-x.amount FROM accepted x WHERE a.id=x.account_id; COMMIT;
SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id=1;
```

**Result**

id | balance
— | —
1 | 970.00

The first insert supplies a row to UPDATE. The second conflicts with the primary key and supplies none. The account loses 30 once, leaving 970.00.
sections.code: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=3 FOR UPDATE; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-15 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+15 WHERE id=3; COMMIT;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The second transfer moves 20 from account 1 to 2 together. The total across accounts must remain unchanged.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-20 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+20 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example's verification shows committed balances 985, 500, and 765. It inspects the completed transfer, not intermediate lock-reading output.

id | balance
— | —
1 | 985.00
2 | 500.00
3 | 765.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Retrying only the last failed command is unsafe. Transaction pooling may use another server connection next time, so do not rely on persistent session settings or temporary tables.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Use transaction-local settings for transaction-scoped behavior. An idempotency key prevents a retried request from applying the same business operation twice.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace lock order and account totals. For retry exercises, check that a repeated request cannot debit again and that local settings end with the transaction.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Short transactions, consistent lock order, bounded retries, and repeat-safe writes solve different parts of reliable concurrent work.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A role is a PostgreSQL identity. It can own objects and receive permissions; LOGIN allows it to open a database session.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Least privilege means granting only what each job needs. A reporting account, for example, usually needs to read selected tables rather than administer the server.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A role is a database identity. Ownership gives the right to manage an object; grants give particular rights such as SELECT. PUBLIC means all roles, not the public schema. REVOKE removes the named grant, but access may remain through ownership or another role. To read a table, a role generally needs USAGE on its schema and SELECT on the table. CREATE on a schema allows creating objects there. The practice role owns its isolated exercise tables but cannot become a server administrator.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: SELECT has_table_privilege(current_user,'products','SELECT') AS can_select; checks effective table access. has_schema_privilege(current_user,'public','USAGE') and the same call with 'CREATE' check schema rights. REVOKE ALL ON products FROM PUBLIC; removes public grants, preserving ownership. pg_roles exposes role properties: rolname is the role name; rolsuper, rolcreaterole, rolcreatedb, rolcanlogin, rolbypassrls, and rolreplication are Boolean flags. Filter WHERE rolname=current_user and alias only the fields requested. These flags describe administrative capabilities; they are different from permission to SELECT one table.
sections.code: SELECT has_table_privilege(current_user,'products','SELECT') AS can_select;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Check one specific right held by the current learner role.

The learner role owns the products table in its isolated database.

```sql
SELECT has_table_privilege(current_user,'products','SELECT') AS can_select;
```

**Result**

can_select
—
t

The result t means true: this role can read products. It does not imply superuser status or access to other databases.

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: REVOKE ALL ON products FROM PUBLIC removes public grants on that table. It does not transfer ownership or remove rights inherited through another role.
sections.code: REVOKE ALL ON products FROM PUBLIC;

sections.title: Expected results

The result of the syntax example is t: the current role can SELECT from products. This does not give it administrative rights.

can_select

t

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Removing one grant may leave access through another role or ownership. Schema USAGE and table permissions are separate. These permissions do not give access to files on the server.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare permission to ownership and RLS. The learner role is intentionally unable to create privileged roles, administer the server, or install unrestricted extensions.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Inspect specific privileges and administrative flags. Explain which permission source is changed by REVOKE before assuming access has disappeared.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Grant the minimum required rights, account for ownership and inherited access, and verify permissions from the intended role.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: SQL injection occurs when application input becomes part of SQL syntax. Value parameters keep input separate from the command's structure.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A customer name may contain quotes or SQL-looking text. It must remain a name, not become a condition that changes which rows are returned.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SQL injection happens when an application joins untrusted input to SQL text and the input becomes a command or condition. Keep the statement fixed and pass external values through the database driver's binding API. A value containing quotes, OR, or -- must remain one value. Parameter placeholders represent values, not table names, column names, keywords, or sort directions. Any dynamic identifiers need a separate, carefully validated construction strategy.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: PREPARE lookup(text) AS SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name=$1 ORDER BY id; declares one text parameter. EXECUTE lookup('Ada'); supplies its value. With two parameters, list both types and use $1 and $2: PREPARE band(numeric,numeric) AS SELECT id FROM products WHERE price >= $1 AND price < $2;. The type controls value interpretation, while the SQL structure stays fixed. In a handwritten SQL string, write an apostrophe twice: EXECUTE lookup('Ada'' OR true --'); passes the literal name Ada' OR true --. Applications should bind that value through the driver rather than manually building this EXECUTE text.
sections.code: PREPARE lookup_customer(text) AS SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name=$1 ORDER BY id; EXECUTE lookup_customer('Ada');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Prepare one fixed lookup and supply a customer name as its parameter.

Customers begin with Ada (id 1, London), Ben (id 2, Paris), and Cleo (id 3, London); the table also contains other customers.

```sql
PREPARE lesson_lookup(text) AS SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name=$1 ORDER BY id; EXECUTE lesson_lookup('Ada');
```

**Result**

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada

The parameter supplies Ada as an exact name value. The same prepared statement could receive Ben without changing its WHERE condition.
sections.code: PREPARE lookup_customer(text) AS SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name=$1 ORDER BY id; EXECUTE lookup_customer('Ada');

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The hostile-looking name Ada' OR true -- is supplied as one text value. Because nobody has that literal name, the intended result is empty.
sections.code: PREPARE exact_name(text) AS SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name=$1 ORDER BY id; EXECUTE exact_name('Ada'' OR true --');

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example is customer 1, Ada. The input is compared as a name value rather than interpreted as SQL.

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Do not concatenate user input or rely on blocking words such as DROP. In the handwritten EXECUTE example, doubled quotes express a literal; application code should use driver binding instead.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Prepared statements also support reuse, but safe value binding does not require manually writing SQL PREPARE. Authorization and allowed identifier choices remain separate responsibilities.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check that changed values cannot change the query structure. Distinguish value placeholders from dynamic identifiers and keep output columns and ordering unchanged.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Keep SQL structure fixed, bind external values with the driver, and validate any separately composed identifiers.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Row-level security, or RLS, controls which table rows a role may read or change. It adds row rules to ordinary object permissions.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A shared table may hold data for different users or teams. RLS can enforce row access centrally instead of depending on every application query to remember a filter.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Row-level security (RLS) adds a per-row permission test after ordinary table privileges. ALTER TABLE customers ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; activates it. Without an applicable policy, access is denied by default. Owners normally bypass RLS; FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY makes the owner subject to it too. Superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS still bypass policies. These exercises use the non-superuser learner role and force policies on its own tables.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: CREATE POLICY vip_access ON customers FOR SELECT USING(vip); permits existing rows whose vip is true. USING controls which existing rows can be read or targeted; WITH CHECK controls permitted new values for INSERT/UPDATE. Policies are PERMISSIVE by default and combine with OR: London OR VIP can admit either group. CREATE POLICY known_contact ON customers AS RESTRICTIVE FOR SELECT USING(email IS NOT NULL); adds an AND requirement. Restrictive policies cannot grant access by themselves: at least one applicable permissive policy must first allow the row, for example USING(true). Policies filter rows; they do not update customer data.

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Let the forced VIP policy filter a query that contains no VIP condition.

Among customers 1–4, Ada (1) and Davi (4) have vip=true; Ben (2) and Cleo (3) have vip=false.

```sql
ALTER TABLE customers ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE customers FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY lesson_vip ON customers FOR SELECT USING(vip);
SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE id<=4 ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada
4 | Davi

The SELECT has no vip condition, yet the forced policy hides Ben and Cleo. All four rows remain stored in the table.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Owners normally bypass RLS; superusers and BYPASSRLS roles still bypass it despite FORCE. Table privileges are still required. RLS does not govern whole-table operations such as TRUNCATE.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Permissive policies combine with OR; restrictive policies add AND requirements. Review views and SECURITY DEFINER functions carefully because execution identity affects access.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check both permitted and hidden rows. When combining policies, work through the Boolean conditions and distinguish row visibility from allowed inserted or updated values.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: RLS adds per-row authorization; test it as the intended role and account for ownership, bypass rights, and policy combinations.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A useful backup contains enough information to restore the required data and structure. A copied result table is only a small part of that job.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Backups protect against mistakes, loss, and corruption. A recovery plan must say how much data loss is acceptable and how quickly service must return.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A backup is useful only if you can restore what you need. pg_dump makes a consistent logical export of one database; a plain SQL dump is restored with psql, while custom-format dumps use pg_restore. Roles and other cluster-wide objects need separate planning. SQLLY does not run backup utilities or write backup files from this workspace. Here you practise safe copies and checks inside the isolated database, then learn why matching a few totals is only part of a restore test.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: CREATE TABLE account_snapshot AS SELECT id,owner,balance FROM accounts; copies query rows and output column types into a new table. It does not copy primary keys, foreign keys, indexes, or the complete database. Before and after a restore, compare count(*), sum(balance), and grouped totals such as sum(stock*price) by category. An orphan check finds a non-NULL foreign key without its parent: WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.id=o.customer_id). A NULL customer ID may be a valid guest order and must not be counted as an orphan. Equal counts and sums can still hide different rows, so also verify keys, constraints, representative queries, and recovery requirements.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE account_snapshot AS SELECT id,owner,balance FROM accounts;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Copy selected account columns and check their balances in the new table.

The accounts table contains balances 1000.00, 500.00, and 750.00 for IDs 1, 2, and 3.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lesson_account_copy AS SELECT id,owner,balance FROM accounts;
SELECT id,balance FROM lesson_account_copy ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | balance
— | —
1 | 1000.00
2 | 500.00
3 | 750.00

The new table contains the same three selected balances. This verifies the row copy shown here, not a full backup or a tested recovery procedure.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE account_snapshot AS SELECT id,owner,balance FROM accounts;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The orphan-check query looks for non-NULL customer IDs without a customer. After a restore, checks like this complement row counts, totals, and application tests.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) AS orphan_count FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.id=o.customer_id);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example's verification contains the three copied accounts. It confirms this table copy, not the completeness of a backup-and-restore process.

id | owner | balance
— | — | —
1 | Ada | 1000.00
2 | Ben | 500.00
3 | Cleo | 750.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A successful dump command is not a tested recovery. Plan retention, access protection, globals, and restore testing; point-in-time recovery additionally needs an appropriate physical backup and WAL archive.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare logical export, row copying, and physical recovery. The SQL workspace teaches safe checks; it does not execute pg_dump or provision an operational backup service.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Verify copied data and reconciliation totals. Explain what each check misses, especially constraints, privileges, and objects outside the copied table.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define the recovery goal, preserve everything needed for it, and prove recovery by restoring and checking a separate environment.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Write-ahead logging, WAL, records changes before their data pages are written durably. Replication sends database changes to another server.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: WAL supports crash recovery. Replication can support availability or additional readers, but introduces questions about freshness, failure, and which server may accept writes.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Write-ahead logging (WAL) records changes before their data pages must reach durable storage. Crash recovery replays the needed records. Physical replication copies storage-level changes; logical replication transfers changes for selected published tables. A replica can repeat an accidental deletion, so replication does not replace a historical backup. SQLLY runs one local primary and does not configure a standby, publication, subscription, or replication connection.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS in_recovery; reports whether this server is in recovery; current_setting('wal_level') reads its WAL setting. Neither proves that replicas are healthy. To inspect primary-key columns, join information_schema.table_constraints tc to information_schema.key_column_usage k using constraint_catalog, constraint_schema, and constraint_name; filter tc.constraint_type='PRIMARY KEY' and tc.table_schema=current_schema(), then order by k.ordinal_position. For logical updates and deletes, replica identity tells PostgreSQL how to identify the old row. ALTER TABLE products REPLICA IDENTITY FULL; uses the old row's full contents rather than its default primary-key identity. It does not remove the key, change rows, or start replication. Grouped row counts and sums can help reconcile copies, but do not measure replication lag.
sections.code: SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS in_recovery;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Inspect recovery status on the local primary.

This example inspects the single bundled local PostgreSQL server; it does not create any replication objects.

```sql
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS in_recovery;
```

**Result**

in_recovery

f means false: this local primary is not in recovery. This is one status check, not evidence that a replication topology exists.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Operational troubleshooting traces a symptom to a specific cause using database errors, application behavior, and system observations.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A failed request might reflect bad data, a missing permission, a blocked transaction, or an unavailable server. Those problems require different responses.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Start with the observed problem, not an administrative command: which operation failed, what error and SQLSTATE did it report, and what should the data look like? A SQLSTATE is PostgreSQL's stable error code. Some operational checks are ordinary SELECT queries: negative totals, paid orders without a shipping date, stale stock records, or products with paid demand but no stock. Each check needs a business rule; a missing value is not automatically an error. The learner role cannot terminate other sessions or change server-wide settings.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: WHERE total<0 defines invalid totals; count(*) counts only those rows. A paid-but-unshipped queue uses status='paid' AND shipped_on IS NULL. To inspect existing safeguards, group information_schema.table_constraints by table_name,constraint_type with table_schema=current_schema(). To compare availability with paid demand, join products to order_items and orders, filter stock=0 and status='paid', then SUM(quantity) by product. For reproducible age checks, DATE '2024-07-10'-updated_on gives integer days; apply the requested >5 threshold and order by age descending. Fixed dates make the same dataset produce the same troubleshooting report tomorrow.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) AS invalid_total_count FROM orders WHERE total<0;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Calculate stock-record age at a fixed reporting date.

Inventory records 1 and 2 were updated July 1; record 3 was updated July 2. The reporting date is July 10, 2024.

```sql
SELECT product_id,updated_on,DATE '2024-07-10'-updated_on AS age_days FROM inventory WHERE product_id<=3 ORDER BY product_id;
```

**Result**

product_id | updated_on | age_days
— | — | —
1 | 2024-07-01 | 9
2 | 2024-07-01 | 9
3 | 2024-07-02 | 8

Date subtraction turns each update date into an age. All three records are older than five days; adding that WHERE condition would retain all three.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A recursive query follows a rule repeatedly. It starts with initial rows, then uses each round's rows to find the next round.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: It can walk an organization chart or connected records when the number of levels is unknown in advance.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A recursive CTE repeats a query using rows produced by the previous round. The anchor produces the starting rows. UNION ALL adds rows from the recursive term, which may refer to the CTE itself. Repetition ends when a round produces no rows. A hierarchy can start at roots (manager_id IS NULL) or one chosen employee. A depth counter starts at 0 and increases at each edge. These employee fixtures form trees; arbitrary graphs may contain cycles, which the next lesson handles.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM numbers WHERE n<5) SELECT n FROM numbers ORDER BY n; shows the anchor, recursive step, and stopping condition. To move down a hierarchy, join the next employee e ON e.manager_id=current.id. To move up, join e.id=current.manager_id and keep manager_id in the CTE. Starting with children WHERE manager_id=2 excludes leader 2; starting WHERE id=2 includes that leader. WHERE current.depth<2 in the recursive term permits children through depth 2 and stops deeper expansion. A final ORDER BY controls display order; recursion itself does not promise one.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM numbers WHERE n<5) SELECT n FROM numbers ORDER BY n;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Walk from Morgan to direct reports and stop after that level.

Morgan (1) manages Noor (2) and Pia (4). Noor and Pia also have reports, but this example stops after one level.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE team AS (SELECT id,name,0 AS depth FROM employees WHERE id=1 UNION ALL SELECT e.id,e.name,t.depth+1 FROM employees e JOIN team t ON e.manager_id=t.id WHERE t.depth<1) SELECT id,name,depth FROM team ORDER BY depth,id;
```

**Result**

id | name | depth
— | — | —
1 | Morgan | 0
2 | Noor | 1
4 | Pia | 1

The anchor adds Morgan at depth 0. One recursive round adds the two direct reports at depth 1; the depth condition prevents another round from adding their reports.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM numbers WHERE n<5) SELECT n FROM numbers ORDER BY n;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The employee query starts with direct reports of employee 2, then finds their reports. Employee 2 is excluded because the initial rows are their children.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (SELECT id,name FROM employees WHERE manager_id=2 UNION ALL SELECT e.id,e.name FROM employees e JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id=r.id) SELECT id,name FROM reports ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example contains 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. ORDER BY n guarantees the display order; recursion alone does not.

n
—
1
2
3
4
5

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: UNION ALL preserves duplicates and does not detect cycles. A link returning to a previous node can run indefinitely unless you prevent revisits or impose an appropriate stopping rule.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare recursion with ordinary CTEs and self joins. A fixed self join follows a fixed number of levels; recursion follows as many as its rule allows.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace the initial rows, one recursive round, and the stopping point. Check whether the starting employee should be included.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define the starting set, the next-step rule, and a termination strategy; order the final result explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A path records the nodes visited on a route through connected data. It helps explain how a node was reached and avoid following a cycle forever.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Paths can produce navigation breadcrumbs or employee ancestry while protecting traversal from links that return to an earlier node.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A path records the IDs visited on one route through a hierarchy or graph. ARRAY[id] starts an integer array, path||next_id appends an ID, and next_id=ANY(path) tests whether it is already present. Rejecting that condition prevents a repeated node on the current route. Names are unsuitable cycle keys because different people can share a name. For readable breadcrumbs, concatenate text instead: breadcrumb||' > '||name. An array can also answer whether a path passes through a chosen ancestor.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: In a recursive employee traversal, build ARRAY[id] in the anchor and use t.path||e.id in the recursive term with WHERE NOT e.id=ANY(t.path). Afterward, WHERE 2=ANY(path) keeps the subtree containing employee 2, including employee 2. UNION (without ALL) removes duplicate complete rows, which safely terminates a finite graph traversal when its only output is node. Adding a changing depth or path prevents that whole-row deduplication from stopping cycles. PostgreSQL's CYCLE node SET is_cycle USING path clause after the recursive CTE tracks repeated keys for you: it includes the cycle-closing row with is_cycle=true and stops expanding that route. Use UNION ALL with CYCLE, then select or filter the marker as the task requests.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (SELECT id,manager_id,ARRAY[id] AS path FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id,e.manager_id,t.path||e.id FROM employees e JOIN tree t ON e.manager_id=t.id WHERE NOT e.id=ANY(t.path)) SELECT id,path FROM tree ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Follow a graph with a cycle and inspect its cycle-closing row.

The directed links are 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, and 3→4. Start at node 1.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE edges(a,b) AS (VALUES(1,2),(2,3),(3,1),(3,4)),walk(node) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT e.b FROM walk w JOIN edges e ON e.a=w.node) CYCLE node SET is_cycle USING path SELECT node,is_cycle FROM walk ORDER BY node,is_cycle;
```

**Result**

node | is_cycle
— | —
1 | f
1 | t
2 | f
3 | f
4 | f

Node 1 first appears normally, then appears with true when 3 leads back to it. That route stops, while the separate route to 4 remains. The final sort groups the two visits to 1 together.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (SELECT id,manager_id,ARRAY[id] AS path FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id,e.manager_id,t.path||e.id FROM employees e JOIN tree t ON e.manager_id=t.id WHERE NOT e.id=ANY(t.path)) SELECT id,path FROM tree ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The graph example uses UNION over node alone. Repeated node IDs are discarded, so the cycle 1→2→3→1 does not keep adding rows.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE edges(a,b) AS (VALUES(1,2),(2,3),(3,1),(2,4)), walk(node) AS (SELECT 1 UNION SELECT e.b FROM walk w JOIN edges e ON e.a=w.node) SELECT node FROM walk ORDER BY node;

sections.title: Expected results
Common mistakes
sections.body: UNION removes duplicates of the whole row. If depth or path changes each time, it may not stop a cycle. A depth cap limits work but does not prove the graph is acyclic.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: PostgreSQL also offers SEARCH and CYCLE clauses. SEARCH computes ordering information; use ORDER BY on it to request the corresponding final order.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace a repeated-node edge and confirm why it is rejected. Distinguish finding unique reachable nodes from returning all distinct paths.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose whether you need nodes or routes, then design cycle protection and ordering for that result.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A recursive rollup totals information across a hierarchy. First find which descendants belong to each ancestor, then summarize those relationships.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A manager's report may need everyone below them, including indirect reports, rather than only employees whose manager_id names them directly.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Separate finding a subtree from calculating its total. First produce pairs (leader_id, employee_id) for each leader and every employee in that leader's subtree. Keep leader_id fixed during recursion while employee_id moves to the next child. Starting every employee as their own leader makes even leaves appear. These fixtures have one manager per employee and no cycles, so each leader–employee pair occurs once; graphs with multiple paths need an explicit deduplication rule.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Anchor SELECT id AS leader_id,id AS employee_id,0 AS depth FROM employees. The next step selects l.leader_id,e.id,l.depth+1 with e.manager_id=l.employee_id. After traversal, GROUP BY leader_id: count(*)-1 counts reports without the leader; sum(e.salary) includes the leader when salaries are joined on e.id=employee_id; max(depth) gives the longest chain. A leaf has no direct children: NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM employees child WHERE child.manager_id=e.id). Filter to leaves before summing leaf salaries. Do not recursively add already aggregated subtotals: that can count the same descendant more than once.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE links AS (SELECT id AS manager_id,id AS employee_id FROM employees UNION ALL SELECT l.manager_id,e.id FROM links l JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id=l.employee_id) SELECT manager_id,count(*)-1 AS report_count FROM links GROUP BY manager_id ORDER BY manager_id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Find one complete team before summing its salaries.

Noor (2) earns 90000.00. Direct reports Owen (3) and Rae (6) each earn 80000.00.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE team AS (SELECT id,salary FROM employees WHERE id=2 UNION ALL SELECT e.id,e.salary FROM employees e JOIN team t ON e.manager_id=t.id) SELECT count(*) AS people,sum(salary) AS total_salary FROM team;
```

**Result**

people | total_salary
— | —
3 | 250000.00

The traversal includes the leader and both reports. Aggregating its rows gives three people and 250000.00; excluding the leader would answer a different question.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE links AS (SELECT id AS manager_id,id AS employee_id FROM employees UNION ALL SELECT l.manager_id,e.id FROM links l JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id=l.employee_id) SELECT manager_id,count(*)-1 AS report_count FROM links GROUP BY manager_id ORDER BY manager_id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: NOT EXISTS finds employees with no direct reports. These are leaf nodes in the employee tree, not necessarily employees with no manager.
sections.code: SELECT e.id,e.name FROM employees e WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM employees child WHERE child.manager_id=e.id) ORDER BY e.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example gives employee 1 five reports and employee 2 two. Employees 3, 5, and 6 have none.

manager_id | report_count
— | —
1 | 5
2 | 2
3 | 0
4 | 1
5 | 0
6 | 0

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: This tree example assumes one route to each descendant and no cycles. In a graph, multiple routes can double-count a descendant; define deduplication before summing.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Connect recursion with GROUP BY and EXISTS. Traversal builds relationships; aggregation decides what those relationships mean in the final report.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Traverse first, then aggregate at the requested ancestor level, with explicit rules for self-inclusion and duplicate paths.
