sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A range stores a span of ordered values together with its boundary rules. PostgreSQL has range types for dates, timestamps, and numbers.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Ranges make questions such as “does this stay include Tuesday?” or “do these reservations overlap?” easier to express consistently.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A range stores boundaries together with their inclusion rules. daterange(check_in,check_out,'[)') includes check-in and excludes check-out: [2024-07-01,2024-07-04) covers the nights of July 1, 2, and 3. @> tests whether a range contains a date. && tests whether two ranges share any dates. -|- tests adjacency: the ranges touch but do not overlap. Thus a checkout and the next check-in can occur on the same date without sharing a night.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: WHERE daterange(check_in,check_out,'[)') @> DATE '2024-07-03' finds stays covering that night. For pairs in the same room, self-join with a.room=b.room AND a.id<b.id to avoid matching a booking to itself or listing both pair directions, then test && or -|-. The * operator returns the intersection: stay_range * daterange(DATE '2024-07-02',DATE '2024-07-05','[)'). lower(result) and upper(result) expose the clipped boundaries; subtracting them gives nights. Filter to overlapping ranges before using these endpoints, because an empty intersection has NULL bounds. These examples have finite dates; unbounded ranges need a separate duration policy.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest FROM bookings WHERE daterange(check_in,check_out,'[)') @> DATE '2024-07-03' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Intersect stays with a reporting window and count only the remaining nights.

Bookings 1, 2, and 3 cover July 1–4, July 2–5, and July 4–6 respectively, with checkout excluded. Report only [July 2, July 5).

```sql
WITH clipped AS (SELECT id,daterange(check_in,check_out,'[)') * daterange(DATE '2024-07-02',DATE '2024-07-05','[)') AS stay FROM bookings WHERE id<=3 AND daterange(check_in,check_out,'[)') && daterange(DATE '2024-07-02',DATE '2024-07-05','[)')) SELECT id,lower(stay) AS stay_start,upper(stay) AS stay_end,upper(stay)-lower(stay) AS nights FROM clipped ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | stay_start | stay_end | nights
— | — | — | —
1 | 2024-07-02 | 2024-07-04 | 2
2 | 2024-07-02 | 2024-07-05 | 3
3 | 2024-07-04 | 2024-07-05 | 1

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Partitioning divides one logical table among child tables. PostgreSQL routes each inserted row to a partition using a partition key.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Large time-based tables can benefit from reading only relevant partitions or removing old partitions together. Partitioning still needs a workload-specific design.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A partitioned parent is one logical table whose rows are stored in child partitions. INSERT into the parent routes each row by its partition key; SELECT from the parent normally reads the relevant children. RANGE bounds are lower-inclusive and upper-exclusive. LIST matches listed values. HASH routes by PostgreSQL's hash of the key, not by the integer key's ordinary remainder. A missing destination causes an insert error unless a DEFAULT partition handles it; DEFAULT is available for RANGE and LIST, not HASH.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: CREATE TABLE dated(id integer,day date NOT NULL) PARTITION BY RANGE(day); declares a parent. CREATE TABLE july PARTITION OF dated FOR VALUES FROM('2024-07-01') TO('2024-08-01'); defines one range; CREATE TABLE other_dates PARTITION OF dated DEFAULT; handles the rest. LIST(category) uses FOR VALUES IN('Office'). HASH(id) uses FOR VALUES WITH(MODULUS 2,REMAINDER 0) and a second partition with REMAINDER 1. Insert through the parent with VALUES or INSERT INTO parent SELECT ... FROM products. A PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint on a partitioned parent must include all simple partition-key columns; PRIMARY KEY(id,day) can support RANGE(day), while PRIMARY KEY(id) alone cannot. Partitioning does not itself guarantee faster queries.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE quarterly_events(id integer,event_day date NOT NULL) PARTITION BY RANGE(event_day); CREATE TABLE q1_events PARTITION OF quarterly_events FOR VALUES FROM('2024-01-01') TO('2024-04-01'); CREATE TABLE q2_events PARTITION OF quarterly_events FOR VALUES FROM('2024-04-01') TO('2024-07-01'); INSERT INTO quarterly_events VALUES(1,'2024-03-31'),(2,'2024-04-01');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Insert dates through a parent table and inspect their destination partitions.

Two incoming dates are July 31 and August 1. The July partition covers [2024-07-01,2024-08-01); the other partition is DEFAULT.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lesson_dates(id integer,day date NOT NULL) PARTITION BY RANGE(day); CREATE TABLE lesson_july PARTITION OF lesson_dates FOR VALUES FROM('2024-07-01') TO('2024-08-01'); CREATE TABLE lesson_other PARTITION OF lesson_dates DEFAULT; INSERT INTO lesson_dates VALUES(1,DATE '2024-07-31'),(2,DATE '2024-08-01');
SELECT 'july' AS section,id,day FROM lesson_july UNION ALL SELECT 'other',id,day FROM lesson_other ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

section | id | day
— | — | —
july | 1 | 2024-07-31
other | 2 | 2024-08-01

The parent routes July 31 into July. August 1 equals the excluded upper boundary, so it goes into DEFAULT. Reading both children shows where each row was stored.

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The dated_notes example adds a DEFAULT partition for otherwise unmatched rows. Its primary key includes note_day, the partition-key column.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE dated_notes(id integer,note_day date,body text,PRIMARY KEY(id,note_day)) PARTITION BY RANGE(note_day); CREATE TABLE all_notes PARTITION OF dated_notes DEFAULT; INSERT INTO dated_notes VALUES(1,'2024-07-01','Ready');

sections.body:
The result of the syntax example's verification shows each date's actual child table, q1_events or q2_events. This is a routing check, not ordinary INSERT output.

— | — | —

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A missing partition causes an insertion error unless a default partition accepts the row. A partitioned parent's unique or primary key must include every partition-key column; expression partition keys add restrictions.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Partition pruning skips children that cannot match a condition. Indexes speed work within partitions; pruning and indexing solve different problems.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test dates on both sides of each boundary and the boundary itself. Check key definitions and where an out-of-range row would go.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose useful partitions, cover intended input ranges, and verify both row routing and the constraints the design can enforce.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An ordered aggregate builds a value from rows in a specified order. A generated column calculates its value from other columns in the same row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Ordered arrays make reports stable. Generated columns keep a repeated calculation consistent without trusting every writer to supply it correctly.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Some aggregates collect values into an ordered container rather than adding them. array_agg(name ORDER BY id) builds an array; string_agg(id::text,',' ORDER BY ordered_on,id) builds text with a separator. Put ordering inside the aggregate: a final ORDER BY only sorts output groups. jsonb_build_object('id',id,'price',price) creates one object from key/value pairs; jsonb_agg(that_object ORDER BY price DESC,id) collects objects into an ordered JSONB array. JSONB object key order is not an element-order guarantee.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: A generated column calculates a value from other columns of the same row: amount numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS(quantity*unit_price) STORED. INSERT names only id,quantity,unit_price; changing quantity automatically changes amount. STORED computes on writes and stores the result. PostgreSQL 18 also supports VIRTUAL, which computes on reads and is the default when neither kind is stated; choose the kind explicitly in these tasks. The expression must be immutable, cannot use subqueries or another generated column, and a virtual expression may use only built-in functions and types. A generated value cannot be supplied directly, except the keyword DEFAULT; it is different from an ordinary default that runs only when an inserted value is omitted.
sections.code: SELECT category,array_agg(name ORDER BY id) AS product_names FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Change a source quantity and watch the generated amount follow it.

A line begins with quantity 2 and unit price 4.50, so its generated amount is 9.00. Only quantity is then changed to 3.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lesson_lines(id integer PRIMARY KEY,quantity integer NOT NULL,unit_price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,amount numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS(quantity*unit_price) STORED); INSERT INTO lesson_lines(id,quantity,unit_price) VALUES(1,2,4.50); UPDATE lesson_lines SET quantity=3 WHERE id=1;
SELECT quantity,unit_price,amount FROM lesson_lines ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

quantity | unit_price | amount
— | — | —
3 | 4.50 | 13.50

The stored generated amount updates to 13.50 without a separate assignment. The expression keeps the line amount consistent with its current base values.
sections.code: SELECT category,array_agg(name ORDER BY id) AS product_names FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The invoice example declares amount GENERATED ALWAYS AS(quantity*unit_price) STORED. INSERT supplies quantity and price; PostgreSQL computes amount rather than accepting a manually supplied value.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE invoice_lines(id integer PRIMARY KEY,quantity integer NOT NULL,unit_price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,amount numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS(quantity*unit_price) STORED); INSERT INTO invoice_lines(id,quantity,unit_price) VALUES(1,3,2.50),(2,2,12.50);

sections.title: Expected results
Common mistakes
sections.body: Outer ORDER BY does not control array elements. array_agg includes NULL inputs and returns NULL for no input rows. Generated expressions must be immutable, row-local, and free of subqueries or other generated columns; virtual columns also prohibit user-defined types and functions.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare generated columns with defaults: defaults provide an initial value, while generated values follow their expression when source columns change.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check ordering inside and outside each aggregate. For generated-column tasks, omit the generated value from INSERT and verify the calculation after writes.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Specify collection order at the aggregate and let generated columns enforce valid row-local calculations.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A gaps-and-islands query finds consecutive runs and the breaks between them. You must first define what counts as consecutive.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: This pattern answers questions about daily activity streaks, uninterrupted bookings, or missing dates in an expected calendar.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: An island is a run of consecutive values; a gap separates runs. First choose the unit: one row per calendar date, or one row per customer and date. Remove duplicate dates before numbering them. For sorted consecutive dates, date minus its row number is constant: both the date and the number increase by one. A skipped date changes that grouping value. Date subtraction needs an integer day count, so cast row_number() to integer.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Build stages: days AS (SELECT DISTINCT occurred_at::date AS day ...), then SELECT day,day-row_number() OVER(ORDER BY day)::integer AS grp. GROUP BY grp and take min(day),max(day),count(*) for each run. For customer streaks add customer_id to DISTINCT, PARTITION BY customer_id, and GROUP BY customer_id,grp. To include customers with no events, compute streak lengths, then maximum length per customer, LEFT JOIN customers and COALESCE to zero. To find missing dates instead, generate the complete calendar with generate_series(start,end,INTERVAL '1 day') and keep NOT EXISTS matches. For room availability, a booking covers day when check_in<=day AND check_out>day; checkout itself is available.
sections.code: WITH days AS (SELECT DISTINCT check_in AS day FROM bookings), numbered AS (SELECT day,day-(row_number() OVER(ORDER BY day))::integer AS grp FROM days) SELECT min(day) AS island_start,max(day) AS island_end,count(*) AS day_count FROM numbered GROUP BY grp ORDER BY island_start;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Show the grouping value that identifies consecutive date runs.

Booking check-in dates include July 1 twice, then July 2, July 4, and July 7. DISTINCT first keeps July 1 only once.

```sql
SELECT day,row_number() OVER(ORDER BY day) AS position,day-(row_number() OVER(ORDER BY day))::integer AS grouping_date FROM (SELECT DISTINCT check_in AS day FROM bookings) days ORDER BY day;
```

**Result**

day | position | grouping_date
— | — | —
2024-07-01 | 1 | 2024-06-30
2024-07-02 | 2 | 2024-06-30
2024-07-04 | 3 | 2024-07-01
2024-07-07 | 4 | 2024-07-03

July 1 and 2 share the same grouping date, so they form one consecutive run. July 4 and 7 have different values and each start a new run.
sections.code: WITH days AS (SELECT DISTINCT check_in AS day FROM bookings), numbered AS (SELECT day,day-(row_number() OVER(ORDER BY day))::integer AS grp FROM days) SELECT min(day) AS island_start,max(day) AS island_end,count(*) AS day_count FROM numbered GROUP BY grp ORDER BY island_start;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The missing-day query generates July 1–7 and retains dates with no matching order. It creates the expected calendar before checking for absence.
sections.code: SELECT d.day::date AS day FROM generate_series(DATE '2024-07-01',DATE '2024-07-07',INTERVAL '1 day') d(day) WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.ordered_on=d.day::date) ORDER BY day;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example has a two-day run on July 1–2 and one-day runs on July 4 and 7. Several arrivals on one date still count as one day.

island_start | island_end | day_count
— | — | —
2024-07-01 | 2024-07-02 | 2
2024-07-04 | 2024-07-04 | 1
2024-07-07 | 2024-07-07 | 1

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Duplicates must not advance the daily counter. Calendar days and business days have different adjacency rules; per-customer streaks also need separate customer partitions.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Relate the pattern to DISTINCT, row_number, date arithmetic, and NOT EXISTS. Window numbering supplies a grouping key; the final aggregate summarizes each run.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test a repeated date, a missing day, and a one-day run. Confirm the entity and date unit before calculating the sequence.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define adjacency, deduplicate at the right level, then form and summarize runs or compare with a complete calendar.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An “every” question asks whether every required item has a match. SQL often expresses this as “there is no required item without a match.”

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Examples include customers who bought every required category or products containing all required tags. Finding any one match is not enough.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: An “every” question asks whether any requirement is missing. For each customer, NOT EXISTS(required item for which NOT EXISTS(a matching paid purchase)) means no required item is missing. This is called relational division. The outer customer row remains one row, however many purchases match. When using counts instead, count DISTINCT requirement keys: buying one category twice must not substitute for buying two categories.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Represent a fixed set with (VALUES('Office'),('Tech')) required(category), or use catalog rows such as products WHERE category='Home'. Correlate the innermost purchase query both to the customer and the required category or product. For all catalog categories, compare count(DISTINCT p.category) in paid purchase groups with (SELECT count(DISTINCT category) FROM products). That grouped approach includes only customers with observed eligible lines; double NOT EXISTS over customers allows everyone when the required set is empty. Choose that policy deliberately. “Every order is paid, and at least one exists” needs EXISTS(any order) AND NOT EXISTS(non-paid order). In this schema status is NOT NULL; if NULL statuses were allowed, explicitly decide whether unknown status counts as non-paid. For arrays, tags @> ARRAY['usb','work'] directly checks that both tags are present.
sections.code: SELECT c.id,c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM (VALUES('Office'),('Tech')) required(category) WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id=o.id JOIN products p ON p.id=i.product_id WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' AND p.category=required.category)) ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Ask which customers have no missing purchase category.

Paid purchases give Ada both Office and Tech items, Ben only Tech, Cleo only Home, Davi Home, and Eli Office. Fara has no purchases.

```sql
SELECT c.id,c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM (VALUES('Office'),('Tech')) required(category) WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id=o.id JOIN products p ON p.id=i.product_id WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' AND p.category=required.category)) ORDER BY c.id;
```

**Result**

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada

Only Ada has no missing category from the required set {Office, Tech}. Repeated Tech purchases do not make Ben qualify.

sections.body: The array example uses tags @> ARRAY['usb','work']. Containment requires both tag values, not just either one, and does not count repeated tag occurrences.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Counting ordinary joined rows can mistake duplicates for fulfilled requirements. An empty requirement set makes the double-NOT-EXISTS condition true for every candidate; decide if that business rule is desired.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare universal matching with EXISTS for “at least one”. count(DISTINCT requirement) can be another approach when its candidate and requirement sets are defined correctly.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Translate “every” into an explicit requirement set and prove that no required match is missing.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A percentile locates a position in sorted values. The median is the 50th percentile: a useful description of the middle of a distribution.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: When a few values are unusually large, an average may hide the typical scale. Percentiles describe the middle or upper end more directly.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A percentile locates a value within a sorted population. The median is the 0.5 percentile; quartiles use 0.25 and 0.75. percentile_cont may interpolate between adjacent values: the median of 12.50 and 15.00 is 13.75. percentile_disc always chooses an observed value: it takes the first sorted value whose cumulative fraction reaches the requested fraction. Fractions must be between 0 and 1. Both functions ignore NULL input values; an empty input returns NULL.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Write percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP(ORDER BY price), then cast its floating-point result to numeric before round(...,2). percentile_disc(0.5) WITHIN GROUP(ORDER BY salary) returns a value of the input type. GROUP BY department computes a separate distribution for each department; a median of department medians is not the overall median. Define the input population before calculating: WHERE status='paid' restricts order totals, while joining order_items to products and grouping by category measures line quantities. If the task says all statuses, do not add a paid-only filter. Several percentile calls can share one SELECT to return the first quartile, median, and third quartile.
sections.code: SELECT round((percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP(ORDER BY price))::numeric,2) AS median_price FROM products;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Compare three continuous percentiles of the same ordered prices.

Product prices in ascending order are 2.00, 4.00, 8.00, 12.50, 15.00, 45.00, 75.00, and 250.00.

```sql
SELECT round((percentile_cont(0.25) WITHIN GROUP(ORDER BY price))::numeric,2) AS q1_price,round((percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP(ORDER BY price))::numeric,2) AS median_price,round((percentile_cont(0.75) WITHIN GROUP(ORDER BY price))::numeric,2) AS q3_price FROM products;
```

**Result**

q1_price | median_price | q3_price
— | — | —
7.00 | 13.75 | 52.50

The continuous quartiles interpolate within that ordered list. None of 7.00, 13.75, and 52.50 needs to be an actual catalog price.
sections.code: SELECT round((percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP(ORDER BY price))::numeric,2) AS median_price FROM products;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The paid-order example filters to paid orders before finding the 90th percentile. Changing that population changes the metric even when the percentile fraction stays the same.
sections.code: SELECT round((percentile_cont(0.9) WITHIN GROUP(ORDER BY total))::numeric,2) AS p90_total FROM orders WHERE status='paid';

sections.body:
The result of the syntax example is a median of 13.75 on Retail, halfway between 12.50 and 15.00. This is different from the arithmetic average.

median_price
—

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A percentile of group percentiles is not the overall percentile. No non-NULL inputs yield NULL; casting an approximate result before rounding does not restore lost precision.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare median with AVG, percentile_disc, and ranking functions. WITHIN GROUP orders aggregate input; the outer ORDER BY orders final report rows.

sections.body: Check the population, fraction, NULL policy, and output rounding. Use both odd and even input counts to understand interpolation.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define the population first, then choose continuous or discrete percentiles according to the meaning of the requested value.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A customer report needs an agreed definition of one result row, eligible sales, and how to show customers without sales.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Revenue, purchase counts, and customer value support decisions only when everyone uses the same business rules.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Start an e-commerce report by deciding what one row represents: a customer, order, line item, or category. Sum orders.total at order grain; sum quantity*unit_price at line grain. Joining order headers to several lines repeats each header total. Revenue here includes only paid orders. A customer report starts from customers and LEFT JOINs paid orders with the status condition in ON, so people without purchases remain. count(o.id) gives zero for them; COALESCE(sum(o.total),0) gives zero revenue.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: For first and last paid purchase dates, filter paid orders and known customer_id, then GROUP BY customer_id with min(ordered_on), max(ordered_on), and count(*). Category contribution uses paid line revenue, aggregated first, then revenue/NULLIF(sum(revenue) OVER(),0). To compare customers with the overall average, build a totals CTE containing every customer, including zeros, and compare paid_revenue>(SELECT avg(paid_revenue) FROM totals). For first-purchase acquisition, use row_number() OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id), keep rn=1, then group by date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date. The id resolves same-day ties. Acquisition month here means first paid order, not the customer's registration month.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id,c.name,count(o.id) AS paid_orders,COALESCE(sum(o.total),0) AS revenue FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY revenue DESC,c.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Build a customer summary that preserves zero-purchase customers.

Ada (1) has paid orders totaling 29.00, 250.00, and 16.00. Fara (6) has no orders.

```sql
SELECT c.id AS customer_id,count(o.id) AS paid_orders,round(COALESCE(sum(o.total),0),2) AS revenue FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' WHERE c.id IN(1,6) GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id;
```

**Result**

customer_id | paid_orders | revenue
— | — | —
1 | 3 | 295.00
6 | 0 | 0.00

At customer grain, Ada contributes three paid orders and 295.00. LEFT JOIN preserves Fara with zero orders and zero revenue.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id,c.name,count(o.id) AS paid_orders,COALESCE(sum(o.total),0) AS revenue FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY revenue DESC,c.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The category report instead uses quantity*unit_price from paid line items. A window sum supplies the total line revenue; NULLIF protects a zero denominator when calculating shares.
sections.code: WITH sales AS (SELECT p.category,sum(i.quantity*i.unit_price) AS revenue FROM products p JOIN order_items i ON i.product_id=p.id JOIN orders o ON o.id=i.order_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY p.category) SELECT category,revenue,round(revenue/NULLIF(sum(revenue) OVER(),0),4) AS revenue_share FROM sales ORDER BY revenue DESC,category;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
In the result of the syntax example, Ada has 295.00 from three paid orders. Fara remains with no paid orders and zero revenue, appearing last in this revenue sort.

customer_id | name | paid_orders | revenue
— | — | — | —
1 | Ada | 3 | 295.00
2 | Ben | 2 | 150.00
4 | Davi | 1 | 90.00
3 | Cleo | 1 | 45.00
5 | Eli | 1 | 25.00
6 | Fara | 0 | 0

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Joining orders to their line items before adding order totals can count each order several times. The stored order total can differ from the sum of its lines. Label and check these two figures separately.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Combine outer joins, grouped summaries, and window totals. A customer's first purchase and last purchase require the same eligibility rules as their revenue.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define the report population and row meaning, aggregate each amount once, and preserve customers the business requires.

exercises.solutionSQL: WITH ranked AS (SELECT customer_id,ordered_on,total,row_number() OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id) AS rn FROM orders WHERE status='paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL) SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS acquisition_month,count(*) AS new_customers,sum(total) AS first_order_revenue FROM ranked WHERE rn=1 GROUP BY acquisition_month ORDER BY acquisition_month;
hints: Choose the report grain before joining detail rows.
Apply paid and known-customer filters consistently.
Use a deterministic tie-breaker for the first purchase.
exercises.explanation: ROW_NUMBER selects exactly one first paid purchase per customer. Grouping those selected rows measures acquisition, not all repeat revenue.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An inventory report compares stock with a target or a defined measure of demand. Quantities and money describe different aspects of the same products.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Replenishment decisions need to show shortages without losing products that have never sold or currently have no stock.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Stock is available quantity; demand is the quantity ordered during a defined eligible history. They answer different questions. Here demand comes only from paid order lines, not pending or cancelled orders. First SUM(quantity) by product, then LEFT JOIN that result to every catalog product, using COALESCE for zero demand. This prevents joins from multiplying stock values and keeps unsold products visible. A warehouse report uses inventory.quantity for each warehouse, not products.stock.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: greatest(20-stock,0) computes the units needed to reach a target of 20 and prevents a negative purchase recommendation. Keep only positive shortages when requested. Warehouse value is sum(i.quantity*p.price) after joining inventory i to products p by product ID. Coverage is stock::numeric/NULLIF(paid_units,0), rounded as requested: zero or absent demand makes the ratio NULL, not zero, because it is undefined. A critical-stock report first filters inventory WHERE quantity<5, then groups by warehouse; count(*) counts qualifying entries and sum(10-quantity) gives the units needed to bring only those entries to ten. The alert threshold and replenishment target are separate rules.
sections.code: SELECT id,name,stock,greatest(20-stock,0) AS units_to_buy FROM products WHERE stock<20 ORDER BY units_to_buy DESC,id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Turn current stock into a clear replenishment quantity.

Monitor stock is 5, Mug stock is 0, and Lamp stock is 8. The replenishment target is 20 units per product.

```sql
SELECT id,name,stock,greatest(20-stock,0) AS units_to_buy FROM products WHERE id IN(4,5,6) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | name | stock | units_to_buy
— | — | — | —
4 | Monitor | 5 | 15
5 | Mug | 0 | 20
6 | Lamp | 8 | 12

The calculation recommends 15, 20, and 12 units. For a product already above the target, greatest(...,0) would return zero.
sections.code: SELECT id,name,stock,greatest(20-stock,0) AS units_to_buy FROM products WHERE stock<20 ORDER BY units_to_buy DESC,id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The warehouse report uses inventory.quantity and product price to total units and stock value by warehouse. It does not use products.stock as an additional quantity.
sections.code: SELECT i.warehouse,sum(i.quantity) AS units,sum(i.quantity*p.price) AS stock_value FROM inventory i JOIN products p ON p.id=i.product_id GROUP BY i.warehouse ORDER BY stock_value DESC,i.warehouse;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example recommends 20 Mug units, 15 Monitor units, 12 Lamp units, and 8 Keyboard units on Retail. These are quantities, not purchase costs.

id | name | stock | units_to_buy
— | — | — | —
5 | Mug | 0 | 20
4 | Monitor | 5 | 15
6 | Lamp | 8 | 12
3 | Keyboard | 12 | 8

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Do not add quantities to currency or mix two stock sources. This project's demand counts paid orders; whether paid also means fulfilled must be defined by a real business.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Relate the report to pre-aggregation, LEFT JOIN, and COALESCE. Stock coverage ratios need an explicit denominator and a rule for zero demand.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check zero stock, stock exactly at the target, no paid demand, and multiple order lines. Identify the source and unit of every reported quantity.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Keep stock, demand, targets, and valuation separate, then combine them at one well-defined product or warehouse level.

exercises.title: Stock coverage against paid demand
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, name, paid_units, stock, and coverage: stock divided by paid units, rounded to two decimals. Include unsold products with paid_units=0 and coverage=NULL. Order by product_id.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A hotel stay occupies nights from check-in up to, but not including, checkout. Revenue and occupancy must use that same boundary rule.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Counting dates incorrectly can charge an extra night or show an occupied room after the guest has left.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A hotel stay occupies nights from check-in through the night before checkout. Full-stay nights equal check_out-check_in, and charge equals nights*nightly_rate. Room totals sum these values by room. A daily report needs a calendar, not just booking start dates: generate each report day and LEFT JOIN stays where check_in<=day AND check_out>day. That preserves days with no guests. Count DISTINCT room for occupancy and sum one nightly_rate per matched booking for that night, with COALESCE to zero.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: For occupancy share, divide occupied distinct rooms by the specified known roster using numeric division and NULLIF(known_rooms,0). Here the roster is all distinct rooms anywhere in bookings; a real hotel needs an independent rooms table. If bookings overlap erroneously for one room, DISTINCT prevents duplicate room counts, but revenue still sums the matched booking rates; flag such conflicts separately. A period report must clip each stay before pricing: greatest(least(check_out,period_end)-greatest(check_in,period_start),0). The inner LEAST/GREATEST selects the overlap boundaries, and outer GREATEST clamps non-overlap to zero. Group all bookings by room, including zero overlap, when the prompt asks to retain those rooms.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest,check_out-check_in AS nights,(check_out-check_in)*nightly_rate AS charge FROM bookings ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Price only the nights inside the report period.

Bookings 1, 2, and 3 cover July 1–4 at 100.00, July 2–5 at 120.00, and July 4–6 at 100.00 per night. Report only [July 2, July 5).

```sql
SELECT id,greatest(least(check_out,DATE '2024-07-05')-greatest(check_in,DATE '2024-07-02'),0) AS nights,greatest(least(check_out,DATE '2024-07-05')-greatest(check_in,DATE '2024-07-02'),0)*nightly_rate AS revenue FROM bookings WHERE id<=3 ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | nights | revenue
— | — | —
1 | 2 | 200.00
2 | 3 | 360.00
3 | 1 | 100.00

Only 2, 3, and 1 nights fall inside the reporting window. Pricing these clipped durations gives 200.00, 360.00, and 100.00 rather than full-stay charges.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest,check_out-check_in AS nights,(check_out-check_in)*nightly_rate AS charge FROM bookings ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The daily report generates July 1–10, counts distinct occupied room numbers, and sums one nightly rate per matching booking. COALESCE displays zero revenue on empty days.
sections.code: SELECT d.day::date AS day,count(DISTINCT b.room) AS occupied_rooms,COALESCE(sum(b.nightly_rate),0) AS revenue FROM generate_series(DATE '2024-07-01',DATE '2024-07-10',INTERVAL '1 day') d(day) LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.check_in<=d.day::date AND b.check_out>d.day::date GROUP BY d.day ORDER BY d.day;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
In the result of the syntax example, Ada's three nights at 100 cost 300.00; Ben's three nights at 120 cost 360.00. Each booking remains a separate row.

id | guest | nights | charge
— | — | — | —
1 | Ada | 3 | 300.00
2 | Ben | 3 | 360.00
3 | Cleo | 2 | 200.00
4 | Davi | 1 | 150.00
5 | Eli | 3 | 360.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Counting bookings is not counting room-nights. Overlapping bookings for one room are a data-quality problem: DISTINCT room avoids duplicate occupancy counts but does not prevent double-counted revenue.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Connect half-open date ranges, generated calendars, and LEFT JOIN. An occupancy percentage also needs an explicit available-room roster as its denominator.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test checkout followed by same-day check-in, a stay crossing the report boundary, and an empty day. Apply nightly prices only to nights inside the requested period.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use exclusive checkout consistently, separate nights from bookings, and define the room-capacity and revenue rules before reporting.

exercises.title: Occupancy against the known room roster
exercises.prompt: For July 1–7, 2024 return day, occupied_rooms, known_rooms, and occupancy_share rounded to four decimals. The known roster is every distinct room anywhere in bookings; occupied rooms cover the night using check_in<=day<check_out. Order by day.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT d.day::date AS day,count(DISTINCT b.room) AS occupied_rooms,r.n AS known_rooms,round(count(DISTINCT b.room)::numeric/NULLIF(r.n,0),4) AS occupancy_share FROM generate_series(DATE '2024-07-01',DATE '2024-07-07',INTERVAL '1 day') d(day) CROSS JOIN (SELECT count(DISTINCT room) AS n FROM bookings) r LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.check_in<=d.day::date AND b.check_out>d.day::date GROUP BY d.day,r.n ORDER BY d.day;

modules.title: Final Projects: Finance, Analytics, and Reporting

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A ledger records money movements; an account balance represents the resulting position. A useful design defines which rules must always hold.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A transfer needs a traceable record and matching balance changes. Recording only one side, or applying a retried request twice, can corrupt financial results.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A transfer record describes a movement; inserting that record alone does not change account balances. Keys identify each transfer, foreign keys require real accounts, CHECK(amount>0) requires a positive amount, and CHECK(source_id<>destination_id) rejects a same-account transfer. Use numeric for exact money values. To apply a transfer, debit and credit equal amounts and insert its log in one transaction. Either all these changes commit or all roll back. A production system also needs authorization, retry-safe request IDs, and an immutable audit trail.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: A posting represents one signed account change: negative delta is a debit and positive delta a credit. PRIMARY KEY(transfer_id,account_id) prevents duplicate account entries in the same transfer; delta numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK(delta<>0) rejects empty movements. Balanced posting pairs sum to zero, but a row CHECK cannot enforce a sum across rows. To apply a batch, give posting_batch one PRIMARY KEY account_id row per account, then UPDATE accounts a SET balance=a.balance+b.delta FROM posting_batch b WHERE b.account_id=a.id inside its transaction. Unique matches avoid ambiguous UPDATE FROM behavior. For account shares use balance/NULLIF(sum(balance) OVER(),0), rounded to four decimals; the window total keeps one output row per account.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE transfers(id integer PRIMARY KEY,source_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),destination_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK(amount>0),CHECK(source_id<>destination_id)); INSERT INTO transfers VALUES(1,1,2,50);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Apply a transfer and record it in the same transaction.

Accounts 1 and 2 start with 1000.00 and 500.00. Apply a transfer of 25.00 and record it atomically.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lesson_transfers(id integer PRIMARY KEY,source_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),destination_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK(amount>0),CHECK(source_id<>destination_id)); BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-25 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+25 WHERE id=2; INSERT INTO lesson_transfers VALUES(1,1,2,25); COMMIT;
SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN(1,2) ORDER BY id;
```

**Result**

id | balance
— | —
1 | 975.00
2 | 525.00

The source loses exactly what the destination gains. Their combined balance remains 1500.00, and the committed log records the movement.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE transfers(id integer PRIMARY KEY,source_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),destination_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK(amount>0),CHECK(source_id<>destination_id)); INSERT INTO transfers VALUES(1,1,2,50);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The account-share report divides each balance by the total balance. A window sum keeps each account row; NULLIF makes a zero total produce NULL rather than a division error.
sections.code: SELECT id,owner,balance,round(balance/NULLIF(sum(balance) OVER(),0),4) AS share FROM accounts ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example's verification shows a transfer record for 50.00. Saving that record alone does not change account balances.

id | source_id | destination_id | amount
— | — | — | —
1 | 1 | 2 | 50.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A CHECK constraint normally validates its row, not that all ledger postings balance. Constraints on the transfer table alone do not prevent overdrafts or implement a complete banking system.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Connect transactions and constraints with double-entry postings, where debits and credits must reconcile. Concurrent updates and request retries need their own protections.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Inspect each key and rule, then verify both account balances and ledger records after atomic tasks. Compare the total before and after a transfer.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Make the invariant explicit, enforce what constraints can express, and keep all related financial changes atomic and auditable.

exercises.prompt: Create transfers(id integer primary key,source_id integer not null references accounts(id),destination_id integer not null references accounts(id),amount numeric(12,2) not null check(amount>0),check(source_id<>destination_id)). Insert (1,1,2,50).
exercises.solutionSQL: CREATE TABLE transfers(id integer PRIMARY KEY,source_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),destination_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK(amount>0),CHECK(source_id<>destination_id)); INSERT INTO transfers VALUES(1,1,2,50);
hints: First identify the result grain: what does one output row represent in ‘Build a transfer ledger’?
Use exact numeric amounts, explicit keys, and atomic updates. A production ledger also needs idempotency, immutable audit history, authorization, and reconciliation.
A toy transfer is not a complete banking system. Cross-row invariants usually require transactions and a carefully designed write interface.
exercises.explanation: A ledger records movements, while a balance is the accumulated result. Constraints and transactions must support a clear invariant. Use exact numeric amounts, explicit keys, and atomic updates. A production ledger also needs idempotency, immutable audit history, authorization, and reconciliation. The reference preserves the prompt’s output grain, NULL policy, and required order on both datasets. Different SQL is accepted when it satisfies those checks.

 (SELECT COALESCE(jsonb_agg(definition ORDER BY definition),'[]'::jsonb) FROM (SELECT pg_get_constraintdef(k.oid,true) AS definition FROM pg_constraint k WHERE k.conrelid=c.oid) defs) AS constraints,

 (SELECT COALESCE(jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(p) ORDER BY p.command,p.using_expression,p.check_expression),'[]'::jsonb) FROM (SELECT p.polcmd::text AS command,p.polpermissive AS permissive,pg_get_expr(p.polqual,p.polrelid,true) AS using_expression,pg_get_expr(p.polwithcheck,p.polrelid,true) AS check_expression FROM pg_policy p WHERE p.polrelid=c.oid) p) AS policies
 FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=c.relnamespace
 WHERE n.nspname=current_schema() AND c.relkind IN('r','p','v','m')

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An analytics metric needs a clear unit: events, people, sessions, or another defined group. Its numerator and denominator must describe the intended population.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: One person may create many events or use several devices. Mixing event counts with people counts can produce a misleading conversion rate.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Define a metric before writing it: what is counted, which people or events qualify, and which time range applies? count(*) counts events; count(DISTINCT customer_id) counts known people. One customer may use several devices, so adding distinct device counts does not give a distinct total across devices. payload->>'device' extracts the device text from JSONB. A daily event ratio is purchases divided by visits; a customer conversion share is purchasing people divided by active people. These are different measures, and neither alone proves that one event caused another.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Use count(*) FILTER(WHERE kind='visit') and the corresponding purchase count for daily event rates. Cast the numerator to numeric and divide by NULLIF(visit_count,0); zero visits gives NULL. For customer rates use count(DISTINCT customer_id) FILTER(WHERE kind='purchase') over the same device population as the denominator. For join-month cohorts, first aggregate paid revenue per customer with a LEFT JOIN, then group by date_trunc('month',joined_on)::date; count customers after that first stage, not joined order rows. A visit-to-purchase funnel first finds min(occurred_at) for each customer's visits, then a correlated min purchase timestamp with e.occurred_at>=first_visit. Customers with no later purchase remain with NULL. This cohort differs from first-paid-purchase acquisition in the previous project.
sections.code: SELECT payload->>'device' AS device,count(*) AS event_count,count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customer_count FROM events GROUP BY device ORDER BY device;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Count events and distinct people side by side for each device.

The six events include two mobile events for customer 1, one mobile event for customer 3, two desktop events for customer 2, and one desktop event for customer 1.

```sql
SELECT payload->>'device' AS device,count(*) AS event_count,count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customer_count FROM events GROUP BY device ORDER BY device;
```

**Result**

device | event_count | customer_count
— | — | —
desktop | 3 | 2
mobile | 3 | 2

Each device has three events but only two distinct customers. Customer 1 appears on both devices, so the two customer counts cannot be added to get the overall distinct audience.
sections.code: SELECT payload->>'device' AS device,count(*) AS event_count,count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customer_count FROM events GROUP BY device ORDER BY device;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The cohort report groups customers by their join month. It calculates paid revenue per customer first, preserving customers without paid orders, then summarizes each cohort.
sections.code: WITH customer_revenue AS (SELECT c.id,c.joined_on,COALESCE(sum(o.total),0) AS revenue FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id) SELECT date_trunc('month',joined_on)::date AS cohort_month,count(*) AS customer_count,sum(revenue) AS paid_revenue FROM customer_revenue GROUP BY cohort_month ORDER BY cohort_month;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example shows three desktop events from two known customers and three mobile events from two. Events and people are different units.

device | event_count | customer_count
— | — | —
desktop | 3 | 2
mobile | 3 | 2

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: count(DISTINCT customer_id) ignores unknown IDs. An event-based purchase rate is not a person-based conversion rate; first-visit and first-purchase ordering must be defined explicitly.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Combine JSON extraction, DISTINCT, conditional aggregation, and date buckets. A cohort is a group sharing a starting characteristic, such as the month they joined.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Write the metric in words before SQL. Verify repeated events, customers on several devices, missing IDs, and customers with no paid revenue.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Name the unit, population, period, and denominator so the reader can understand exactly what each metric measures.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A reliable report has explicit business rules, correct calculations, stable output, and checks that reveal missing or inconsistent data.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Other people will maintain and use the report. They need to know what its totals include and why they can trust them.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A reliable report fixes its business definition before combining tables. Here revenue comes from paid orders. count(*) includes guest orders, while count(DISTINCT customer_id) ignores NULL and counts known customers only. date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date sets one month key. Keep header revenue at one row per order: aggregate quantity*unit_price per order before LEFT JOINing it to orders. This retains orders without lines and guest customers, and prevents a multi-line order from repeating its header total.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: For growth, first aggregate monthly revenue in a CTE, then use lag(revenue) OVER(ORDER BY month_start) in another stage. Compute (revenue-previous_revenue)/NULLIF(previous_revenue,0), rounded to four decimals: the first month and a zero previous value give NULL. LAG compares observed months; a missing calendar month needs a calendar stage if the report requires one. Year-to-date uses sum(revenue) OVER(PARTITION BY extract(year FROM month_start) ORDER BY month_start ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) after monthly aggregation. For reconciliation, compare each header with COALESCE(line_total,0), then group the discrepancies by month. Before changing a mismatching report, check status/date filters, missing lines, join duplication, guest handling, NULLs, currencies, tax, shipping, discounts, refunds, and rounding. A difference is evidence to investigate, not proof that one source is wrong.
sections.code: SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,count(*) AS paid_orders,sum(total) AS paid_revenue,count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body:
Compare each monthly total with the previous month before calculating growth.

Paid order revenue is 354.00 in May, 131.00 in June, and 124.00 in July 2024. Pending and cancelled amounts are excluded.

```sql
WITH monthly AS (SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY month_start), compared AS (SELECT *,lag(revenue) OVER(ORDER BY month_start) AS previous_revenue FROM monthly) SELECT month_start,revenue,previous_revenue,round((revenue-previous_revenue)/NULLIF(previous_revenue,0),4) AS growth_rate FROM compared ORDER BY month_start;
```

**Result**

month_start | revenue | previous_revenue | growth_rate
— | — | — | —
2024-05-01 | 354.00 | NULL | NULL
2024-06-01 | 131.00 | 354.00 | -0.6299
2024-07-01 | 124.00 | 131.00 | -0.0534

LAG supplies the previous observed month. June falls by about 62.99%, and July by about 5.34%. May has no previous month, so its growth is NULL.
sections.code: SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,count(*) AS paid_orders,sum(total) AS paid_revenue,count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The reconciliation example adds up the line items for each order, then uses LEFT JOIN to keep every order. When there are no lines, their total is zero. The difference column subtracts the line total from the stored order total.
sections.code: WITH lines AS (SELECT order_id,sum(quantity*unit_price) AS line_total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) SELECT o.id AS order_id,o.total AS header_total,COALESCE(l.line_total,0) AS line_total,o.total-COALESCE(l.line_total,0) AS difference FROM orders o LEFT JOIN lines l ON l.order_id=o.id ORDER BY o.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result of the syntax example contains May, June, and July on Retail. July has three paid orders but only two known customers, because the guest order still contributes revenue.

month_start | paid_orders | paid_revenue | unique_customers
— | — | — | —
2024-05-01 | 3 | 354.00 | 2
2024-06-01 | 3 | 131.00 | 3
2024-07-01 | 3 | 124.00 | 2

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: An order total can differ from the sum of its lines because of tax, delivery, discounts, or rounding. Check the reason for each difference. Decide how the report should show months with no matching orders.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Bring together CTEs, outer joins, windows, NULL handling, and reconciliation. Reporting rules should agree across detailed checks, monthly totals, and growth calculations.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check missing customers, no lines, duplicate joins, zero denominators, and period boundaries. Explain discrepancies at order level before comparing overall totals.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A report is complete when its rules are understandable, its edge cases are checked, and its totals can be reconciled.

exercises.prompt: Return month_start, revenue, previous_revenue, and growth_rate as (revenue-previous)/previous rounded to four decimals, NULL when previous is absent or zero; use paid orders only and order by month_start.
exercises.solutionSQL: WITH monthly AS (SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY month_start), compared AS (SELECT *,lag(revenue) OVER(ORDER BY month_start) AS previous_revenue FROM monthly) SELECT month_start,revenue,previous_revenue,round((revenue-previous_revenue)/NULLIF(previous_revenue,0),4) AS growth_rate FROM compared ORDER BY month_start;
hints: First identify the result grain: what does one output row represent in ‘Month-over-month growth’?
Break the report into named stages, test empty and duplicate cases, compare totals, inspect a plan, and communicate which facts the data can support.
Do not hide unknown customer IDs or silently mix cancelled sales into revenue. Explain every business filter and denominator.

exercises.title: Cross-check order and line totals
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, header_total, line_total, and difference (header minus line total) for all orders, with a zero line total if no lines; order by order_id.
exercises.solutionSQL: WITH lines AS (SELECT order_id,sum(quantity*unit_price) AS line_total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) SELECT o.id AS order_id,o.total AS header_total,COALESCE(l.line_total,0) AS line_total,o.total-COALESCE(l.line_total,0) AS difference FROM orders o LEFT JOIN lines l ON l.order_id=o.id ORDER BY o.id;

exercises.title: Explain a revenue reconciliation mismatch
exercises.prompt: A paid-order report sums orders.total. A line report sums quantity*unit_price after joining order_items. Their totals differ. Explain at least four checks you would perform before changing either query. This answer is self-assessed; no English string matching is used.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT true AS discussed;
hints: Compare the exact eligible order sets and result grains.
Look for missing lines, duplicate joins, guest customers, and different status or date predicates.
Consider business amounts outside line prices, such as tax, delivery, discounts, and refunds.

exercises.modelAnswer: First compare status and time filters so both reports use the same eligible orders. Check whether inner joins remove guest or line-less orders. Verify join cardinality so header totals are not repeated for each line and lines are not duplicated by another relationship. Reconcile per order before comparing grand totals. Check whether header totals include tax, shipping, discounts, refunds, or rounding that line totals exclude. Inspect NULL handling and currency units. exercises.title: Year-to-date paid revenue
exercises.prompt: Return month_start, revenue, and year_to_date from paid orders. Aggregate by month, then accumulate revenue within each calendar year in month order. Order by month_start.
exercises.solutionSQL: WITH monthly AS (SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY month_start) SELECT month_start,revenue,sum(revenue) OVER(PARTITION BY extract(year FROM month_start) ORDER BY month_start ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS year_to_date FROM monthly ORDER BY month_start;
hints: Fix the eligible paid-order set before combining facts.
Never sum a header measure at line-item grain.
Reconcile at order grain before rolling the result up to months.
exercises.explanation: Aggregate detail orders before running the window. Partitioning by year resets the accumulated total at a year boundary.

exercises.title: Monthly header-to-line reconciliation
exercises.prompt: For paid orders, return month_start, paid_orders, header_revenue, line_revenue, and difference (header minus lines). Include guest orders and orders with no lines. Aggregate line totals per order before joining; order by month_start.
exercises.solutionSQL: WITH lines AS (SELECT order_id,sum(quantity*unit_price) AS amount FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) SELECT date_trunc('month',o.ordered_on)::date AS month_start,count(*) AS paid_orders,sum(o.total) AS header_revenue,sum(COALESCE(l.amount,0)) AS line_revenue,sum(o.total)-sum(COALESCE(l.amount,0)) AS difference FROM orders o LEFT JOIN lines l ON l.order_id=o.id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;
hints: Fix the eligible paid-order set before combining facts.
Never sum a header measure at line-item grain.
Reconcile at order grain before rolling the result up to months.
exercises.explanation: Preaggregating lines prevents repeating a header total once per line. LEFT JOIN keeps line-less orders, and no customer join discards guest revenue.
